Uniform Title: Nareśvaraparīkṣā Main Title: Nareśvaraparīkṣā of Sadyojyoti with the Prakāśa Commentary by Rāmakaṇṭha Author: Sadyojyoti
Commentator: Rāmakaṇṭha Editor: Śāstrī M. K. Description: E-text transcribed from the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, Volume 45.

Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: 13/04/2007. Publisher: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State. Year of Publication: 1926.
Place of publication: Srinagar; Country of publication: India. *Nareśvaraparīkṣā*
by Sadyojyotis, together with the commentary *Prakāśa* composed by the venerable teacher Rāmakaṇṭha.
Combined with the preface by the venerable Professor Rāmamūrti Śarmā, edited by [Name].
Ācārya Śrī Rāma Jī Mālavīya, Ācārya and Director of the Department of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Tantra, and Āgama.
Thus,
the Vice-Chancellor of Sampurnanand Sanskrit University.
Vārāṇasī, in the year 2056 of the Vikrama era; 1921 of the Śaka era; 2000 of the Christian era.
The *Nareśvaraparīkṣā* composed by the venerable teacher Sadyojyotis,
[with a commentary] composed by the venerable teacher Rāgakaṇṭha, son of the venerable Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha.
The first section, accompanied by the commentary named *Prakāśa*,
[is dedicated] to Śaṅkara, the jewel in the ocean of objects of knowledge, who possesses immeasurable luster.
I shall describe the examination briefly, preceded by the examination of the person.
Having bowed to that supreme Nāreśvara, who consists of the nature of power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimad),
the literal meaning [of the text] is now elucidated in this examination of Nareśvara.

He states the purpose of this treatise with the word "Now" (*atha*): the investigation of God (*īśvaraparīkṣā*) is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) being undertaken; its purpose, however, is the production of knowledge concerning the Supreme Lord, which is the means for the highest good (*śreyaḥ*)—as will be explained.

At the conclusion of this treatise, however, because the Blessed One is the essence of the entire ocean of objects of knowledge— such as the principles (*tattva*) and the worlds (*bhuvana*)— he is of the nature of a jewel; this very point is expressed by the word "Śaṅkara," for he is sought after by all like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) as the one who brings about the highest good.

The relationship is characterized by that of means and end, which constitutes the accomplishment of the purpose; thus, for every discerning person, engagement with this [treatise] is established. By this, although Hari, Hara, Hiranyagarbha, and others are established as lords (*īśvara*) in other systems, they are not *Śaṅkara* (the Auspicious One), and therefore discerning persons do not [engage with them].

He shows that they proceed toward investigation. Now, how is it that he alone possesses such a nature, by virtue of which he is of immeasurable splendor? For he is the *prakṛti* (primordial matter) for those who propound the doctrine of *prakṛti* and *Īśvara*; he is *brahman* for those who know *brahman*; or he is *Nārāyaṇa*.

By the followers of the Pāñcarātra, Īśvara is postulated as the material cause of the world; however, since that very fact entails his lack of consciousness—just like clay and other such materials—he is necessarily one of limited power. Furthermore, even for the Sāṅkhyas, although [the self] consists of the *guṇas*, because they admit that *prakṛti* is the agent, Īśvara is indeed admitted to be a non-agent.

Even by those who maintain that the Lord is a transformation (*vikāra*), it is admitted that the Lord— who is accepted as Brahman, known as Hiraṇyagarbha, possessed of great majesty, and characterized by the fourfold nature—
is of limited power due to his association with creation and dissolution; this is also true for those who [maintain] him to be a particular kind of *puruṣa*.
Īśvara is described as such because of his association with an excellence of intellect and other qualities, and because he is untouched by the afflictions (kleśas) and so forth;
yet even by those [who hold this view], since intellect and the rest must necessarily perish due to their being manifest entities, his power must be admitted to be limited.
As for those, however, who proclaim Īśvara to exist through conjunction with the mind (*manas*), [the same critique applies].
Since those internal organs (manas) lack consciousness and are manifold like jars and other objects,

they must be admitted to be impermanent by virtue of being effects, and thus their power is limited; furthermore, even if the mind were eternal, its conjunction [with the self] would still be impermanent, as in the case of a liberated soul.

In that case, this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) is indeed unavoidable. If it is argued that because [the self] is all-pervasive, there is a conjunction with the mind even for liberated souls, then they too would be Lords (īśvara), which contradicts your own scripture.
If it is argued that even when there is conjunction, the mind functions as an instrument due to the power of unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), [then the same applies] to the Lord.

In the absence of that [power], there would follow the consequence of his being non-omnipotent. If it is argued that the Lord is always in conjunction with the mind by means of his own power (*śakti*) alone, this is nothing at all, because there is a circular dependency: he possesses power because of the conjunction with the mind, and there is conjunction with the mind because of his power. But this Supreme Lord...

By virtue of the method to be explained, his power is unimpeded everywhere and at all times; thus, he is called Śaṅkara because of his immeasurable splendor. For this very reason, unlike other treatises which begin with a formal salutation, there is no commencement here preceded by a *namaskāra*, since the removal of all obstacles is achieved simply by stating the subject matter (*tatparīkṣā*) of the work. The composition of the treatise [proceeds] as follows:
Or rather, it is because of the manifestation of its inherent capacity. And thus says the Śruti:
"The gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not harm that practitioner in whose heart that supreme Śiva-tejas shines. || 1 ||

And this investigation is only possible by being preceded by an investigation into the person (puruṣa), since some say, "All this is the Person alone; therefore, what is the use of a Lord (īśvara)? Others, however, [hold that] because things arise and perish by their own inherent nature at every moment, there is an absence of a presiding controller. Still others...

"May one live happily as long as life lasts"—since there is an absence of any object to be governed by karma and the like, they ask, "What then is the use of a Lord? Thus, an examination of that [the Lord] is not possible without an examination of the person (puruṣa); therefore, first of all, that very [examination of the person] is commenced.

He who, through awakening, is the knower and the agent, and having awakened, proceeds toward that which is to be known, and is the enjoyer of the fruit of such activity—he is what is called "the person" (puruṣa) in this context. || 2 ||
The Knower is said to be endowed with the power of knowledge; however, unlike the various schools of Sāṃkhya, or like the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, he is not eternally inferable,
because he manifests himself spontaneously by virtue of his own nature as the illuminator of all objects.
And because it is impossible for [the self] to be inferable— we shall explain this later— the agent is endowed with the power of action,

since it is by that very power that movement and so forth are experienced in the body and other such things; however, unlike the Sāṅkhyas, he is not a non-agent, as that would contradict one's own experience, nor is there merely a connection with power.

[If it were transformed], there would follow the consequence of selflessness (*nairātmya*) because even the conscious power (*cicchakti*) of the Self would be absent; rather, transformation means vibration (*spanda*) or the attainment of another form, and that is not possible for this [Self] precisely because of its being the agent of such [transformation].
Thus, we shall explain that there is no contradiction in its conjunction with the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) just as with the power of consciousness. And so forth.
This form of the self is a composite whole, not existing in its individual parts. Furthermore,

one acts only after having ascertained through the intellect itself— by means of perception in the form of cognition characterized by conceptual determination— and not, as the followers of Jaimini and others maintain, solely through that which is eternally inferable.

We shall explain that this is because it is experienced in exactly that way. Furthermore, the object to be known is indeed a distinct entity, and not—as the proponents of Śūnyavāda hold—mere consciousness, nor—as certain Vedāntins hold—an unreal non-entity;
for the latter, being indefinable, is characterized by a total absence of all causal capacity.
There is an impossibility of [the Self] having the nature of an object of knowledge; or, if such a connection were possible, it would not possess that status [of being the knower].

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "having known the object of knowledge," the cognition of that object is not a property of the Self, because—unlike the followers of Jaimini who maintain distinctions—it is common to all without exception.
Because it would otherwise follow that everything is both the knower and the object of knowledge,

[the author] shows by the word "proceeds" (*pravartate*) that the very nature of the knower is self-luminous. Thus, preceded by such an understanding, one performs actions— whether their results are visible or invisible— such as those involving cause and effect.

And he begins to act. However, in the position that [the Self] is not the agent, since agency is admitted to belong to primordial matter (prakṛti) alone, then—without being impelled by that [matter]—his causal activities would proceed spontaneously and haphazardly, as if out of helplessness or madness; thus, there is a contradiction with the fact established by experience that the Self is its own agent.
Everything will be established hereafter. Furthermore, [the self] is the enjoyer of the fruit of activity; thus, it is non-momentary.

For if it were momentary, the performer of acts such as giving would be one person and the enjoyer of their fruit another. Therefore, [the self exists] by way of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which is a stable grasper of a single, uniform form at all times.
We shall explain that there is a contradiction with experience, which serves as the basis for all worldly transactions. Thus,

the person who is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) in each individual by virtue of being qualified by such attributes is demonstrated here in this system by means of refuting all other conflicting views.
The meaning of the proposition. || 2 ||
Regarding this, he first states that there is no contradiction with direct perception:
"Conventional usage is completed by the fourfold set beginning with the agent.
For all proponents [of philosophical systems], this has been firmly established since time immemorial as being grounded in experience.

Worldly convention must be followed, and that [convention] consists entirely of activities such as cutting and cooking, which are characterized by the fourfold set beginning with the agent (kartṛ) and so forth; this is an illustration based on the distinction of grammatical factors (kārakas) tied to action,
which, according to the circumstances, may in some cases involve one, two, or three [factors].

It is observed that [an action] is being accomplished by means of up to six [factors]; for without action, the entities such as the agent and the instrument would be mere things, and would not attain the state of diverse *kārakas*, nor does action exist without them.

Now, what is the use of this discourse on the distinctions between action and its factors? For objects such as seeds, characterized as a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and endowed with their respective states, will produce the specific effect such as a sprout by virtue of being causes through their mere prior existence; thus say the proponents of the absolute causality of the cause (*kāraṇaikāntavādin*).
The Jains say that this is incorrect, because:
"This [distinction] cannot be established by those who maintain extremist views. (3)

For in this way, since the status of being a cause would be indistinguishable for both the killer and the victim, or the giver and the beggar, merely by virtue of their prior existence with respect to a single effect— such as the act of killing or the act of giving— it would follow, against your own tenets, that they must share identical results.

If it is argued that this is not so because of a difference in essential nature, since that very causal complex (*sāmagrī*) produces an internal distinction [in one case but not the other], we say no; for this argument is trivial, as both [the killer and the victim] are equally at fault and are causes [of the act], just as the killing belongs to the killer, so too does it belong to the victim. If it is argued that this was stated with reference to the distinction between one's own and another's continuum (*saṃtāna*), let it be so.

There is indeed no difference in the actual application [of consciousness]. If it is argued that even this difference exists in some sense due to the distinction between one's own and another's continuum, then this very doctrine of specific actions and factors— consisting of the distinctions of agent, object, and so forth,
which serves as the cause for seen and unseen fruits— is established by conventional usage.
It cannot be established by those who maintain the doctrine of a single cause;

therefore, the theory of causal efficiency (kārakavāda) must be accepted in order to establish it—thus, the meaning of the proposition remains uncontradicted. This same principle should also be applied to acts such as giving (dāna). || 3 ||

But is it not the case that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this entire conventional practice based on differentiation is unreal, since Brahman—the single essence of bliss—is alone real? As it has been said:
"This one neither kills nor is killed" (Gītā 2.19).
This too is incorrect; for instance:

there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever to establish the oneness of all things, because perception and inference have difference as their object, since they depend respectively upon the senses and inferential marks.

On the contrary, since those two [perception and inference] are sublaters of that [non-duality], if it is argued that they do not sublate it here because their object is mere existence (*sattāmātra*), then, since the distinctions between perception and so forth would be unestablished, let there be an absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*), for non-duality alone is what is possible from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). To this we say: no, because of the absence of means of valid cognition.
We shall state that this very [reason] is unestablished.
Now, if you claim that the authoritative means here is scripture (*āmnāya*), [we reply:]...
And thus it is heard in scripture:
"Brahman alone is the supreme reality; there is no diversity whatsoever here.
This is like foam, or indeed nothing at all, or like a bubble, or indeed nothing at all."

If it is argued that even when the object is already established— as in the case of a ritual act— the authority of the Veda does not belong to the Upaniṣadic portion by way of being a mere explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) through syntactic unity with the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), but rather that its status here is indeed that of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);—
Nor by that which makes those latent impressions manifest. || 4 ||

This sacred tradition (āmnāya) is not an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of establishing the non-duality of Brahman as an existing reality, because it is admitted that Brahman, being a nature transcending all conceptual constructions, is not an object [of cognition];
for if it were an object of that tradition, then the tradition itself would also possess reality.
Because that which is non-existent cannot be its object, it lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);

thus, the reality of non-duality (*advaita*) is not established, since the relationship between a means of knowledge and its object (*pramāṇa-prameya-bhāva*) is dependent upon duality. This is so unless—[if] this [non-duality], which consists of all forms of difference...

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be accepted as being [indirectly] a proof for the non-dual Self through its illumination of the nature of the impressions of ignorance regarding practice; for they say, "The realization of the Self is 'not this, not this'.
Consequently, because its object is not a real entity, it is like the collection of statements such as "the son of a barren woman is walking."
Furthermore, due to the absence of validity, non-duality itself remains unestablished. || 4 ||

If this is so, then since difference is real, let it be that for each body, for each object, and at every moment, a distinct consciousness—which is the locus of the "I-sense" (ahaṅkāra) regarding external objects that are themselves not the locus of the "I-sense"—is established by experience as the grasper; let there be no other thing called a "Self" (ātman). Thus [they argue].
The Vaibhāṣikas [reply]:

"The existence of that which has reached the conditions for perception yet is not perceived, and whose nature is unperceivable, is indeed difficult to establish; this is true. For this very reason, from an effect one can only infer the cause-in-general, just as from the sense-faculties and so forth."

Only something similar is inferred; and that is simply the preceding cognition itself, accompanied by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by an even earlier cognition—a fact established for both disputants—which serves as its cause, just as it does for cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth. Thus, how [could there be any doubt]?

The establishment of another unseen cause that is entirely dissimilar [to the observed one]. As it has been said: "When something necessarily occurs whenever X is present, if one postulates something other than X as its cause, there would be an infinite regress of causes in all cases."

Thus, because its status as an effect is not established— as it is for cognitions such as those of blue and so forth— desire indeed arises concomitantly with a cognition of having the same agent, which is established by the capacity for recollecting that [object] was previously experienced as a means to pleasure and the like; therefore, it is distinct from other types of cognition.

The fact that [consciousness] is excluded from being an effect—despite its similarity to the body, another consciousness, and so forth—leads to the inference of a specific, stable knower; thus is the proof of the self (*ātman*). For it is not possible elsewhere [than in the self] that "I who am the seer am the very same as the one who desires," because [the self] is not unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*). Indeed, it is not...

It is established that this [cognition] co-exists with the knowledge of having a common agent (*samānakartṛtva*) with that [object-cognition]; for if that were established, the self would be said to be directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) because it is the object of that cognition—thus there would be a contradiction with the accepted doctrine that the self is eternally inferable (*nityānumeya*). But surely, for that very reason, that [self] belongs to all selves...

It has been stated that [the existence of the Lord] is established by the capacity for the investigation of the means to happiness and so forth. What is this "capacity" (sāmarthya) by which His proof is achieved? It is simply "inexplicability otherwise" (anyathānupapatti). Of what does this belong?
Not, first of all, of desire, because desire arises precisely from the knowledge of such investigation. Or else—

"It is not the case that its [the self's] existence is untenable," you might say; however, even you admit the arising of that [memory] precisely from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience. Well then, that very impression is not tenable without a permanent substratum (*dharmī*); therefore, its [the self's] existence is established, and not merely from impermanent seeds of madness.

The refinement [of a cloth] by lac and so forth is established through the redness of its flowers and the like; thus, we do not understand how that [refinement] could be established in anything other than a sequential continuum of consciousness, since it is absolutely unestablished elsewhere.
Apart from the mere ostentation of formal arguments, what else is there whose establishment would allow even that [refinement] to be established?
Knowledge, which serves as a qualification of the reason, is established.

By this, the inference of the self (ātman) as stated by the Vaiśeṣikas—based on inhalation, exhalation, closing and opening of the eyes, life-functions, movements of the mind, modifications of the other sense organs, memory, and so forth—is also refuted. For instance, [this applies] to that which has the nature of moving horizontally.
The upward and downward propulsion of the vital air (vāyu) is not possible without a supervisor; like one blowing into a bellows, some agent must be postulated.

Likewise, for the closing and opening of the eyes and other functions dependent on the limbs of the body, there must be a supervisor endowed with effort, as in the case of a mechanical man; this applies to the life-force (jīvana) as well.
Because it is the effect of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), it is the substratum of those qualities; and since even the mind (*manas*) is insentient,

like a chariot or similar objects, there must be an impeller possessed of effort, just as the sight of a fruit such as a pomegranate— which possesses an exceedingly sour taste— induces a transformation in the gustatory faculty consisting of saliva, much like the presence of many windows [reveals the interior].

Some synthesizer of all sensory objects must be postulated; and that is simply consciousness itself, existing as a continuous stream which—by virtue of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and other factors—is established by both disputants as the performer of all the aforementioned purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*). Thus, what else could it be?

It is established. Furthermore, as for the inference of the self—the possessor of qualities—by means of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), on the grounds that desire and so forth are not objects of visual perception, and thus, being qualities like taste and the like, do not persist as long as the substance [in which they reside] (such as the body), thereby precluding them from being specific qualities of the body and so forth; that too [is established].

Because the example is unestablished and there is a lack of pervasion (vyāpti), the reason is inconclusive; for neither for us nor for the Sāṃkhyas is the "quality-ness" (guṇatva) of taste and so forth established as something other than a collection of color, taste, and the rest.

Because no substratum (dharmin) such as a mango fruit is perceived [separately], the designation of difference—namely, "the taste of the mango"—is indeed appropriate for the purpose of indicating that it is a part of a whole, just like saying "the Dhava tree of the forest is beautiful. To whom, then, does this desire belong? It belongs to the object of desire (karma).

It is from the village and so forth itself. Now, as for the question "of what cause?", it is said: it is of that very specific cognition which is seen immediately following [the object], consisting in the ripening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a preceding cognition.
How then is the worldly conventional usage of agency, such as "Devadatta's desire," employed here?

Alternatively, it is indeed appropriate [to say this] for the purpose of demonstrating a connection with a continuous stream of specific knowledge—just as one might say that the flow of the Vitastā river has been utterly destroyed at its very root by the practice of false reasoning (*kutarka*).

Or, even among those who maintain the existence of a self (*ātmavādin*), how could Devadatta [be the authority], since his own self alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this case? How then...?

If it is argued that worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) is merely imagined because it is not logically tenable by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then enough with such practice! For it is precisely valid cognition that must be pursued to establish what is true and what is otherwise; and since that is the same in the other case as well, one desires a specific kind of cognition, not some quality belonging to anyone.

Although the Sāṃkhyas have presented the argument for the sake of another (*pārārthya*)—based on the analogy of beds and so forth—as an inference established by the opponent regarding the body and its organs, that too merely proves consciousness as something admitted by both parties; thus, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Now, [one might object]:

Because consciousness is impermanent, it is composite by way of succession; therefore, something else that is non-composite and supreme must be inferred from that. True, provided that such a pervasion (*vyāpti*) were established;
for in the case of the examples of composite things, their being "for the sake of another" (*parārthatva*) refers only to objects such as the composite body and so forth.
The word "siddham" (established) means that only such a cognition is established; even at the end,
for the sake of avoiding infinite regress, one must admit some such [cognition] alone, and not another that is not of that nature, for it is not so.

A thing that has not been observed in the example and whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished cannot be proven by a reason through its own power; for this [reason] is a signifier (*jñāpaka*), not a producer (*kāraka*).
Nor should it be said that cognition (*jñāna*) is unestablished for us, because this is indeed the manifestation of the object (*arthaprakāśa*).

This [cognition] is indeed experienced as well-known to the entire world; yet it is not a property of the object, because it is experienced internally as distinct from the object, and because if it were a property of the object, the object—being indistinguishable for all people—would entail the undesirable consequence that it would be perceived by everyone simultaneously. Nor is it an inherent nature of the person.

Since that [consciousness] is unestablished, and even if it were established, because there would be no distinction from that which is non-luminous, it too would be of a non-luminous nature; thus, total blindness of the entire world would result. As it has been said:
"For one who perceives an object that is not itself perceived, the vision of the object is not established."

Since consciousness is established by experience as having the specific nature of illuminating its object—just like a lamp which, by virtue of having the single nature of self-illumination, illuminates the object—it cannot be denied. This has been stated: "In the Vibhāṣā system, the cognition and the object are born together, like a form and a lamp."
The aggregates are empty of another, namely a self in the form of an enjoyer and so forth—
thus say those who propound the emptiness of self.
Regarding this, the Teacher says:
"Non-existence cannot be asserted with respect to the cognition that is the witness of all;
therefore, the emptiness of all entities is sublated by awareness. (5)

If this is so, since the nature of the subject— which is the essence of cognition engaged in the direct realization of all objects— is established by perception, it is impossible to demonstrate the non-existence of the self,
because it is established by experience; for "being an enjoyer" is said to be "being a knower," and that is precisely what [the self] is.

And you have stated that the ultimate nature of the self is established by experience even for yourselves; therefore, what else remains to be proven? [The opponent objects: But we maintain that this consciousness, which is the apprehending subject, is indeed distinct with respect to each object and at every moment.
It has been demonstrated that there is no such entity designated as "self" (ātman) that serves as a witness to all objects;

and if it is argued that this [consciousness] itself is that [self], then let there be a difference in name at most—but every proponent of the self must show that it possesses a stable form—if this is said, we reply: not so.

We have stated your own admission as a supporting factor; for indeed, a difference in experience among all cognizers who establish the system for each respective philosophical school is impossible, since that [non-difference] is established by its very nature. As they say:

"The fool and the wise man are alike in their cognition and their expression. Therefore, let this very self-evident experience, well-known to all the world, be examined: is it something entirely new at every object and at every moment?

Does the apprehender manifest as appearing in the form of distinct moments through the two preceding and succeeding experiences, or does this manifestation appear here as a stable form that is always non-different? Even when there is a difference in the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the object of apprehension, it has not attained any differentiation within its own self.

In all three periods of time, it is that which has transcended its own prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and its subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*); even amidst the perception of the arising and passing away of various mental modifications such as the diverse means of valid cognition, it is the experiencer of the unshakable stability of that which perceives them; and even during the intervals between those modifications, its light remains undiminished.

Since even in states such as deep sleep, one's own consciousness remains unbroken and is always cognizable through its own self-luminosity, it is established by each individual’s own self-awareness as that which is denoted by the term "Self"; what need is there, therefore, for any other means of proof? And it is precisely by relying upon this very undivided and imperishable self-consciousness that [one proceeds].
All actions are undertaken by everyone with the expectation of results at a later time; however, if that [consciousness] were momentary, all worldly transactions would collapse,
since all experiences would perish immediately after being felt for a mere instant.

Since [the self] arises in another moment, who acts, where, or for what purpose? For indeed, action is not possible for one who knows the nature of the moment and perceives that "I am not" and "this is not mine" in the subsequent moment; thus, [the self] is devoid of effort and established solely in the manifestation of its own essential nature.

Otherwise, this world would be devoid of the cognition of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, free from false knowledge, and empty of various cognitions such as investigation and understanding;
thus, there would be a contradiction with universal experience, because such [cognitions] are necessarily preceded by the manifestation of a stable grasper.
It might be argued: "Granted, this manifestation as a single, stable grasper is indeed undeniable;

however, it is not self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*), but rather is merely superimposed by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)—which are mistaken due to perceiving similarity—upon the stream of moments of the grasper that is being experienced, like [the illusion of] water."

The notion that there is a unity [of the stream] like that of a flowing current is merely an illusion; for this very reason, because it constitutes the grasping at a self and is thus the root of all misfortune, the Blessed One, the Sugata, undertook the effort known as the cultivation of the antidote—the object of which is selflessness—in order to bring about its pacification. As they say:
"The effort for the sake of removing false superimposition [is undertaken] even though there is no enjoyer"—

this is incorrect, because it is experienced internally as an object (*karman*) due to its distinctness from the [subjective] domain; for if this were merely superimposed, then [it would have to arise] from the superimposer in the form of a grasper (*grāhaka*).
Otherwise, the cognition of Devadatta would appear as if it were an object, like [the statement] "the cognition is stable"; however, this is not the case for this experience.

Rather, because its intrinsic nature consists of an internal grasper by virtue of illuminating the object, even at that time it is experienced as being indeed stable in the form of the subject who falsely superimposes that [stability].

For even that [momentary cognition] does not appear as having the nature of a single moment by itself; indeed, if it were not so appearing, superimposition would be impossible, because superimposition consists in the synthesis of a prior and a posterior [cognition] and is therefore removable only by a stable awareness. Nor, moreover, can this be said of that which is momentary in nature.
Because it has as its object a long duration comprising both prior and subsequent moments simultaneously, it is non-conceptual— since conceptualization consists in the nature of superimposition—
just like the appearance of a whirling firebrand; for this very reason, even though it has as its objects both words and their referents simultaneously.

It has been stated by you that the cognition of a yogi is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). If it is argued that this is because its objects have been synthesized (*yojita*), this is of no consequence, since synthesis is impossible given that all things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*). For this very reason, even a series of multiple conceptual moments (*vikalpakṣaṇa*) occurring in succession cannot be superimposing (*anāropaka*).

Thus, because superimposition is impossible, conceptual construction has subsided. Furthermore, the nature of the grasper cannot be made into an object of grasping, such that one could say stability has been superimposed upon it through superimposition within itself.
Since conceptual construction is non-conceptual with respect to its own self, for this very reason, even the status of being an object of the notion of "I" does not belong to it.

It is not that [the subject] arises anew; rather, even then, it is precisely the nature of the manifestation of the cognition that appears with stability in that very form. For the destruction of the nature of the grasper is never experienced, even throughout the three periods of time—this has been stated. Indeed, that which possesses prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is said to have arisen; but for this [subject], there is none.

That destruction which has perished is such that there is no cognition of its non-existence at either the prior or subsequent limit; therefore, it cannot be said that it is produced or ceased at every moment. Furthermore, we shall explain later that the nature of consciousness cannot be something not self-cognized. Thus it stands.
Because the permanent and the momentary are mutually contradictory in nature— just as,
for instance, momentariness established by valid cognition in the case of lightning and the like excludes non-momentariness—
so too, since superimposition is impossible upon the nature of the subject (the grāhaka).
It is logical that stability, as it appears, undoubtedly excludes momentariness;

nor can there be a sublation of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) in its being such [i.e., stable], because even that which is considered a sublater is itself self-aware by that very same stable nature, for otherwise it could not function as a sublater.

Furthermore, because there is no error [in our position], for we shall demonstrate that even an erroneous cognition is erroneous only with respect to its object (*ālambana*) and not with respect to itself. Nor does the acceptance of something established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in a manner other than it actually is win over the minds of the wise, unless there is a sublater (*bādhaka*).

If it is argued that the non-arising of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is precisely the subverting proof against a stable [entity], we say no; for we shall explain that its arising occurs in that very [stable entity] itself.
Thus, the nature of manifestation which grasps as eternally uniform and stable is indeed not superimposed.

Since [the Self] is established by self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) in every person as the witness of all objects, for that reason the thesis that "the aggregates (skandhas) are devoid of a causal Self" is indeed refuted by direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Thus, with this much, the word "knower" (jñātā) from the Sūtra of the Proposition has been explained. || 5 ||

If this is so, then because the nature of the apprehender is indistinguishable with respect to all objects, the distinction between cognitions for each respective object—such as "this is the cognition of blue, not of yellow"—would be unestablished. For there are not two separate perceptions: one of the object and another of the self; and since [the cognition] consists in the perception of the self...
When there is the apprehension of an object, since the self (ātman) is without distinction [from it], that [consciousness] is also without distinction;
consequently, because even the distinction of the object is not established, there is a contradiction with experience. [Objection:
But surely consciousness is experienced as non-different from that which illuminates the object, and thus it possesses the object.

If this is so, then because there is no cognition of another self, it is indeed the case that what was stated—“There is never an eternal means of valid cognition, because the distinction between entities is established”—is true. [Objection: But surely the self is also cognized. [Response: That is incorrect, for this is one single form of consciousness.

We observe a manifold manifestation consisting of joy, sorrow, and other various forms; for if that [manifestation] is consciousness (*saṃvit*), what else could the Self (*ātman*) be? Or, if it is the Self itself, what else could consciousness be?

Indeed, it is not tenable to claim that the nature of consciousness differs from one philosophical system to another, such that this [distinction between the two] would apply to the followers of Jaimini.

If it were called "form" (rūpa), its establishment would have to occur through the power of the object itself—just like blue, yellow, and so on—since it is impossible for it to be otherwise for each individual person. True; this nature of consciousness is indeed one.
However, by the force of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "I know this blue," the self (*ātman*) is also experienced as an object, just like the external thing.

We reply: For this very reason, because there is a reflection upon the "I-component" (ahamaṃśa) as being included within the cognition, the Prābhākaras maintain that perception itself, accompanied by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the self. If this were so, then [one would have to say] "a forest of *palāśa* trees" or "a heap of *māṣa* beans."

If it is argued that, by the force of such cognitions as "forest" and so forth, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the existence of a distinct entity—such as a forest-mass—that is separate from the *palāśa* trees, beans, and so on, because it is directly perceived (*adhyakṣasaṃvedya*), [we reply: no, for nothing other than those [individuals] is perceived by that [cognition]; thus, this reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is false. If that is so, then...

Since there is an inconclusiveness here, enough with this further deliberation. Let it be investigated whether this [consciousness] belongs to a self that possesses an object, or whether it is merely imagined, like a forest and such.
Furthermore, there is no other thing called a "self" apart from the object and the consciousness that apprehends it.

If it is argued that "it is perceived"—and thus that [perceivedness] is merely imagined—and furthermore, that being an object of perception does not constitute the Self because it is an object of consciousness like a jar or similar things, and that there is no fault because it is perceived precisely as the subject (pramātṛ), we say:
no, because of mutual contradiction; for being a subject consists in being the illuminator, not in being the illuminated.
If it is argued that "if [consciousness] were an object of illumination, its status as an illuminator would be untenable; therefore, let it be the self of that very illuminator,

since in reality it is not a different form from the fruit characterized by consciousness," then it has already been stated that if there is a difference [of consciousness] with respect to each object, there is no-self (nairātmya), whereas if there is no difference, the distinction between objects cannot be established.

By this, the position of the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas— that although there is no distinction in the self with respect to each respective object, a distinct cognition inherent in that self arises as the illuminator, and therefore there is no contradiction— is refuted.

Therefore, if there is no difference between cognition and its object, then due to the diversity of objects, there is simply selflessness (*nairātmya*). But if there is a difference, then because of the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator, let it be cognition alone; what is the use of some other internal impediment? What can we do? Even so, [the self] is indeed purified through inference, for it has already been stated: "But is it not the self?"

The followers of Kumārila (Kaumārilas) maintain that this [consciousness], as the grasper, shines forth indeed without having acquired any distinction for each respective object by virtue of its own immediate self-manifestation; however, by the power of that [consciousness], a property called "the manifestation of the object" arises as something distinct for each object. Therefore, since the distinction between objects is established, there is no fault. But even that is incorrect.
Since an object is non-distinct with respect to all [knowers], it would follow that it is manifest to the entire self;

thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that everyone is omniscient. If it is argued that this is not so because [the manifestation] is produced by a specific self, like an action that is reached [by the agent], that is incorrect, because if that [object] is not manifested, that [production] is also unestablished; but if it is manifested...
The claim that it resides in both [the self and the object], like the attainment of a village, belongs only to the proponent of consciousness (saṃvit-pakṣa), and that has already been refuted.

Even if it were a property of the object, this property—whether it be ownership, sonship, and so forth, or the manifestation of an object produced by light while excluding owls and the like—would be related specifically to that particular self. In that case, [the objection does not apply].

"Therefore, there will be no over-extension [of the argument]," it was said. Furthermore, this [manifestation] must be either the very end of the object's manifestation, or it must have the form of the object as its content. In the former case, the object would manifest by itself at that time; thus, because the self (the subject) does not manifest as before, [the object] remains unestablished. But now—

How can an object that is manifest be unestablished? True; [if it were] "by itself," as in the case of another self (*ātmāntara*), then it would indeed be unestablished for that other self. But surely it manifests by virtue of that [other self]. What follows from this? For that [other self], it does not manifest—thus it remains forever indirect (*parokṣa*). Now, as for the second alternative, in that case, regarding the object...

It must be stated: what is this illumination? Is it not simply the self-luminosity of the Self? True; however, because that [self-luminosity] is devoid of distinction, the determination of specific objects is not possible—thus this very defect remains.
[Objection: But surely, the determination of specific objects for the Self arises from the cognition of the specific forms imparted by those objects.
Since [the self] is of the nature of that [consciousness], this fault does not apply; thus conclude those who maintain the five-fold basis. As they say:
"Experience (bhoga) in the self is the grasping of the reflection of that which is to be experienced. And it has also been stated by the Sautrāntikas:
"It connects this [cognition] with the object; for indeed, there is no connection except through the form of the object.
Therefore, the conformity to the form of the object (*meyarūpatā*) is the means (*sādhana*) for the apprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya*).
Regarding this as well, is the manifestation of the reflection of the object distinct from the manifestation of the self, or is it of the same nature as that?

Or rather, if there were difference, the very same fault already stated would apply; but if there were non-difference, since this [cognition] would—like the grasped and the grasper—not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality, it would be merely imagined like the cognitions in dreams and so forth.
Consequently, because the object would lack stability, the occasional nature of cognition would be untenable, just as in the case of dreams and the like.

Because there is deviation [in the inference] when an object is inferred from the occurrence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth, and because even in the absence of an external object, the manifestation of multiple forms in succession would otherwise be inexplicable, it has been stated that there is indeed selflessness (*nairātmya*):
"Though the nature of cognition is undivided, it is seen as such by those whose vision is perverted."
"The cognition of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject appears as if it were possessed of duality.
Regarding this, the Teacher also says:
"Nor is there an absence of the object, since it is experienced."
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that not only is the position of the emptiness of the self refuted by direct perception,
but the position of the emptiness of objects (*artha*) is as well. He states this because this object is experienced and manifested through experience as being connected with external space.
The meaning is that the manifestation of the duality of the grasped and the grasper is established by experience. For that which is manifested cannot itself be the nature of the manifestor,
because the manifestor appears as distinct from it due to its being the self-nature of that manifestation— as has been stated— since the status of being both self and other is logically untenable.

And because all conventional transactions would be absent. If it is argued: "True; from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this conceptual transaction of the grasped and the grasper is indeed unreal," then from what [is this known]? If it is argued: "From the previously mentioned subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," we say no.
If it is argued that since the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is based on duality, that [cognition] is likewise unestablished for him,

and therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it has only its own self as its object and thus excludes difference from external objects— this is true, provided it were experienced in that way.

However, it is experienced that [the object] has indeed a distinct domain; or else, if there were no distinction, there would be a lack of validity for conceptual and other types of cognition as well, because they would have only themselves as their object due to the impossibility of an external object. True;
however, those [cognitions] lack validity because of the manifestation of a duality in the form "I know the blue. If that is so, then...
Because they appear, duality is indeed real, just like non-duality; for if it were unreal,

its appearance would be impossible, since that which is non-existent cannot logically manifest, and thus the manifestation of something whose nature is ignorance is not tenable— this is your [position].
[The opponent says:
"It is true; because one acts toward an object through the determination of that object based on its own internal appearance, [the cognition] lacks validity regarding that [external] object.

[The author replies: Let it be so regarding the object itself; however, with respect to its own appearance—which is of the nature of illumination—just like the subjective aspect (grāhakātman), it possesses the nature of being manifest.

If it is argued that [the means of knowledge] must indeed consist of the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then non-duality (*advaita*) is untenable; if it is replied that this is not so because even that has a non-dual object from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), then there is no distinction from indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpa*). For, according to the accepted principle that "all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is saṃsāra," the absence of conceptual construction entails the absence of saṃsāra. This is not [the case].
If it is argued that [cognition] is conceptual because it functions by determining duality even within its own non-dual nature, we say no;

for this [cognition] is not conceptual with respect to its own nature. Even if it were conceptual, since duality is merely the object of determination, its very nature remains that of cognition; so how could it be unreal?

If it is argued that [cognition is unreal] because purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is not obtained from it, this is poorly instructed advice from the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*).
However, if consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is real, what other purposeful action could there be apart from the cognition itself?
Thus, even dreams, the double moon, and so forth, are not unreal; for that which has appeared is not non-appeared.

This follows from the logical principle that [a thing] exists. If it is argued that there is the production of another cognition, even that exists for them, so there is no unreality. If it is argued that there is a continuous state due to the persistence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then, because it is connected to beginningless latent impressions, it consists of the manifestation of conceptual cognition.

The reality belongs only to the two [subject and object] as they function in a continuous stream, not to the non-duality imagined by you; thus, there is no contradiction. If it is argued that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have unreal objects because they consist of a reflective awareness of what precedes and follows, and thus manifest a distinction between objects that are not present, [we reply]: if that which is not present is unreal, then...
How could it appear? If it does appear, then like non-duality, it must be real.

For you, reality consists precisely in having consciousness as one's essence; since, unlike for those who propound external objects, there is no capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣamatva*) other than that [consciousness], this kind of argument being stated here is not a valid proof.

Because this [argument] is a proof specifically for those who maintain the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*). If it is argued that [the mind] is unreal because the grasped and the grasper are established in another [object] and thus do not abide in their own nature, then how can cause and effect be real? If you say they are also not [real], then—

Because of the absence of causes such as the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), even for a continuum of non-dual representation (*advaya-vijñapti-santati*), a restriction by way of place, time, and nature is untenable; thus, everything is inconsistent. Now, if it is argued that there is no fault because the conventional [subject] depends on something else, since those two [place and time] exist only in a specific form—

If it is argued that this is the same in the other case as well, and thus there is no unreality [of the object], because proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādins) accept that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has an unreal object— [we reply that] the reason for their acceptance is sublated by you; even if it were not sublated here, non-duality (*advaita*) would still not be established from that very fact, since duality alone [would remain].

Regarding this, the New Śākyas maintain that there is merely the designation of non-dual appearance because conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is of such a nature, but there is no actual appearance by which [the object] would entail the consequence of being real. This is incorrect,
because [such appearances occur] in states such as daydreaming.

Because there is an experience of the conceptualized form of the blazing, radiant, and so forth within conceptualizations such as "fire," and because a systematic determination cannot attain the status of being a determination by denying that experience—this has already been stated.

If it is argued that this is merely the appearance of the form of the apprehended object, we say no; for that [appearance] is non-different from the conceptualized form, and if there were a difference, [the argument would fail].

This is because, like the forms of cognitions of grass and so forth belonging to one who is moving, they lack the status of being objects of determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) due to their being self-cognized as non-different from consciousness itself. As they say:
"How can that form which is determined by certain [cognitions] be their object?"

If it is argued that [the theory] is impossible because the conceptualized form cannot be established as either unreal by virtue of being the self (ātman) or as external, then let there simply be this lack of establishment;
there is no impossibility, because it is being experienced, or else some kind of establishment must exist.
It is precisely of that nature. As it was said by the ancient Buddhists:
"There is no manifestation of a clear object for that which is permeated by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Conceptual construction is a corruption because it manifests as a non-entity and because it is deceptive.
And it is said: "It is a pseudo-perception.

Furthermore, because even that which is conceptualized appears [in cognition], and because existence consists precisely in appearing, both [the conceptualized object and its appearance] are real; thus, non-duality is not established. [Objection: In that case, it will be established in non-conceptual [cognition]; [Response: No.
For that too is perceived in exactly the same way; thus it has been stated. As those of vast intellect have said in the *Śabdakaṇikā* and other works:
"That pair indeed consists of the internal reality and the external reality."
"Whatever might be the practitioner, in reality, there is nothing whatsoever. Consequently, the claim that "the nature of cognition is also undivided" is likewise untenable.
[Objection: Even so, it follows that consciousness alone is established as having a dual form, consisting of the apprehended and the apprehender.
The objectivity of the apprehended [is as follows]. As it has been said: "There is no other object to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there another experience of it;
due to the absence of both the apprehended and the apprehender, that very [intellect] shines forth by itself."
It does not appear as an object by virtue of its distinctness from cognition, nor as the means for accomplishing a specific purposeful action,

nor as that which is being sought; rather, it is only upon the attainment of that [cognition] that purposeful action is established, whereas in the case of its non-attainment, there is a lack of correspondence with reality (*ayathārthatva*).
If you argue that there is no lack of an object in cognitions such as those of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell because [the object] is admitted [to exist],

then, since acts such as giving and the like, as well as the karma consisting of merit and demerit such as violence, would be unestablished, the Lokāyata materialist position alone would be worthy of worship for you. If it is argued that there is no fault because such cases have as their object the form of cognition itself, then—
In dreams and the like, many auspicious actions such as acquiring or giving wealth,

as well as violent acts such as the killing of enemies, would be accomplished; for who indeed would engage in service, agriculture, and so forth, or in [the pursuit of] elephants, horses, weapons, and the like, which are to be achieved through excessive hardship?

One would then be engaged in [useless] means of accomplishment—this contradicts experience. If it is argued that those [means] are also essentially the manifestation of a qualified cognition, we say no; for in the absence of an object, that qualification cannot be established. This is of no consequence, as there is also the property of mutual assistance [between them].

The same [argument] does not apply even to the Jina, because there is no cognition of another. If it is argued that this fault does not apply to him because of his omniscience, [we reply: since for him too, as in dreams and so forth, there is only the cognition of his own form, mere limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatā*) is impossible under this position; how then could there be omniscience? It is not so.
If it is argued that [the object] is known because it is perceived as a condition for its apprehension (*adhigatipratyayatvena*), what indeed is this so-called "condition for apprehension"?
It is merely proximity (*sannihitamātratā*). But how can one who is blind from birth discern whether or not an object is present here?
Nor is it possible for us to establish this for him. As they have said:
O best of the Śākyas, the accomplishment of all purposes by the Blessed Ones is indeed inconceivable.
This which you say is far too little; for everything is inconceivable to the ignorant, since only the wise have authority in this matter.
If it is argued that he knows [it] by way of its forms (ākāra), then what is this relationship of "door" and "one who possesses the door" in his case?

Because cognition does not arise regarding objects that are spatially remote from us— such as those perceived merely by their own form— just as it does not arise regarding objects [perceived] by ourselves; yet, in reality,
because the appearance of that [object] is produced by the object itself, and because that [appearance] is a cognition of the object as it truly is, [cognition] exists.

If it is argued that there is a relationship of door and doorkeeper, and that therefore the experience of the object exists not directly but rather through the inference of the object in this manner—[we reply] no; since that [inference] too is a cognition, its status as having that [external object] as its domain is untenable because it perceives only its own internal form. If that is so, then because of its purity, everything [is known] by the power of its own cognition alone.

If it is argued that this [cognition] knows an external object, then, if that were so, because others are not pure, that [cognition] would likewise be non-omniscient with respect to all objects and would be formless (*anirākāra*); thus, there would be no absence of an object. If it is further argued that the Vaibhāṣika system alone should be accepted as primary:

Consequently, the claim that "there is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect" is untenable; thus, the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) is refuted. Now, one might object: "Even for you [the proponents of consciousness-only], since the cognition of an object is non-different from the self-cognition [of that consciousness], and since there is no differentiation of the cognition for each respective object, the experience of objects would be impossible. This undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows according to the reasoning already stated.

This has been stated [by others], but [it is not so] because the Self is the illuminator of proximate objects. Indeed, being the illuminator of proximate objects is the very nature of the Self, as is established by experience, just like a lamp or similar objects.
For instance, whatever object is proximate, this Self is experienced as illuminating each one of them by its own power alone.

"How can this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) arise from the non-establishment of a specific object? [If one asks this,] it is improper to say, "But how is this logically consistent? For there is indeed nothing that is inconsistent when it is observed; for in the case of "fire burns, but space does not," it is impossible to state any other ground for logical consistency than such observation. Now, if...

What benefit has been conferred upon it by the presence of the object? None at all. How then does it manifest that very object? It has already been stated that it is because its nature (*svabhāva*) is such. For even if a benefit were conferred, one never observes something that is not of that nature to be a manifester. [Objection: But then, since it manifests what was previously unmanifested in the absence of that object, it [must be dependent on it].
"How can it be said that 'it has its own nature' (svabhāva)? Because there is no difference from its essential form (svarūpa).

For its essential form, being of the nature of the manifestation of the object, is at all times undifferentiated, beyond conceptual construction, and is said to be the illuminator. If so, why does it not manifest the object?"
Because of its non-proximity; for how could that which illuminates what is proximate illuminate what is not proximate?
What, then, is the difference between the illumination of blue and the illumination of yellow? None at all. For it is as if they were illuminated simultaneously;
since there is no distinction between them there, there can be no distinction even through a difference in their constituent parts. Thus it is said.

Otherwise, it would follow that there could be no appearance of variegated cloth and the like, since they would have to be analyzed down to their individual atoms. Nor should it be argued that such an appearance is constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), because for one whose eyes are open, these objects appear instantaneously and simultaneously; furthermore, at that time, conceptualization is impossible and is not even experienced. As it has been said:
Nor do these conceptual constructions arise or perish entirely unnoticed, such that they would remain unperceived even while existing.
[Objection: Since conceptual cognition is also unitary, how can there be a variegated appearance consisting of multiple natures?

For example, although there is a diversity of various objects to be illuminated— such as blue, yellow, and so forth— there is no division in the single nature of cognition being experienced; yet, despite that non-duality of cognition,
it does not follow that the diversity of objects such as blue and yellow is unestablished.
Because you yourselves accept that a single [entity] possesses the power to manifest in multiple ways, so too,
even in the case of sequential manifestation, it is because a single experience, whose nature is luminosity, is endowed with the power to manifest in multiple ways.
It must be accepted that the state of being multiple manifestations established in a temporal sequence is proven by experience.

Nor is there the fault of the non-establishment of the difference between objects due to the non-difference [of the light]; for no difference whatsoever is experienced within the nature of the Light between the manifestation of spatial sequence and the manifestation of temporal sequence. But [one might object]:

In the *Dikkramaprakāśa*, it is stated that because no differentiation is perceived within the nature of light (*prakāśātman*), there is no contradiction in a single entity performing multiple functions— just as a lamp performs the burning of the wick, the consumption of the oil, and the production of its own cognition of light; thus, there is no contradiction in the coexistence of powers (*śakti*).

In the course of time, however, because the powers of manifestation (*prakāśa-śakti*) consist of mutual negation, they differentiate the object through their diversity, just as the powers of a jar, a cloth, and so forth do. As it has been said:
"For power, being differentiated by existence and non-existence, differentiates the object itself; it does not [differentiate it] otherwise."
Furthermore, [the argument] based on the difference of effects is incorrect because it is unproven;

for even in that case, there is no distinction between the existence and non-existence of power, since it has been stated that the luminous self is always perceived in a single form, as a nature free from superimposition. Nor is it the case that...

Since there is no power where there is no effect— according to the principle that causes do not necessarily possess [their effects]— and since even here the distinction between entities is not established, it is logical that there is merely a collection of powers,
not a contradiction; furthermore, this is like the case of the senses and so forth, where the imperceptible substratum [is inferred] from the difference in effects.
A difference in essential nature does not follow from a difference in powers, because its non-difference is established by perception;

for you yourselves accept that a single entity, like a lamp, can be the performer of multiple functions, and it has been stated that the self is established by perception as being non-different. Therefore, even in its case, [non-difference] does not result from a difference in powers.

It is not logical to postulate a difference [between cognitions] on that basis; thus, just as there is simultaneous manifestation, even in the case of successive manifestation, no difference in objects is established. How, then, is it that the cognition "this is the cognition of a jar" is distinct from the cognition of the jar itself?
"Even that cognition which occurs as 'a jar' is one that falls upon an object" (Vākyapadīya 3.105).

Thus, the various types of worldly cognitions do not arise from a difference in the nature of the apprehender (*grāhaka*), because that [apprehender] is experienced as being always of a single form, consisting of the manifestation of non-difference; rather, [the difference arises from the objects].

Because of the distinction in determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), and because knowledge (*jñāna*) is indeed determinative cognition, since knowledge is a quality of the intellect (*buddhi*). As it has been said: "The intellect is traditionally held to have eight qualities; it is characterized by determinative cognition. We shall demonstrate this later. Thus, the expression "having understood" (*buddhvā*) is also [to be explained].
"Each step has been explained.
Now, one might object: whatever is cognized is of the very nature of consciousness, just as the cognition of blue and so forth;
and since blue and so forth are cognized, they too must be of the nature of consciousness. Therefore, [how can there be] anything that is not of the nature of consciousness?

Because external objects are not perceived, all cognition is devoid of an object; thus say the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādins*) by means of another formal argument (*prayoga*), as they have stated:
"Is perception [of an object] due to identity with it? It is simply the appearance of that [object]."
What would this mean? That "that external object is directly experienced. To this, he says: "To say that 'consciousness alone is directly perceived' is stated without foundation. (6)
Since even you do not maintain that cognition is graspable by another cognition,
this [argument] is also untenable because the probans (sādhana-dharma) is unestablished in the example; for even for you,
the cognizedness of cognitions such as "blue" is not established due to their momentariness.
Because it is impossible for another consciousness to arise at the time [of the first], and because in the case of the example,
a reason whose connection to its own probandum is unestablished cannot prove that probandum, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga). || 6 ||
Now, out of fear of this defect, it may be argued that consciousness is an object of cognition because it generates another consciousness;
as they say:
"If it be asked how that which exists at a different time can be an object of perception, those who know declare its status as an object."
"Those who know the reasoning [of causality] understand that it is precisely the state of being a cause that is capable of imparting its form to cognition.
To this, he replies:
"Even if it were an object of apprehension, not every cognition would be devoid of an external object. (7)

If this is so, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because consciousness—even though it is not by nature non-conscious—is nevertheless cognizable; therefore, the object (*artha*) will likewise be cognizable. Alternatively, if the reason is "because it is cognizable while being of the nature of consciousness," then it is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of blue.

Since it cannot be established that consciousness is an object of cognition by virtue of its being of the nature of consciousness, this thesis of yours—that all cognition is devoid of an object—is not proven. || 7 ||
Here he presents the opponent's view: "Now, if cognition is held to be perceptual because its nature is that of experience,
then in this case the reason is not being cognizable by another consciousness, but rather self-cognizability itself."
Consequently, neither the fallacy of the unestablished reason (*asiddhi*) nor the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) applies to the probans.
This also he refutes:
"There is no non-existence when an object is present before one, since it is within the range of experience. (8)

If this is so, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); for it is not established that blue and other objects of cognition possess the nature of consciousness (*saṃvitsvabhāvatva*), but rather that they simply possess the state of being cognized (*saṃvedyatā*). Therefore, since the reason is unestablished, with respect to the object such as blue—which is indicated by the demonstrative "this" (*idantā*) and is an established subject (*dharmin*) proven by perception—[the reason fails].
Neither non-existence nor the refutation of externality is established. || 8 ||
He states that this very point is established by direct perception: "For this alone is clearly the distinction between the object of cognition and the cognition itself:
the former, which has the form of experience, is experienced by the latter. (9)
For the nature of consciousness is established by experience as being self-luminous and luminous to others;
since the object is also [established] by virtue of being cognized by that [consciousness], the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) is not thereby proven.
Now, if both the self and the object are thus experienced, one might ask: "Which is the self? It is not so.
We know this, for even animals are not deluded regarding the distinction between self and other;
yet this one is an animal even among animals, seized by the forgetfulness of false views, and is truly pitiable.
Or how could it be that, while both knowledge and the object of knowledge are manifest, knowledge alone [is the nature] of entities?

The object is pure. Now, since no difference in form is perceived between the object itself and the cognition of the "I-object," the system of the Sugata is well-established; for even that which has the form of impurity is accepted as such through the relationship of the one to be trained and the trainer.
But has it not been said:

"This mind is luminous by nature; the impurities are adventitious"? If so, this very [luminosity] would be the self-nature [of the object], and thus there would be no non-perception of a difference in form between the object and its cognition.
"Even if it were established, the perception [of the self] would nonetheless be distinct.
By this, the inference of insentience in the self based on its existence, substantiality, agency, and so forth, is rejected, because it is refuted by direct perception. || 9 ||
Furthermore, by means of another argument, the proponent of emptiness [states]:
"The object is not distinct from consciousness, because it was not apprehended previously at the time of the arising of consciousness."

That which is invariably perceived together with something else is not a different entity from it, just as the second moon appearing in the cognition of two moons is not different from the single moon;
and blue and other such objects are invariably perceived together with the cognition of blue. Therefore, without that [cognition], they [the objects] do not exist.
Because there is no cognition of a "prior" and "posterior," it follows that even for that [cognition], there is no difference from the object;
thus, by establishing that blue and so forth are of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), the refutation of their externality is established as a matter of course.
As they say:
"Because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension, there is no difference between the blue object and the cognition thereof.

However, the Teacher [Dharmakīrti] has demonstrated that even in the absence of the blue object, the existence of the illuminator of blue is established; therefore, this proof is unestablished (*asiddha*). Now...

This is stated with reference to Buddhist determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*); for even in that case, since it exists during states such as daydreaming even when the object is unreal, it is [considered] unestablished.
Thinking thus, and accepting its distinction based on the distinction of the objects of cognition (*prameya*), he says:
Thus, it is stated that [the reason] is inconclusive. || 10 ||
The meaning is that, having thus accepted [the opponent's position], the means of proving it is said to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
How so? He says:
"It is not perceived prior to the operation of the eye or prior to illumination."
In the world, form is not perceived as non-different from those two. || 11 ||

In this context, because the discussion concerns perception (*upalambha*), the word "eye" (*cakṣus*) refers specifically to the eyeball (*golakam*); its "activity" (*vyāpāra*) is the state of being wide open. The necessity of perceiving form (*rūpa*) together with that light is established;
however, since the eye's activity is not itself the nature of light, nor is the nature of light the eye's activity, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).

Furthermore, since you yourselves have formulated a formal argument (prayoga) for the purpose of refuting external objects, it is not logical to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) on the grounds that light and so forth are of the nature of consciousness; for precisely because of that [very reason], they remain unestablished as the probandum (sādhya). Now, even in the case of form (rūpa) that is not light...

Since there is no fixed rule that perception occurs simultaneously with light when objects are apprehended by other creatures such as owls and the like, there is no inconclusiveness [of the reason]. How then do they perceive form even when it is shrouded by darkness, as if by a cloth? It is not that darkness lacks reality, for it consists essentially of shadow.

Because this is admitted by the proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādins), and because it is possible for even people like us to have our vision obstructed by it; furthermore, if it were a real entity, as long as that which has the nature of obscuring form has not ceased, how could there be the perception of form by that eye?

If it is argued that their form is manifested by the power (*śakti*) alone, then that power itself must be the illumination, because it is the illuminator of form. If, on the other hand, it is claimed that the power will be non-illuminative in nature, then how can it illuminate?
For it is not possible for that which is non-illuminative in nature to possess the quality of being an illuminator, just as it is impossible for darkness to do so.

That power must be admitted as being of the very nature of light; therefore, the simultaneous perception with light is necessarily restricted to form, and since it is not itself of the nature of light, this reason is indeed inconclusive. [Objection: But surely form is perceived by yogis even without the operation of the eye and without light?

In this case, because there is no necessity of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*), there is no lack of definiteness (*anaikāntika*) regarding the object. In the phrase "not in the world," the qualification [is applied];

therefore, while these [objects] are perceptible to people like us, the necessity of simultaneous apprehension certainly exists, yet there is no identity [between the object and its cognition]. Thus, [the reason] remains indeed non-definitive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, for the proponents of emptiness, the long-established distinctions between monasteries, groves, shrines, and so forth—which are established by experience—would not be tenable; thus he says:
"The continuum of consciousness of blue and that of white [are distinct] despite being formless."
Even regarding cognition possessing a form, there is no rule [of certainty] without qualification. || 12 ||

This entire variety of rivers, oceans, mountains, and so forth, characterized by the distinctions of continua such as blue, white, and the like, is determined to be the means for accomplishing distinct causal functions; it cannot be without a cause, because it is subject to the constraints of place, time, and nature. As they say:
"Existence or non-existence must be eternal, because they do not depend on any other cause;
for it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of things is possible.
Nor is [the world] caused by consciousness, because [consciousness] possesses form from the very beginning.
Because it would not be established in this world; for even if that [consciousness] were admitted to possess form,
