since the nature of consciousness is without distinction everywhere and at all times, everything would possess every form everywhere and at all times— thus there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the previously mentioned rule regarding the diversity of the world would fail to be established.
He states that very point of the argument:
"The proponents of consciousness (vijñānavādins) have reached the conclusion that representation is of a single form alone," as they say:
"Entities possessing that or another form are produced from causes possessing that or another form.
Therefore, whatever has the same cause as something else possesses the same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as it;
for example, the second moment of consciousness has the same form as the first, arising from a single non-dual moment of cognition. Wherever...

In that case, there would be no identity of form, nor even identity of cause, as in the case of two cognitions in the system of the Sugata; and since, according to the Vijñānavādins, the cognition of rivers, oceans, and so forth arises from a cognition of the form of a mountain with an identical cause, it would necessarily be of one and the same form.

"But surely, for those who maintain the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), the cognition of rivers, oceans, and so forth in a dream—which arises from the same cause as the cognition of a mountain—is not of an identical form; thus, [your argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*. To this, he replies:
"But if there is no real entity, what causes the distinction between blue and other [colors] within consciousness? (13)

There is no inconclusiveness [of the reason], for those who maintain the reality of external objects do not accept that consciousness alone is the cause; rather, they hold that external things themselves are the causes according to their respective conditions by means of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
For you, however, because external objects do not exist, consciousness alone is [the cause] in all cases.

The consequence that [the world] would have causality has been stated. No; since we also admit the existence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), this appearance of diversity is produced by them and is not caused by cognition alone—thus, there is no such consequence.
As it has been said:
Formative activity (saṃskāra) born of knowledge and being the cause of knowledge is called latent impression (vāsanā). Thus [ends verse 13].
Regarding this, he says:
"The claim that [the world] is produced by latent impressions (vāsanā) is a statement impelled by the wind;
it is equal to the ravings of a madman."
Why is this so? He says:
"For you, no latent impression other than that which arises from momentary cognition is tenable. (14)
For that latent impression (*vāsanā*) is not something other than consciousness,
since you do not admit the existence of anything else— such as a sense organ— independently of consciousness; rather, it is produced from a preceding moment of consciousness.
Vāsanā is simply a specific cognition that serves as the cause for a subsequent moment of cognition;

therefore, it has already been stated that there is no distinction [between them]. Consequently, this [objection] amounts to nothing. For us, however, because the intellect (buddhi) is stable, various other properties capable of being perfumed (vāsana-dharmas) are possible. Thus [ends the argument].

[The cognition] depends on some other factor— such as a particular state of the body, or the equilibrium or disequilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), or karma which yields the fruits of pleasure and pain by revealing things as they truly are, or the grace of a deity, which serves as the cause for the ripening of specific latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

The state of possessing a specific form is indeed established. Now, one might object: even in the case of momentary things like a flame, a latent impression (*vāsanā*) such as paleness or redness produced by causes like grass or leaves is clearly observed.
No; this is not so, because that [paleness or redness] is its very nature. For its nature is indeed specifically produced by that grass.

Furthermore, it is precisely that which is produced by the leaf and so forth that is specific, and not some indeterminate latent impression (*vāsanā*). If this is so, then let the nature of some preceding moment of blue-cognition also be specifically characterized, by virtue of which [it could produce] a dissimilar mountain-form.

It would follow that [the cognition] would produce an infinite series of cognitions having the form of taste and so forth—this is an undesirable consequence. No, for since that [cognition] produces a moment similar to itself, a continuous stream (dhārāvāhika) of cognitions is not admitted. But if it is argued that because of the difference in moments, that cognition of blue is indeed different [each time], and thus there is a difference in the effect; then [we reply]:

Since there would be no distinction between moments, nothing whatsoever could produce a similar effect; consequently, because consciousness— whether in the form of a single continuum or as the body and so forth— would be non-existent, all worldly conventions would cease to exist.
Because your conventional discourse has its root in the continuum [of moments]. But surely, some moment of cognition of blue and so forth may also be a similar cause? No;

in that case, there would be a difference in the effect due to the difference in the moment—this is the aforementioned undesirable consequence. Nor even by way of being the nature of the cognition of blue...

Because of their difference, that cognition which is the cause of a similar moment is indeed one thing, and that which is the cause of a dissimilar moment is another. One must state what kind of cause belongs to what; for the proponent of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādavādin*), it is such that whatever is perceived from whatever [cause], that [cognition] belongs to that [object]. Thus, these...
Like dogs at a place where one has leaped from a cliff, imagining causes for every single thing that comes their way and wondering "from what does what arise?",

those whose intellects have not developed regarding the means for what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted should be avoided from afar by the discerning; for [the discerning] act solely for the sake of attaining the beneficial and abandoning the harmful.

Because one engages in the desire to know the means for achieving that [result]. Now, it might be argued that this [desire] will have the continuum (*saṃtāna*) as its object; but no, because that [continuum] is impossible due to the impossibility of the production of moments (*kṣaṇa*), since it consists of a flow of moments.
Thus, in order to avoid all such lack of restriction, the external object being experienced is real.

It must be admitted that the nature of the object of illumination is distinct from the nature of the illuminator; therefore, its non-difference from this [illuminator] cannot be established merely by their simultaneous perception—this is the point of the proposition to be understood, which has thus been explained. || 14 ||
Furthermore, even if there is non-difference due to the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), it does not follow that the self (*ātman*) is non-existent; thus he says:
"Non-existence in the self is not tenable, since [the self] is the object of the 'I'-cognition (*ahaṃpratyaya*).
This is because the 'I'-cognition has the self as its object, given that its nature consists in a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that apprehends a stable [subject].

There will indeed be a rule of simultaneous perception together with the self as the object of determination; thus, since both are established as being of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), they possess reality, and there is no absence of self (*nairātmya*). This is not so, however, because the self has been described as transcending conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by the Teacher in the *Mokṣakārikās*.

Furthermore, because its being an object of intellectual cognition (*buddhibodhyatva*) has been refuted, the fact that it is the objective domain of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*) is simply unestablished for the opponent. True; however, just as in the case of cognitions such as "the Self," even that [notion of "I"] is accepted as having that [Self] as its object for the sake of conventional usage, albeit through a certain degree of remoteness. Thus, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*). But [one might object]: [The text continues: *nanuṃ*... (Note: The provided fragment ends here).

Furthermore, because determination (*adhyavasāya*) has a non-real object as its domain, for us, its non-existence together with the determined object is not established. This might be correct for one who maintains the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), but for you, since that which is not of the nature of cognition is unperceivable, determination itself must be perceivable.
Since existence belongs to that which is determined as having the nature of consciousness—just like the object of determination—there is no lack of proof for its coexistence [with consciousness].

If this is so, then this [reason] is unestablished for the proponent (*vādin*), because it is accepted that the self is apprehended through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) even in the absence of the notion of "I. True; [it is accepted] in the case of the notion "I."

In this context, the reason [for the necessity of simultaneous apprehension] is the state of being an object of determination (*adhyavaseyatā*) which coexists with the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*); and since that state does not exist at that time [of the initial perception],
the rule of simultaneous apprehension is not unestablished (*asiddha*), for the state of being touched by determination is one thing, while the state of being determined is another.

The nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpatā*) has been demonstrated in the *Svāyambhuvodyota* itself in the context of the discernment between the intellect (*buddhi*) and consciousness; however, it is not discussed here as it is of no utility in this case. As you yourselves have also stated:
"For the self of cognitions is impossible to designate by convention, as it does not partake of anything else."
"Therefore, their self-cognition is not associated with verbal expression.

For this very reason, because it differs from both [the previous types of cognition], we shall demonstrate that it does not have the character of apprehending what has already been apprehended, but rather possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of that alone.

[Objection: But surely, since the notion of "I" is observed only with respect to the body—which is not the Self—in such cognitions as "I am fair" and "I am thin," the reason [adduced] is contradictory. To this, he says:
"And nowhere is the notion of 'I' ever seen to be devoid of [the qualities of] the object [of cognition], even when that object is something other [than the Self]. (15)

It is not so, because [the self] is qualified. For the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya), when qualified by other entities such as "fair-complexioned" and so forth, applies to the body through figurative usage (*guṇavṛtti*), just like the notion of a "lion" applied to a young brahmin;

however, when unqualified by those [attributes], it applies primarily to the Self alone. And it is precisely this [fact of being qualified] that is stated here as the reason, and not [the mere existence of the notion].
Since it includes a qualification, there is no contradiction at all. || 15 ||

If this is so, then since no other self (*ātman*) as an object of cognition is perceived apart from the conditions (*pratyaya*), the notion of "I" is likewise without an object— just like the notion of the unity of a forest— and thus the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished; to this, he replies:
Furthermore, cognition is clearly observed in some cases to manifest as both agent and object;
thus, in the thought "I see this," the duality is established with clarity. (16)
True; it would be without an object if the Self did not manifest by itself through its own nature as the illuminator of all objects.
However, it has been stated that it always manifests through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) precisely as being beyond conceptual construction (*vikalpātīta*).
And this notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), having that [Self] as its object according to the aforementioned method, is in some cases expressed as "I am this."

In cases such as "I clearly perceive," a very distinct experience is observed within a specific type of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*); thus, like [the cognition] of a forest and so forth, it is not without an object due to its unity. Therefore, the previously stated argument of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*). If this is so—
The argument that "the non-duality of the self is established because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension" results in the subversion of [your own] desired position;
for even in your own view, self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*) is not something to be rejected, as this [argument] is intended for that very purpose.
However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), even this reflective cognition (*parāmarśabuddhi*)—such as "I perceive this"—is [not ultimately real].

The Self, by virtue of being the illuminator of all objects, is to be perpetually reflected upon as their source; whereas the object, being that which is illuminated by it, is perceived sequentially. Thus, because they are determined to be absolutely distinct, these two are clearly [differentiated].
Thus, the claim that there is no distinction [between them] is untenable; therefore, there is no subversion of our desired position. As it has been said:
"This indeed is clearly to be understood as the distinction between cognition and its object:
the former has the form of experience, while the latter is experienced. (16)

"Is it not the case that there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) here, because we observe even a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose object is non-dual, such as in the phrase 'nanv ayam' and so forth? To this he says:
"For every cognition indeed manifests both an agent and an object."

Even such reflective cognitions as "this is a jar" cannot logically have reflection itself as their sole object; for, lacking reflection within its own self, it cannot be established as having that nature, just like an object of another's reflection. This [cognition] must also [possess reflection] by way of its own self.

If it is argued that [the existence of the Self] is not established because there is no awareness of it at that time, we say no; for even an awareness that is not reflected upon is established, just like the awareness of grass and such objects by those who are walking. As they say:
"In reality, consciousness, though existing, is [unestablished] due to the absence of reflective awareness."
"Just as the cognition of grass and such things belongs to the traveler, it is established as if non-existent.

Therefore, that [object] must be investigated as being indeed without an agent; and when the object is investigated as having the self as its agent, by implication the self itself, having become subordinate to it, is also investigated. Thus it is said.
Since all reflective awareness (*vimarśajñāna*) necessarily has both an agent and an object as its domain, there is no lack of logical necessity (*anaikāntikatā*).
He states that this is also established by inference: "Because the triad is recollected, [one concludes] 'I have seen that. (17)

Since memory, which has as its object such reflective awareness as "this is a jar," is observed to have as its objects the agent, the object, and the instrument, it necessarily implies a non-verbal reflective awareness of the agent prior to [the awareness of] the object and the instrument; thus, every reflective awareness has a dual object. For this very reason:
Investigation does not have a non-entity as its object, because, like perception, it conforms to the presence and absence of the entity.
Others have also said:
"There is indeed an initial non-conceptual cognition called mere observation (ālocana)."
It is like the cognition of infants, the mute, and others, arising from a pure object.
"Furthermore, that [cognition] which is subsequently determined by the intellect through the properties of the object, such as genus and so forth, is also accepted as being perceptual. [Objection:
But surely, even in the absence of a real object, the conceptualization of things like a jar is observed in cases such as daydreaming. [Reply: True; for this very reason—

The distinction between these two [types of cognition] is due to their having real and unreal objects respectively, just as there is a distinction between perception and its semblance. Now, one might object: even for that which is considered to have a real object—such as the reflective awareness "this is that same jar"—it proceeds by way of having been previously perceived; yet now, in the absence of that prior perception...
It is not the case that [the cognition] has a non-entity as its object because of the impossibility of that [prior perception], since the absence of prior perception is unestablished;
for it has been stated that the very illumination of the self is the perception of the object, and that exists at all times.
Therefore, even the state of having been previously seen is, at present, nothing but the entity itself; thus, in the case of a jar or the like, it does not have a non-entity as its object.

"We shall state later that momentariness is unestablished. If that is so, then even when one touches [an object] in total darkness, the mental conceptualization ‘this is a jar’—which lacks reflection on the form and other qualities not perceived—is a mental construction based on memory and has no real object. No, for those [qualities] are bound to the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*).
Because even those things that are not perceptible at that time are inferred from the specific mark (liṅga) characterized by contact.
As it has been stated by you as well:
"The cognition of form and so forth, which depend on the same causal complex, occurs even when they are not present [to the senses]."
"By means of the inference of causal properties, like the transformation of fuel by smoke.
Nor is even the deliberation (*vimarśa*) of inference concerned with non-entities (*avastu*),

because it possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by following the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of real entities, just like perception and its subsequent deliberation.
This has been stated by you as well:
"Since [cognition] would be absent if the object were non-existent, it possesses the status of a means of valid cognition even in the case of perception;
if its nature is restricted [to that object], then both [perception and inference] are equal in being caused by that [object]."
Nor can its having a non-real object be established by the fact that its appearance is indistinct,
because this would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since even in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), such an appearance is possible for an object situated at a distance;
furthermore, even scriptural investigation (*vimarśa*) pertains to a real entity (*vastu*) by means of the knowledge of the author of that scripture.
Because it is dependent [on a reliable source], it is indeed true to reality, like the reflective inquiry produced by hearing the words of a non-deceptive father or similar authority.
As it has been stated by you as well:
"This object is desired, provided it is possible to know it with excellence."
However, let it be granted that a deliberation excluded from perception, inference, and scripture—
like a deliberation concerning a castle in the air— is devoid of a connection to a real object and thus has an unreal object;
yet, the deliberation "I perceive this" does not have an unreal object, because its object is the self and the thing as they are experienced by consciousness.

However, because it is a specific kind of perception according to the method already stated, it is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, the self is established by this as well. Consequently, the thesis-statement "by cognition" (*bodhena*) has also been explained. || 17 ||

Thus, although the absence of the conventional usage of "existent" regarding the self has been refuted by the presence or absence of proving and subverting means of valid cognition, the Lokāyatikas say: "Therefore,
[the self] is thus distinct from the body and so forth, by virtue of being the witness of all objects..."

The self is indeed of a non-different nature, being the object of the notion of "I" which is self-cognized; however, it perishes at the time of death and is therefore unstable, like a jar and other such things, because it possesses the quality of having an origin. Nor is this reason unestablished.

Since the production of that which is of the nature of consciousness is observed when there is a specific transformation of semen, blood, and so forth, and it is not observed in their absence—just as smoke [is absent] in the absence of fire—its status as an effect is established; for this reason it has been said: "Indeed, the body arises fully endowed with consciousness."
He refutes this as follows:
"Furthermore, the permanence of the person here is understood precisely from memory;
permanence means existence even prior to birth."

The absence of production from the specific transformation of semen, blood, and so forth is understood from the reason that a person possesses recollection immediately upon birth. In this regard, he first establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this reason:
For [a memory] does not arise in one person regarding an object experienced by another. || 18 ||
For remembrance is certainly determined within oneself after the stage of childhood to be preceded by an experience of a specific single substratum; because,
from a vivid experience occurring in one substratum such as Devadatta, [remembrance arises] in another substratum.
Since remembrance is not observed in the case of Yajñadatta and others, the pervasion is established by the fact that remembrance is preceded by an experience of a single qualified locus. || 18 ||
He also states the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*):

"That by which joy and so forth are characterized, when that [joy] has arisen, as in the case of youth or old age, is preceded by the experience of an object, its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the manifestation of that [impression], and memory. (19)

When a person has been born—that is, when one who has acquired a body has come into existence—immediately after birth, by virtue of which cause joy and so forth are observed, since [otherwise] the expansion of the face and other such signs would be inexplicable;
by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), postures, the striking of articulatory organs, and the like are meant. As they have said:
"The initial arrangement of the instruments [of action], the upward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa),
and the non-obstruction of the [various] locations do not occur without prior consciousness.
And that [consciousness] is not, like one who is insane, produced by the agitation of wind and other humors, even when it is unobstructed therein.

At that time, it does not arise from the experience of everything; rather, it arises from the impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited in the intellect by whichever experience of the object sought— such as pleasure— or its means occurred in a person situated in youth or other stages of life.
In the world, it is observed that whatever memory arises from awakening must have a specific cause; thus, wherever there is joy and so forth, there must necessarily be such a memory.
Therefore, it is stated that the presence of this [memory] as a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) is established through inference based on an inference (anumitānumāna). || 19 ||

[Objection: But surely, even in the absence of a prior experience of pleasure and so forth, joy and the like are observed in a person who has reached a stage such as youth; thus, since that [joy] is established through memory, [the reason] is inconclusive. To this he says: "Nor is its experience observed, because [it occurs] during the experience [of something else]."

Because, regarding the object of experience, that person's experience of pleasure and so forth at that time is not perceived— meaning it is determined to be non-existent— due to the absence of the means of pleasure such as drinking milk;
therefore, the phrase "in the absence of the experience of pleasure and so forth" is specified as the cause of joy and the like.

Since the recollection of pleasure and so forth, when it is being applied and is not distinguished by non-deviation, leads to the inference [of its cause], there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
Therefore, it is inferred that a person has transcended to another state of existence. || 20 ||

Therefore, from memory characterized by signs such as joy—which has established pervasion (*vyāpti*) because it is preceded by the experience of a specific single cause, and so forth—an individual person infers a previous existence that transcends the present life; however, this does not mean that birth occurs simultaneously with the body. This is because... [the text continues].
If this [self] were an effect of semen and blood, then its existence and non-existence would depend on the existence and non-existence of those [semen and blood];

however, these two [dependence and independence] are not possible, because one cannot perceive their prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or their subsequent destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) by oneself, and because another's consciousness cannot be perceived by another. And just as...

The capacity of the *sthānas*, *karaṇas*, and so forth to convey meaning is likewise demonstrated here by the Teacher (*ācārya*) in his *Rauravavṛtti* through the verses refuting the highest liberation (*paramokṣanirāsakārikā*):
"Even when [the object] has been experienced in another birth, memory is observed to arise."
"And she would have hunger because of her approaching for the sake of milk.
This must be understood from that very [scriptural passage]. || 20 ||
In this way, his garland of births must be understood as beginningless;
thus, by this sequence, the beginningless continuity of birth for the person is established.
And therefore:
Because of its connection with beginningless phenomena, there is the possibility of being indestructible and so forth. || 21 ||
For you have stated that this [self] is impermanent because it possesses the quality of being produced, like a jar and so forth;
however, since it is beginningless, that [impermanence] is not possible—thus it is established that the self is indestructible. || 21 ||

But surely, even though this [individual self] is beginningless, upon liberation there will be its destruction— just as in the case of those who advocate the merging of the supreme self, or like the proponents of the extinction of a lamp— [this applies] even for those who maintain the existence of the individual self (jīvātman).
To this, he says:
When consciousness is pure and liberated due to the abandonment of all afflictions,
our liberation does not consist in the destruction of the self; rather, we shall explain that it is the cessation of all bondage and the manifestation of omniscience.
Thus, the thesis-statement "and [he] is the enjoyer of the fruit of activity" has been explained with reference to results pertaining to the next world;
now, in order to demonstrate it with reference to results pertaining to this life, [the author states]: "the grasping self is momentary."
The Śākya position is not only untenable because of the existence of the subverting proofs previously demonstrated, but also because of the absence of any proving proof; thus he says:
For there is no means of valid cognition for momentariness, since no difference [between successive moments] is perceived. || 22 ||

For this position is refuted by perception—just as the claim that "sound is inaudible"—because no difference [between subject and object] is observed; for, according to the method previously stated, their non-difference is revealed by the perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) as something not superimposed. Furthermore, there are no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Just as [the claim] "all objects are knowable" is refuted by its own words, so too is this [position] refuted by its own words,

because this statement of the thesis regarding its momentariness is untenable; for your own admission is that a "moment" is a time devoid of priority and posteriority, yet this statement is brought about by multiple moments.
"How could a moment bring about [the effect]? This is a contradiction. True;

for this very reason, we do not accept the formal statement of a thesis (*pakṣaprayoga*), because the probandum (*sādhya*) is established solely from the mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics.
Well then, let that mark be stated here. [It is as follows: "Whatever exists, all that is momentary; for if there were an absence of momentariness..."
The reason is precisely that which is called "existence" (*sattva*), because [the opponent claims] there is an absence of existence [in the subject] while the nature of the apprehender exists.

If this is so, this reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of existence with non-momentariness is established everywhere in examples such as a jar. [Objection: But surely lightning, a flame, and so forth are not examples here?

For that [object] also consists of multiple moments because it falls within the range of perception for people like us; furthermore, since even you do not admit that those who do not perceive everything engage in linguistic convention regarding a single moment, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) if it is of the nature of a moment. [Objection: But surely "pure existence" (*śuddha-sattva*) is the reason here. [Response: If that were so, it would be unestablished (*asiddha*), for indeed—
The mere existence [of a thing], devoid of non-momentariness, is established even in some other locus (dharmyantara). Now,
since conceptual cognitions (vikalpa) are intent upon specific portions by way of exclusion from dissimilar classes,
[the quality] "red" [is applied] even to a jar and so forth.

Since the conceptualization of "existence" (sattva), proceeding by excluding redness that is the object of other conceptualizations such as "earthen" or "circular," takes as its object existence itself in its pure form, how can it be unestablished?
As it has been said:
"As many as are the superimpositions of parts, so many are the determinations through their removal;
and there are just as many words, for that reason they have distinct domains."

This is correct: [conceptualization] has other phenomena as its object, but not non-momentary things, because without that [momentariness], conceptualization would be untenable. For every conceptualization attains the status of being a conceptualization by proceeding on the basis of what was previously perceived, thinking "this is that very same thing.
Conceptualization is the act of joining; it is so called because it functions through such joining.

Because it would follow that [the self] is non-conceptual; for it is precisely through synthesis (*yojanā*) that there is a determination of non-momentariness with respect to the self, just as there is with respect to an object. Indeed, even if momentariness were present in the self, a synthesis such as "this is a jar" would not be possible, since [the self] is not denotable by a specific word. As it has been said:
"Only when those [objects] have been seen does practical activity proceed through desire based on memory, which arises from the power of consciousness. Therefore,
because it consists of such conjunction, the self, like the objects to be conjoined, also functions as the conjoiner.
Since that [momentariness] has become a subordinate factor, it is indeed determined as non-momentary by every conceptual construction;
thus, just like redness or other such qualities, even non-momentariness cannot be excluded by the conceptual construction of existence.
Therefore, the pure reason known as "existence" (*sattva*) is simply unestablished (*asiddha*). If...

This reason is therefore pure; because it is concomitant with one of the two—either the eternal or the non-eternal—it cannot exist outside both as a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*). Consequently, like "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) in the case of the non-eternality of sound and so forth, it is an uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason. However, it is not [inconclusive] in the sense of being concomitant with what is observed [in the similar class].

Therefore, it has been stated that [the reason] is both pure and contradictory. Furthermore, because all existing things are pervaded by momentariness, it is impossible to provide a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) of something ultimately real that is non-momentary; this is because there can be no exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣa).

A purely positive (kevalānvayin) reason would be non-probative, because it has been stated that only a reason possessing the three characteristics (trirūpaka) is probative. It is not the case that the absence of the reason from the counter-example (vipakṣa) constitutes the third characteristic, such that this fault [of being non-probative] would arise; rather, it is the negative concomitance (vyatireka), consisting in the absence of the probans where there is an absence of the probandum, for that very reason.

That which is other than that, opposed to it, and its absence is called its "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*); and since that exists for this [reason], it is not a case of pure positive concomitance (*kevalānvayi*). As it has been said:
"Therefore, a dissimilar example is not required here, nor is a locus necessarily desired."
"Even in the absence of that [the object], because of the statement 'it is not there,' that [non-existence] is understood.

If this is so, then this reason has a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*), because the object to be understood from the statement is itself of a doubtful nature—just as in the case of the argument, "This portion of ground possesses a treasure. For [only] if [the object] were of a certain nature...
Since the probandum is established by the mere statement of the thesis, what is the use of this laborious presentation of a fallacious reason?

[The opponent replies: "But even in the absence of a dissimilar instance (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), there is a certainty of negative concomitance (vyatireka) for this [reason] by virtue of the force of a subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the counter-example; thus, it is not a case of doubtful negative concomitance."

If that is so, then that very subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) should be presented first; for without it, this statement of the reason is equivalent to not stating it at all. [Objection: "Because for an entity that is non-momentary, a cause of destruction is impossible. [Response: This is not [the case], because [that reason] is contradictory (*viruddha*). For the impossibility of a cause of destruction implies non-destruction.

It establishes [the fact of destruction], but not momentariness. If that is so, then it is qualified by the term "observed": for if jars and the like possessed a non-perishable nature, a cause of destruction—whether observed or inferred through such factors as being produced—would be entirely ineffective; conversely, if they possessed a perishable nature, such a cause would be redundant.

Because destruction is established by its very nature (*svabhāva*), and since there is no distinction in that nature, the destruction of an existing thing at every moment is established. If this is so, [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it has been demonstrated that no cause for the destruction of the perceiving self is observed, and [destruction occurs] solely from what is seen to perish.

By this, the exclusion of this reason from the counter-example (vipakṣa) would be established; however, because the destruction of atoms and so forth is not observed but remains merely possible, this reason again has a doubtful exclusion from the counter-example and is therefore inconclusive (anaikāntika). And it is not...

We shall explain that the cause of destruction either lacks the capacity [to act] or is simply redundant. If that is so, then let this subverting proof—namely, that for an eternal entity, purposeful action (arthakriyā) is contradicted by both succession and simultaneity—apply everywhere to the contrary position; [the opponent replies: no.

This [reasoning] is also invalid because its locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhatva*); for you do not accept any eternal entity upon which this reason could be established. If it is argued that it is indeed a valid reason because it is established for the opponent, then how is it established? If it is argued that it is established because the subject (*dharmin*) is established, [then...]

From what source is this established for him? If it is by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is certainly established for the proponent as well, since a valid cognition has a real entity as its basis; so how can there be a rejection of permanence?
On the other hand, if it is said that it is established for him merely through an assertion (*abhyupagama*) without a valid cognition, [then...]
If this is so, how could that which is non-existent establish a real entity (*vastu*), for it has been stated that the establishment of a real entity comes from a real entity?

[Objection: But surely, wherever causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) occurs through either succession or simultaneity, there is momentariness; whereas in the absence of momentariness, there is an absence of causal efficiency through either succession or simultaneity.

By demonstrating merely the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between two properties (*dharma*), there is no fault of the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhatā*) because some substratum (*dharmin*) is being relied upon; as the author of the *Alaṅkāra* said: "This is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*); therefore, there is no unestablished locus."
"If it were thus, then this [reason] would also not be accepted as being both [present in the subject and absent from the dissimilar instance].
If it were thus, then because it lacks the property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*), this would simply not be a valid reason (*ahetu*).

If it were to establish the exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*), for indeed, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone are not the definition of a reason.

Since it has been stated that only a reason possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) is a valid logical mark, and as we shall demonstrate later, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is also unestablished (*asiddha*) in this case; Dharmottara, however, says: "Existence (*sattva*) is indeed pervaded by succession and simultaneity; therefore, by the absence of succession and simultaneity..."

The absence of a sentient being (*sattvābhāva*) is here the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*); therefore, there is no fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*) for this absence, because it is established in a permanent subject (*dharmin*), just as in the case of a hare's horn and the like. Indeed, this fault applies only to a reason (*hetu*) that is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*). For this very reason [it does not apply here].

"The reductio reason (*prasaṅgahetu*) is that which culminates in the reversal of the consequence (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*). This is incorrect, for even you maintain that a reason must be necessarily connected to its own probandum (*svasādhyapratibaddha*). As it has been said:
"Either from the relation of cause and effect, or from an essential nature (*svabhāva*) that acts as a restrictor..."

"The rule of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva-niyama*)—[is not established]... Thus, since no connection (*pratibandha*) is possible for a reason that consists in non-existence—an absolute non-entity—it follows that such a reason is not a valid reason (*ahetutā*). As the *Alaṃkāra* [author] also said:
"If the reason consists of mere non-existence, what could be established by whom, and where?
Thus, it has been stated that there is a lack of proof (*asiddhatva*), because a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) does not exist in the form of non-existence;
for instance, in the case of things such as a rabbit's horn.
Since it is merely an object of conventional usage such as non-existence by virtue of being constructed through conceptualization, its status as something purely imaginary is established;

however, it is not established as the means (*sādhana*) for anything, and thus there is no contradiction. For this very reason, non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) functions as a means of proving non-existence by force of the determination of cognition, whereas in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), it pertains to the real entity (*vastu*).
You yourselves have stated that when a superior entity is established from a [previously] superior entity, it is nothing other than a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*):
"The formulation alone differs; the meaning does not differ in every case."

This is nothing at all. Others, however, say: that very thing which is intended as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), such as a pot, is likewise [intended] as a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*); and since the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is established with respect to that, how can there be the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*)? If it were thus, this [fallacy] would be produced by human whim.
The distinction between the similar class (*sapakṣa*), the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), and so forth, does not exist in reality;

therefore, [a reason] such as "being one or the other of the subject or the similar class" is a fallacy of inference (*anumānābhāsa*). Furthermore, it is impossible for the similar class itself to be the dissimilar class, because the presence and absence of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) are absolutely contradictory; thus, this [distinction] does not exist in reality.

The status of being a dissimilar instance (vipakṣatva) is attributed to jars and the like by virtue of their being similar instances (sapakṣatva), and is then negated by a subverting means of valid cognition (bādhaka-pramāṇa):

"If jars and the like were non-momentary, then for a non-momentary entity there would be a contradiction with causal efficiency (arthakriyā) in terms of either succession or simultaneity; yet it does perform causal efficiency; therefore [it is momentary]."
Regarding the claim that [the reason] is "momentary": it is argued that just as if there were no fire here, there would be no smoke;

yet since there is smoke, there must be fire here—because there is no contradiction, the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*) does not apply—that too is incorrect, because the contradiction is not established, since it is precisely non-momentary things such as a jar [that persist].

The causal efficiency of milk, ghee, and so forth is observed to occur sequentially, whereas that of a lamp and the like—such as the burning of the wick and the consumption of the oil—is seen to occur simultaneously;
how, then, can their contradiction be established? For that [lamp] possesses a single nature, yet its causal efficiency occurs sequentially.

Because [simultaneity] is impossible, [the agent] would have to perform all effects belonging to subsequent times simultaneously; yet such a one performing them simultaneously is not observed, and thus contradiction is established. No, for this reason too is unestablished (*asiddha*) due to a difference in locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*), since [it applies only to that which] produces multiple objects of action simultaneously.

That intrinsic nature (svabhāva) which is seen to produce those effects simultaneously, such as a lamp and the like, is indeed established as having a single nature that produces multiple purposeful actions (arthakriyā) all at once; however, that which is seen to produce an effect sequentially is established as having a single nature that produces multiple purposeful actions only in succession, not simultaneously—thus there is no contradiction. Now, for what purpose does it act sequentially?

We shall explain later that because it possesses such an intrinsic nature, it is as if simultaneous. Thus, since there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); it is not a valid means of proof for momentariness. However, the new Śākyas say: "It does not [exist] in its counter-example..."

Furthermore, the ascertainment of non-existence by virtue of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) arises precisely from an investigation based on the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) with the thing itself; for when existence is investigated,
it is excluded from the non-momentary by that very essential connection, just as the nature of heat is excluded from the non-burning.
This— that [the argument] resting upon momentariness finds its repose in the process of returning—
is established by a thorough investigation into the very nature of things;
therefore, the previously mentioned defects, such as the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), do not apply.
If this inquiry is thus stated to consist of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or of intuition (*pratibhā*),

as the elder grammarians have said: "There is nothing that is unprecedented," then because it is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would be either perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).

If it is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is a contradiction with your own tenet; however, if it is not a valid means of knowledge, how can the certainty of the absence of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) be derived from it, since only that which is a cause for the certain determination of existence or non-existence is a valid means of knowledge? [Objection:

But surely, even through the investigation of the nature of things, for those who know the method of reasoning (*naya*), there exists a form of inference (*ūha*) whose object is a thing not present before them.
Certainty is indeed seen to be certainty. True; it arises solely from the inference of capability (yogyatā) and not from anything else.
As you yourselves have stated:
"The production of an effect which is inferred by means of a complete cause..."

"Because it does not depend on any other object, its own nature has been described. Furthermore, what is the meaning of the statement that "investigation is based upon a necessary connection" (*pratibandha*)? Does the establishment of the necessary connection result from the investigation, or does the investigation take place once the necessary connection is already established? In the former case...

If [the relation] were established through investigation, then even for a jar and a cloth—which are absolutely unrelated in this world—an essential connection (*pratibandha*) would arise through such investigation;

this would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Now, if the second position is held, then since the connection is established by perception—just as in the case of fire and its capacity to burn—this subsequent investigation is merely a conventional usage preceded by memory.
Thus it would be stated, and therefore there is no comprehension of a new (previously unknown) object from that [statement]. As it has been said:
"When those very things previously perceived are seen again, worldly activity proceeds through desire based on memory, which arises from the power of consciousness."

Furthermore, since no connection whatsoever has been established between existence and momentariness, an investigation into that subject is untenable; how then could this reason be excluded from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), such that it might possess the status of a means of valid cognition for establishing momentariness? || 22 ||
Even if one were to accept the position of momentariness (*kṣaṇika-pakṣa*), there would be the consequence of no liberation; thus he says:
"There would be the consequence of rebirth, for the affliction (*upaplava*) is without cause.
For ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are the causes for the origination of this cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), which is of the nature of suffering.
It is sung [in the scriptures]:

"As it has been said—'Because of the cause of bondage, which consists of the misconception regarding suffering and excessive craving, he for whom these two do not exist is not subject to rebirth. Thus it is stated.

Nor is it logical for those two to be the cause, because it is accepted that here the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)— consisting precisely of the preceding moment of cognition of blue, yellow, and so forth— is the cause, and no other is possible. As it has been said:

"When X exists, Y necessarily comes to be; if one were to postulate another cause for it besides that [X], there would be an infinite regress of causes in all cases. Therefore, since there is no other efficient cause and this [result] has only this much as its cause, [it follows that...].

Because of the recurrence of the ruinous nature of cyclic existence as before, there would be no possibility of liberation characterized by cessation, nor of the path which consists of the cultivation of that which is opposed to its origin; this applies to all four: suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

"The Noble Truths are indeed non-truths. Or rather, let this be so even indirectly; [yet] it is only the cause of the affliction of passion and the like, and not of the nature of the grasped and the grasper. Thus he says:
The sign (nimitta) must be correctly explained for the sake of establishing the object of measurement and the means of measurement. || 23 ||

For where there is the distinction between the grasped and the grasper, even for you, ignorance and craving are established; however, since these two are impossible in the case of persons free from passion and in the case of the omniscient ones, it is incorrect to posit them as the cause in this context. || 23 ||
Now, one might object: "Is it not established that these two [the eye and form] serve as the basis for the distinction between the grasped and the grasper even in dreams? To this he says:
"Other cognitions, such as those occurring in dreams, are intended to serve as the illustrative examples."
For even those [qualities] produced by latent impressions (vāsanā) become firmly established in the subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra). || 24 ||
For even in that case, the status of those two as causes is not established by any means of valid cognition; rather,
it is simply through the observation of form and so forth, which results from the latencies of experience conditioned by karma, that [the appearance occurs] in accordance with that experience.
Because of the experience of suffering and so forth, and because forms and other objects do not appear in the dreams of those born blind;
furthermore, as was stated previously, the theory of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is only tenable for those who maintain the existence of a stable self, not for the position of momentariness.
How then are the appearances of error not without an object?

Because it appears in the form of two moons and so forth, it does not have a non-existent object, for that which is non-existent cannot appear; nor does it have a distorted object, because it is unreal in those respective forms due to the aforementioned fault; nor does it have the self as its object, because the self is unchanging; rather, [it is as follows]:

It has been stated elsewhere that [these cognitions] have as their objects only the forms of the intellect (buddhi) as refined by the latent impressions of determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya-vāsanā*):
"The parts of the reality of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-tattva*) appear as if situated externally. Thus, even these [cognitions] do not have delusion as their cause.
He demonstrates this very point:
"For even by the proponent of cognition (Buddhist), the entire range of objects of knowledge, means of knowledge, and so forth, has been taught;
because they are included within [consciousness] and because they exist, there is no falsity in them either. (25)

For it is not possible for the proponents of consciousness (vijñānavādins) to assert the non-existence of this distinction—the nature of which consists in the grasped, the grasper, and the act of grasping—because it is established by experience;
rather, its very nature is that of consciousness. Therefore, because it is apprehended as being included [within consciousness], it is also of the form of consciousness.
Because this [duality] exists, its falsity—its nature as a cognitive distortion—is not tenable;
rather, it must be of the very nature of consciousness. Since it cannot be removed, and because duality is thus unestablished, there would be no liberation at all. || 25 ||

Now, one might object: since the manifestation of the grasped and the grasper is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it must be of the nature of a cognitive distortion—just like the notion of a self in what is not-self—and cannot be the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
For indeed, perception shows that all this, such as a jar and so forth, which is the grasped, is not distinct from the grasper.

Because it is an object of apprehension; for if there were a difference [between subject and object], there would be a mutual lack of apprehensibility, as in the case of the cognitions of Devadatta and Yajñadatta.
Yet such [apprehensibility] does exist; therefore, there is simply the non-existence of duality. As they say:
"In ultimate reality, there is nothing whatsoever that is an object of apprehension or an apprehender."
"This creation, produced by ignorance, is indeed a delusion for people.
Therefore, he says:
"The statement that perception is indeed knowledge is itself a false statement."
Since everything is cognized and there is no sublation whatsoever. (26)

This [objection] also does not constitute a sublation because they are mutually non-contradictory; for even this sublating cognition has as its object an entity that is itself being sublated, since if it did not have that as its object, the negation of it would be untenable, and thus its status as a sublater would be impossible. Therefore, since everything that is to be apprehended is unsublatable...

It is not so, because [the object] is being perceived; rather, it is of the nature of a cognitive distortion, like the notion of a self in what is not-self. Therefore, there is no redundancy here in the passage beginning with "perceptual cognition itself," because the objects of proof (sādhya) differ. || 26 ||
Furthermore, he states that this reason of yours proves the opposite of the nature of the subject (*dharmin*):

"Because it is an object of cognition, like an external object, an infinite regress would follow; for if the object is cognized by consciousness because it is an object of cognition, then knowledge itself [would likewise require another knowledge]."
Since it would be cognized only by being graspable by another cognition, there follows the undesirable consequence of its not being self-cognized;
and if that [second cognition] were also uncognized, its status as the grasper of the first would be untenable, leading to an infinite regress of "that [cognition] and yet another."

"Surely, even if it is unknown, cognition, like a sense organ, will apprehend another cognition; therefore, there is no infinite regress. To this, he replies by restating the previous argument: "If a cognition apprehended by another cognition were to function with respect to an object... (27)
There might be no distinction between those two [the sense organs and the means of knowledge] as long as it has never been seen otherwise.
This is logical for the eyes and so forth, because they are instruments (*kāraka*) with respect to the direct perception of objects;
however, this is not the case for indicators such as logical marks (*liṅga*) and words, which lack self-luminosity.

Since it has never been observed that anything possesses the quality of illuminating an object of apprehension, and because cognition itself is a cognizer, the establishment of its capacity to apprehend another cognition is not possible without self-luminosity;
thus, there follows the undesirable consequence that everything would be imperceptible. As it has been said:
"For one whose apprehension is not itself perceived, the perception of an object is not established. Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, he states that this reason is unestablished for the proponent: "And consciousness is imagined by him as the internalization of its own parts. (28)
Even for the Vijñānavādin, the multiplicity of a single consciousness—which has jars and so forth as its nature—must be postulated. As it has been said:
"If this variegated consciousness were one, then it would be even more variegated than that."

Thus, since a distinction must be postulated down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) which is a mere portion of cognition, the perceptibility of objects such as jars—which are intended as external entities—is not established; this also contradicts experience. (28)
Moreover, since it is impossible even to postulate another stream of consciousness (vijñānasantānāntara),
for what purpose would there be the composition of treatises or acts such as giving?
Thus, he states that this [view] results in the total collapse of all worldly conventions:
Furthermore, there is no distinct object of cognition that constitutes another mental continuum;
since the object of thought is merely its own form, it follows that everything would be non-existent. (29)
For bodily and verbal activity is observed in one's own body to be preceded by a specific consciousness;
thus, because such [activity] is seen in another's body as well, consciousness is inferred by everyone.
However, for the Vijñānavādins, since everything that is cognized is merely its own form (ākāra), it is like a dream.

Since another body is not established, this appearance is false; how, then, can there be the establishment of another stream of consciousness (*jñānasantāna*) from that? Even if it were established, its status as a distinct objective support (*ālambana*) is not proven, because even that distinct [object] would lack [the capacity for] an object in relation to a cognition—whether that cognition possesses an image (*sākāra*) or is devoid of an image (*nirākāra*).

Because it is impossible to make [an external object] the content of cognition, that [object] is established as being known only as consisting of its own form (the form of the cognition itself). As it has been said:
"Having observed an action preceded by cognition in one's own body, one perceives it elsewhere [in an external object]."
"If it is known [that there is no external object], this same principle applies even to mere consciousness (cittamātra).

This too is incorrect; for if that were so, the consequence would be the absence of all worldly transaction (vyavahāra), as in the question: "Who would do what for whom? Therefore, [the external object] must indeed be real.
The distinction between the grasped and the grasper must be admitted; thus, because non-duality cannot be established due to its irreversibility, there is indeed no liberation for you.

Now, regarding those who, while accepting the existence of external objects, maintain that their apprehender must possess a form— those who say, "We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and the cognition"— it is said in reply to them: "In this world,
the path of the intellect of a yogi whose senses are well-guarded..."
Therefore, it is perceived as having its objective form cast aside. || 30 ||
Even that cognition which has sound and other objects as its domain does not possess their form;
it consists of the determination of those [objects], and thus the notion that it possesses their form is an error. (31)

This might be so, if no difference in form between the object and its cognition were perceived; however, that difference is indeed perceived. For instance, in the case of a yogi who has withdrawn all activity of the sense organs—and for that very reason whose experience of the forms of all objects has ceased—there remains only pure consciousness.

It is observed even in your own scripture that the nature of consciousness manifests as a continuous stream; otherwise, it would be impossible for the non-dual [consciousness], which is not represented by objects, to undergo any change. And this has been stated by those skilled in the inner science (adhyātma):

"Then there is the subsistence of the seer in its own nature. Thus, the grasper is established as indeed distinct from the form of the object; therefore, precisely because of that distinction, at the time of the determination of sound and so forth, it is simply the state of being the determiner of those [objects].
Since the nature of the apprehending subject is established through experience, it can be accepted;
however, because it contradicts the experience of having the form of sounds and so forth, the theory of "cognition with forms" (sākāravāda) is also merely an error.
Explaining this very point, he says:
"For the object itself possesses form, since it is apprehended as having that [form].
For the object is indeed differentiated by various forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth, [which are distinct] from the nature of the grasper."

Since it is experienced internally in the form of a present object, yet is perceived as having a definite form connected with an external location in the manner of an "in-front" object, it is logical that it must indeed be distinct from that formless cognition.
Having spoken thus with respect to the nature of the apprehender, he also says with respect to the determination [of the object]:
"The object is apprehended first, and consciousness afterwards; such is the established order. (32)

For when there is an immediate contact between the sense organ and its object, first there is the pure object itself, devoid of any determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*); subsequently, however, even a determinative cognition such as "this is a jar" is experienced.
Therefore, their identity is also untenable. [Objection: But surely, the *puruṣa* perceives the object as determined by the intellect (*buddhi*).
This is the accepted position of all those who maintain the distinction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*);

therefore, your established doctrine—that there is first a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) and subsequently a self-awareness (*saṃvedana*)—is logical, and it is not something observed in the Buddhist system. True; this [distinction] applies only in cases such as the appearance of memory and so forth, but not...

Because there is contradiction with experience in every case; for it is not logical that there should be a difference in experience according to each philosophical system, since that [experience] is established by the nature of the object itself.

Indeed, it cannot be asserted—even by those who are most skillful—that "blue is blue only for the Buddhists, whereas for the Jains it is yellow. For this experience is established by the inherent power of the object.
Being experienced as consisting solely of initial non-determination, how could it otherwise be established? As they say:
"There exists first a perceptual cognition that is indeterminate."
It is like the cognition of infants, the mute, and others, arising from a pure object.
Furthermore, that cognition by which the object is subsequently determined through properties such as birth and so forth is also accepted as being of the nature of direct perception.
Thus it is rightly said; such is the established position. || 32 ||

[Objection: Surely an object cannot be the causeless [source] of cognition, because that would lead to the consequence of infinite regress; and if it were a cause, then the same would apply to the sense organs and so forth. Therefore, it is logical that [cognition] possesses the very form of that [object]. To this, he says: "Know that for a thing to be a generator is its being a benefactor (upakāritā) toward the cognition."
Therefore, because of the connection with the organs of action, there is grasping, not of a [specific] form. || 33 ||

Since it is said that with respect to cognition (*buddhi*), the object’s status as a producer, its being a benefactor, and its state as an object (*karmatā*) are nothing other than its being the apprehended (*grāhyatva*), therefore neither the assumption of the form of that [object] nor an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is tenable; thus he says: "due to the connection with the sense-faculties. This is so even though there is no distinction in their being apprehended.
Only that object which is connected with the sense-faculties is apprehended, and nothing else; for it has been said:
"When there is contact of a person's sense-faculties with what is existent, the arising of cognition is perception.
Therefore, because the position of formlessness (*nirākāra*) alone is established by experience and is uncontradicted, its reality is proven.
The position that [cognition] possesses an aspect is indeed erroneous; therefore, the conclusion is that non-duality is not established even in liberation.
But even so, since there is a lack of evidence for the object of cognition in the case of non-momentariness just as there is in the case of momentariness,
it would be of the nature of an error even due to doubt regarding whether it is momentary or non-momentary; thus, in the case of non-momentariness—
He states the proof: "Therefore, even though there is deviation from this recognition, stability is apprehended in some things as being the very nature of the entity. (34)
Not only is stability established in the nature of the grasper itself according to the method previously demonstrated,

but it is also established in the object that is grasped by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*); for there is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) "this is that jar" precisely as something stable, and this is not something that even you yourselves do not determine.
It has already been shown previously that stability regarding objects cannot be denied. Now, one might argue:

"In the case of hair, nails, and so forth, which grow back after being cut, the perception of stability must be based on similarity. To this he replies: "But in some cases, there is deviation due to the force of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*)."

Even though there is another object that is uncontradicted, since there is no sublater for the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of silver when there is real silver, there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). If it is argued that "in this case too, there will be a sublatant means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," [the author] says "no," because it is impossible, stating "that which is apprehended. This is because of this stability (*sthairya*).

By perception (*pratyakṣa*), which grasps the actual object (*vastu*), [the object] is indeed grasped beforehand, just like blue and so forth; for if the nature of the object were not grasped when it is determined (*adhyavasita*), there would certainly be a sublation (*bādha*), as in the case of mother-of-pearl being determined as silver or the determination of the stability of hair and nails, but this does not occur when [the object] has been grasped.

Because, as in the case of the determination of blue, there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress. Now, one might object that since stability consists in pervading multiple points of time, its apprehension by perception—which grasps only the present—is not possible; to this he says: "because the thing exists as its own nature."

Stability, too, consists in nothing other than the very nature of the thing itself; for if it were not its nature, stability would be impossible for that thing, and every object would be seen as having a form that perishes at every moment, like a rapid stream of water emerging from the mouth of a canal. Thus [the opponent argues].
There is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*), because an object is apprehended precisely as having a stable nature. As it has been said:
"For when silver is being apprehended, it is apprehended as persisting for a long time.
Nor is it tenable to claim that the cognition of stability is an error arising from the production of successive, similar [moments].
To say this is also unestablished; for this [argument] would only be tenable if momentariness were established.

Yet, up to the present day, it has not been established for anyone what its nature is or by which means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) it is established. Nor can it be maintained that even the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing is not apprehended when the thing itself is apprehended.
Because there is no difference [between them] when it comes to speaking. As you yourselves have said:
"When the single nature of an object is itself directly perceived, what other part could there be that is not seen and yet must be examined by means of valid cognitions?"

Thus, even perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not [establish the object's permanence], because although it grasps only the present, its nature is stable; furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the contact between sense organ and object is present, but neither the object nor the cognition thereof is perceived, since that cognition has the self as its very nature. || 34 ||
He demonstrates this very point: "For when the nature of an object is grasped again and again by a single cognition, then tell us, by what can its stability be prevented? (35)
For in this way, even for Bodhisattvas, when their wives, mothers, and so forth, or their teachers, servants, and so forth, are seen again and again, appropriate conduct toward them is justified;
otherwise, there would indeed be a reversal. [Objection: But is it not the case that motherhood belongs to the continuum?
If it is argued that it is "the state of being the wife," we say no; for even that, in reality, is impossible apart from the possessor of the continuum (*santānin*).
Since the motherhood belongs only to that very momentary entity (*kṣaṇa*) from which [the child] is born, that alone must be accepted as such.
Therefore, regarding the fifth moment, the rule applies: "the fifth [mother] from the maternal relatives."

If [the status of] being a wife were to arise from mere conduct, it would be entirely consistent with your own view; thus, the animals—who are devoted solely to the actions prescribed by your doctrine—have already won. Or else, how could there be stability in mountains and such things, which always appear in a single, unchanging form? (35)

An objection is raised: "But surely, even in the case of mountains and the like, there is necessarily a distinction [of the mountain] due to the presence of contradictory properties such as coldness and heat produced by winter and summer; therefore, stability is untenable. To this, he says:
There is no distinction based on the difference between cold and so forth without a cognition of distinction;

for there is no [distinction] in the mountain-soul— which is manifested by, or produced from, cold, heat, and so on— just as there is none in the cold and heat themselves that consist of summer, winter, and the like.

The distinction of intrinsic nature occurs either simultaneously— as in the case of a cognition with an aspect (*sākārajñāna*)— or sequentially, as in the case of form and so forth, which are bound by a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrīpratibaddha*), because they possess a manifold yet unitary intrinsic nature. For a cognition of a jar or similar object, though unitary, possesses multiple forms and is indeed bound by a single causal complex.

You have already accepted that [the object] has a nature consisting of multiple contributions, such as form and so forth; otherwise, due to the conceptualization of a distinction for every individual atom, the appearance of a gross form would be impossible because of the lack of multiple contributions, and consequently, the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) could not be established.

It was stated that there would be the consequence of the non-arising of a specific effect; likewise here as well, there is no contradiction because one accepts that [the entity] possesses, sequentially, multiple forms and multiple natures of assistance.
But [one might object]: how can there be multiple forms and multiple powers of assistance therein simultaneously?

Unity is appropriate in the case of a collection (*samuccaya*) and the like; however, in the case of succession (*krama*), because mutual exclusion is necessarily present, there is only difference (*bheda*). Even in that case, it is precisely through mutual exclusion that [properties such as] broad bases and bellies, or multiple capacities for assistance, [are established].

Because [the whole] persists; otherwise, the mass would appear as nothing more than a mere atom, and even the collection of color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities would produce only a single effect—thus everything would be inconsistent. Therefore, in that case, the one [whole] possesses multiple forms and is endowed with the power for multiple auxiliary functions.

Just as that [simultaneous perception] is logically possible because of such an inherent nature (*tathāsvabhāvatva*), so too here, for one who perceives even a mountain or similar object as being unitary, stable in form, and possessing an inherent nature such that it possesses multiple forms and multiple capacities for assistance sequentially,
its existence is established; thus, due to the impossibility of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmāyoga*), there is no distinction based on coldness and so forth.
Furthermore, difference exists only where there is a distinct cognition, as in the case of a jar and a cloth;
whereas where cognition is non-distinct, there is non-difference, as in the case of a cognition having the form of a jar—thus there is no contradiction. As it has been said by you yourselves:

"For one whose sensation is undivided, that which is not so must indeed possess division. If this [sensation] were not established as a means of proof, then the proof for division would not be established.
Thus, having provisionally accepted [the opponent's position], he states the division based on the distinction between cold and so forth:
And as long as there is non-difference from that [object], so long is non-difference established. || 36 ||
Just as there is a distinction between cold and heat produced by the differences of cold, heat, and so forth,

even though mountains and the like are distinct, for as long as there is no difference in the cold characterized by winter or in the heat characterized by summer, for that long there is non-difference; likewise, there is stability in the mountains and such.
By what could this be prevented? For it is through the conjunction of contradictory properties that difference is established;
yet that [difference] does not exist for such a duration of time. Thus, stability for that duration of time is indeed proven. || 36 ||
"Surely, since it must perish by its very nature from another [cause], it would perish even earlier due to this lack of distinction;
thus, momentariness is established. To this, he says:
"But when something dissimilar arises, that [previous state] ceases because of the cause."
The destruction of the conscious self and likewise the birth of that which is insentient; || 37 ||

Therefore, when from that mountain or other object— which possesses the nature of coldness— another very different object possessing the property of heat arises due to auxiliary conditions such as sunlight, then that [heat] exists prior to that very cause, namely the sunlight and so forth.

The nature of coldness in mountains and such things is set aside through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because it is understood in that way; it is not [set aside] by nature alone. Therefore, how can there be the consequence of momentariness?
Furthermore, we shall explain later how defects such as the incapacity or futility of a cause of destruction are not [actual] faults. From that...

And for this reason, at that time, even the cognition of recognition ceases there, since there arises from it the birth of mountains and the like—which are insentient, distinct, and characterized by heat.
And this very thing they call the transformation of attributes (*dharmapariṇāma*) for those who maintain the doctrine of stability. || 37 ||
Now, how does this single [cause] produce these three distinct effects? To this he says:
"And by its own nature (*svabhāvena*), there would be no variety anywhere in existence.
If this were not admitted, then in this entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), by its own nature—

If manifoldness—the capacity to perform multiple effects—did not belong to anything at all, then even a lamp and the like would not produce their various effects, such as burning the wick and consuming the oil; this would contradict direct perception.
Therefore, this must necessarily be accepted.
Furthermore, on the view that all things are momentary, the relationship between cause and effect cannot be known;
thus he says:
"Since prior and subsequent moments are not cognized, how can there be the state of being cause and effect? (38)

The doctrine of momentariness is based on the denial of action; thus, the causality of fire and so forth does not arise from its connection with a specific action, but rather from its prior existence, whereas the subsequent existence of smoke and so forth constitutes its effectness.
Furthermore, because these two states of priority and posteriority— like "prior" and "posterior"— are mutually dependent in nature,

they cannot be apprehended at the time of grasping each individual moment; nor is it possible for you to have a separate cognition that grasps both moments, since [all cognitions] lack the persistence of two moments.
Because of the admission of [the existence of] entities, the claim that "the causal relation is established by perception and non-perception" is also untenable. || 38 ||
