[Objection: But surely, since the momentary fire (*vahnikṣaṇa*) has smoke as its causal nature (*dhūmahetusvabhāvatva*), when that [smoke] is apprehended, it is already apprehended.

If this is so, then since it also possesses the property of being knowable by an omniscient being (*sarvajñajñeyatva*), it follows that when [the omniscient being] apprehends that [property], he must also apprehend it. [Response: No, because even upon apprehension there is no ascertainment (*aniścaya*). [Objection: No, because of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
Since even certainty is impossible, this [objection] amounts to nothing. However, this fault does not apply to the position that things are non-momentary;
thus he says:
"The causal totality (sāmagrī) is established as manifesting the capacity of that which is of a stable nature."

The causal complex consisting of fire and so forth, being stable, is established as the determiner of its own capacity to produce effects such as smoke that are related to itself; for it is when that [complex] is stable that the discernment of the relation of cause and effect is possible, not when it is momentary— this is the meaning.
He demonstrates this very point: "An object whose capacity is manifested is suitable, however, with respect to the task to be performed. (39)
A causal entity becomes one whose causal capacity is manifested only in relation to an effect that is suitable and non-momentary. || 39 ||

When stability and the perfection of the true mind are established, there is vision both simultaneously and sequentially; likewise, there is authorization and action according to the power of the totality of conditions.

When stability has been established by means of a more firmly grounded proof, then just as simultaneous perception occurs in certain cases— such as at a performance of actors or wrestlers— and sequential perception regarding various objects on a path while walking is likewise possible, so too this [perception] occurs sequentially, while that [other] effect occurs simultaneously.

This is the authorization [of the position]. Furthermore, due to the acquisition of a specific collection of causes, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is possible both simultaneously in some cases and sequentially in others; however, for a momentary entity, there can be no sequence precisely because of its momentariness. Even in the case of simultaneous production, since [the effect] is non-existent prior to its arising, it exists at the same time as the moment of its production.

Furthermore, because there is no possibility of an effect when [the cause] is simultaneous with it, and because for that which has already arisen, destruction follows immediately, purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is simply not possible. Now, one might object: "In the second moment, an effect will arise from it, just as destruction does. If this were so, then because it is separated by destruction, that very [moment]— [...is not the cause].

The word "that" [refers to the cause], because momentariness has not been established; for if the second moment of the jar or other object were to arise from non-existence—which is separated by that [interval]—it would be without a cause, and as it has been stated, it would therefore be either eternally existent or eternally non-existent.
Thus, regarding the momentary...
Because it lacks causal efficiency either successively or simultaneously, there follows the undesirable consequence that it is not a real entity. || 40 ||
Furthermore, regarding the relationship between the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge here, he says:
"And there is no means of knowledge for another [person] for the sake of establishing an object constructed by oneself;
for since everything perishes immediately after its arising due to momentariness, what [means], for whom, or where [could it exist]?"
The establishment of "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and so forth is entirely unestablished.

Now, one might argue that this systematic arrangement of means of valid cognition and the like is merely inferential, constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) arising at a time subsequent to [the perception]. No, because of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
Having stated that [inference] is impossible even for those two, he says—admitting it for the sake of argument:
"Without conceptual construction and the like, there is no object; nor is there a logical mark (liṅga), because it is not an object [of perception]. (41)

Since you accept that [the object] exists as something devoid of meaning due to its lack of an objective referent (*artha*), there is no room here for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and so forth;
by the inclusion of "and so forth," even the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), which consists of the superimposition of a self (*ātma-adhyāropa*), is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is it inference, because you also accept that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), it too is simply without an object (*nirviṣaya*). It is not...
And it is not tenable that [the object] is beyond the scope [of cognition], for it would then be established as being like false knowledge. || 41 ||

Now, one might object: "Since it has been stated that 'the logical mark (liṅga) is said to have a universal (sāmānya) as its object because particulars are not established,' inference is not without an object for us. To this, he says:

For even from what you have stated, there is an awakening regarding that which possesses a universal [property], due to memory and because of certainty; otherwise, neither of these two would exist. (42)

In that case, since the universal would be an object of valid cognition, it would follow— just like the particular— that it possesses existence (*sattva*); consequently, it would also be apprehended by sensory perception (*indriyajñāna*), even though you claim it is not,
because its object is remembered in exactly the same way as "this is a jar," which consists of both the universal and the particular.

Because of this certainty; otherwise, even the existence of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) would not be established. Since both of these would then not be real entities consisting of the universal and the particular, everything would be unestablished. Therefore, the universal must also be accepted as existing. (42)
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: Because it is apprehended in another individual, its distinction [from that] is intended;
therefore, even when an individual perishes, that [universal] remains for that long. (43)
Because that universal is perceived as existing in another individual even when a particular instance has perished,

its stability is established for as long as the destruction of all instances— such as occurs with the universal of "mosquito" and so forth— has not yet taken place; thus, [the claim] that "all conditioned phenomena are momentary" is refuted.
It is indeed sublated. || 43 ||
Now, [the author] says that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the universal (*sāmānya*) is indeed merely imagined:

"Excluding the universal, the individual (*vyakti*) does not accomplish human enjoyment. For pleasure and so forth are experienced in two ways: as pertaining to sense objects (*vaiṣayika*) and as consisting of self-conceit (*ābhimānika*). Among these, [pleasure pertaining to sense objects...]
It has been established that the former [cognition] is produced by the contact of cold and so forth, and has as its cause only the particular (svalakṣaṇa);

however, the latter, because it consists of conceptual determination (adhyavasāya) arising from conceit (abhimāna), is established as having as its object things such as kingdoms, which are capable of being reflected upon in terms of priority and posteriority. And it is not the case that...

If you maintain that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) exists as it truly is, then it is indeed caused by the universal (*sāmānya*); therefore, because it establishes pleasure and so forth, the universal—just like the particular—is not a non-entity.

If it is argued that the causality for that [cognition] belongs to the cognition itself and not to the universal, we say no; for it is just like the case of the object which is the particular characteristic.

Even for a cognition whose object is a universal, since it consists essentially in the manifestation of pleasure and so forth, and because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself, the object alone is the cause.
Now, he addresses those who seek to prove momentariness on the grounds that [otherwise] the causes of destruction would be either incapable or redundant:
"Because the destruction of an object arises from the destruction of its cause and so forth, and not by way of its own nature. (44)

Because of the aforementioned stability established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is the destruction of the object through the destruction of its cause, just as a phlegmatic disease is destroyed by the destruction of the phlegm and so forth.

By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is meant that [destruction occurs] from the cause of destruction; and in some cases, destruction arises from the cause itself, and thus [it occurs] from the cause of destruction.
Because [destruction] occurs due to the presence of external factors such as a mallet for a jar and the like, and not from its own nature alone;
for if it were due to its own nature, then since that nature would be without distinction, destruction would be established even prior [to the impact], whereby momentariness would be proven. || 44 ||

Now, do the causes of destruction produce its destruction as something non-different or different from it? If it is non-different, then destruction is simply the entity itself; and since that is produced by its own cause alone, those [causes of destruction] would be useless. Even if it is different, one must state whether destruction is a non-entity or an entity.

In that regard, because a non-entity is absolutely non-existent, it is impossible to act upon it; therefore, those [causes] lack capacity due to being ineffective. However, if it were an entity, then this [destruction] would be a different thing from the jar, like a cloth, and thus could not be its destruction. Thus [it is argued].

As before, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its being perceived. [Objection: This consequence does not arise because that [destruction] has been produced as having the nature of the pot’s destruction. [Reply: No, because the pot itself has not been produced. [Objection: Then its destruction will occur from that [cause]. [Reply: No, for in that case too the same consequence applies, leading to an infinite regress (anavasthā). Therefore, [destruction] is indeed causeless.

Destruction must be admitted; and since it is impossible for there to be a restriction of place and time for that which is causeless, the destruction [of things] at every moment is established. Therefore, he says:
"Nor is destruction ever causeless, as is the case with functional entities."

The destruction of entities is not causeless, because it follows the positive and negative concomitance of causes such as a mallet, just like their arising. For this very reason, it is not a non-entity; rather, it is indeed an entity consisting of shards and so forth. Indeed, the destruction of a jar and the like consists in its becoming the nature of shards and so forth.
Nothing else is established by direct perception, because that [other entity] lacks substantial reality and thus falls outside the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it has been said:
"Just as a snake’s coiled state or the collective state of scattered parts, so too do some explain the birth and destruction of existing things."
If this were so, then destruction would be said to be merely an effect (*kārya*). It is not so, because it is a transformation (*vikāritva*);

for an effect, such as a jar, is established as having the capacity to hold water and so forth while its form remains unaltered, whereas destruction is a transformation characterized by the attainment of another state. This very [distinction] constitutes the relationship between the original material and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*).

The great-minded ones think thus: even the world says that milk which has turned sour is "lost. But when curd is produced, what has happened to the milk such that it is no longer perceived? This is merely the talk of fools; it is indeed destruction. Because it has been destroyed, it is not perceived; for it has been stated that curd consists of the very nature of that destruction.

[Objection: Is it not the case that non-existence (*abhāva*) consists precisely in the cessation of an entity (*bhāvanivṛtti*), since we observe it to be so even in cases such as "there is no jar here"? [Reply: True; however, destruction (*nāśa*) does not consist of that [mere cessation], but rather is of the nature of another entity (*vastvantara*), as has been stated, being established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Non-existence, on the other hand, is merely the cessation of an entity, because it is absolutely non-substantial (*atyantāvastutva*).
It is not even an object of valid cognition;

rather, in cases such as "there is no jar here," it is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whose fruit is purely conventional usage, consisting in the discernment of an error regarding the association with other objects restricted by place and so forth. As it has been said by you yourselves:

"Because non-existence lacks the nature of form, those words which express the form of non-existence are established as denoters of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) without even being suspected [of denoting a positive entity].
Thus, it is not that non-existence is an effect; rather, it is only non-existence, whose nature is the absence of an object, [that is so].
The fault is that the cause of destruction is either incapable or redundant.

But for those [who hold] that destruction is indeed the very nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, an entity perishes solely due to its own nature of destruction and not from another cause, because it is impossible to destroy that which does not possess such a nature; and for this very reason...
The non-deviation between being produced and impermanence is established because of their identity (*tādātmya*), and not otherwise.
As it has been said:
"Because destruction is causeless, it is necessarily connected to its own nature."
For it is not necessarily accepted that dependent phenomena must exist.
To those who say this, he replies:
"Nor is it non-different from the object, because it is not perceived as having the nature of an object. (45)

For whatever is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an object is necessarily established when that object is established, just as "treeness" is established when "śiṃśapā-ness" is established. However, that which is not established when another is established cannot be its intrinsic nature, just as "cowness" is not the intrinsic nature of "treeness. Furthermore, upon the establishment of an object, there is neither its destruction nor [the emergence of] a non-entity (*avastu*).

That [duality] is perceived within the self as being absolutely contradictory, because their coexistence is impossible due to their mutual exclusion. As it was stated by the Teacher in the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikā*:

"Two contradictory properties, existing at the same time and residing in a single substratum, bring about their own disappearance through mutual destruction. Thus, because [the second] does not arise when that [first] has been produced, destruction is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the object. But surely, in the case of a second...
At that moment, it exists for him—how then could it be without intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), precisely because it is an effect? [Objection:
But surely, its being described as an intrinsic nature is due to its independence from other causes.
[Reply: In that case, this would be a conventional (*sāmayika*) intrinsic nature, and thus no real entity (*vastu*) is established by it, since otherwise it would not be so.

Because it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress; since there is no necessary connection of identity between being produced and destruction, and since you do not necessarily admit their non-identity, the perishability of a produced entity cannot be inferred from its state of being produced.
"Since destruction is not the intrinsic nature [of things], this fault does not apply. If that is so, then you have merely accepted our own position. (45)
And there is no deviation in inference; thus he says:
"Just as that which brings about non-difference proceeds for the sake of establishing the object, so too does it proceed for its destruction; thus the destruction of what has been born arises. (46)

Just as auxiliary causes such as the staff, the wheel, and the string operate for the sake of producing an object like a jar, so too do auxiliary causes such as a mallet operate for the sake of producing its destruction in the form of potsherds and the like— thus, whatever is produced [is subject to destruction].

That which necessarily perishes upon the presence of auxiliary causes, but that which does not perish is not a product—just like the self (ātman) and so forth—is established through the existence of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Therefore, it is logical to infer impermanence from the state of being a product in the case of sound and other such things; it is not [logical] for you, because of the impossibility of establishing negative concomitance (vyatireka).

Because this [reason], being purely positive (*kevalānvayin*), lacks the capacity to prove [the conclusion]. Now, as for what was said— that there is no need for a hammer or other such causes for that which has a perishable nature— that is incorrect, because it is precisely upon the proximity of the hammer and so forth that its nature consists in the transition to another state.

[Objection: But surely, since dependence on something that provides no assistance is illogical, when there is assistance by a hammer or the like, that previous pot has perished by its very nature, and this other one, assisted by it, has arisen; thus, [the pot] is indeed momentary. [Reply: No, for it has already been stated that this is due to its having such a nature. For it possesses such a nature by virtue of its own cause.

An entity is that which, being always unassisted, undergoes modification upon the proximity of a hammer or similar instrument, and not otherwise; in this regard, direct observation alone is the proof. Furthermore, the intrinsic natures of entities do not deserve to be subjected to questioning. By this—

Since a stable entity possesses the nature of performing purposeful action when such auxiliary causes are present, the contradiction regarding the successive performance of purposeful action by that stable entity must be resolved. [Objection: But surely, in the absence of auxiliary causes, its nature is distinct from that which produces [the effect], precisely because it does not produce [it] at that time. [Response: No, for even then—

Because its nature is to produce the effect when the auxiliary causes (sahakārin) are present, and it remains that very same [nature] even when they are absent, there is no difference; for there is no change in its nature throughout the three periods of time,
though due to the absence of the auxiliaries, it does not [produce the effect] previously.
Regarding the arising of an effect: it is only its proximity and non-proximity that differ, not the difference in the entity itself. [Objection:

But then, proximity and non-proximity must produce a difference in the auxiliary causes, since they possess contradictory natures. [Response: There is no contradiction even in that case, for that [difference] also...

When its own auxiliary causes are present, [the cause] possesses the nature of being present together with them; likewise, when those [auxiliaries] have their own auxiliaries present, and so on for each subsequent one, there is no lack of restriction.
This is because the diversity of all things is governed by the restriction of their inherent natures, including that of the auxiliary causes.

When earth and the other [elements] are in proximity with the seed and its causes, that which acts as their cause is indeed similar to them by nature; for it is by virtue of this nature that they produce the effect, such as the sprout, only when those [causes] are present and not at other times— thus, the nature of all these things is to be the producers of that [effect].

"Mutually dependent upon proximity"—thus all causal factors (*kārakas*) are designated as "cooperative" (*sahakārin*), and not individually. Nor is there a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and although they all possess efficacy, there is no contingency of multiple effects arising when they are in mutual proximity.
Because it possesses a nature that accomplishes a single effect; likewise, because in the performance of various distinct purposeful actions,
when various corresponding auxiliary conditions are present,
it possesses a single nature that produces multiple distinct effects in succession.

Even when performing various distinct purposeful actions, there is no difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); for example, just as a single person, Caitra, who performs multiple tasks such as reaping, cooking, and eating, possesses the respective natures of performing those specific acts of reaping, cooking, and so forth, sequentially, depending on the presence of various auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) such as sickles and pots.

Even though there are states such as cutting and cooking, there is no difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because that which possesses such an intrinsic nature exists therein simultaneously, just like a lamp. For a lamp indeed accomplishes multiple effects, such as burning the wick, consuming the oil, providing illumination, and producing self-cognition.

It has already been demonstrated previously that you have accepted an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), but not a difference in intrinsic nature based on a difference in effects; likewise, in this case as well, because a stable entity is never dissociated from its intrinsic nature of performing that effect when its auxiliary causes are present, it must always do so.

However, because the proximity of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) occurs sequentially, even though multiple effects are produced in succession, there is no difference [in the cause], since its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) remains undifferentiated. For the Buddhists, the primary weapon for introducing the meaning of negation (*nañ*) is indeed the establishment of a difference in the essential form (*svarūpa*), and this is not the case here.

For those [entities] whose nature is obscured by phenomena that possess a single, eternal intrinsic nature, that [capacity for causal efficiency] exists; thus, it is not the case that causal efficiency is impossible for a stable entity through either successive or simultaneous action. || 46 ||
[The opponent objects: "Surely destruction will occur even without a cause, from another causal factor, or even from the self (*ātman*) and so forth;
thus, since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established, this reason of yours is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). To this he replies:
"Even if there were a negative concomitance, that object [of the reason] does not arise for him."
What can we do about this contradiction? For when something is directly perceived, no sublation exists. || 47 ||

The destruction of that which is the object of the negation—the self and so forth—is not possible for that which serves as the cause of the negation, because of their mutual contradiction. This is the meaning: when a contradiction with destruction has been established by valid cognition for a particular thing in a certain way, destruction cannot occur for that very thing because of that contradiction, just as [destruction does not occur] for coldness.
The heat arising from another cause, or the cold that is the counteragent of heat, is inferred;
as it has been stated by you yourselves:
"The cognition of contradiction arises because that which possesses its complete causes ceases to exist when another thing is present."

Not for that which is non-contradictory. For the contradiction between a cause and that which possesses origination—such as a jar—and that which possesses a cause is established by perception; therefore, it is proper to conceive such [origination] through inference only in the case of things of that nature, and not in the case of that which is unoriginated and causeless, such as the Self (ātman). Indeed, [inference] does not apply to what is already seen through perception.
In some cases, a deviation [from the rule] might be plausible, because if there were the possibility of smoke and the like occurring even without fire in another location,

it would follow that all inference would cease to exist. Now, if it is argued that this is established by the nature of things— that what does not arise from something cannot arise from it even once— then:

The postulation of causeless destruction for uncreated things such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth is mere conceptual construction; therefore, its exclusion [from the subject] is established, and thus there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*). || 47 ||
He demonstrates this very point:
"Since the state of being produced is pervaded by the presence of a cause for destruction in every entity, it will therefore not deviate from impermanence. (48)

Existence (*bhāva*) is arising (*utpāda*); since destruction pervades every entity that possesses arising— just as heat pervades cold— and because it is established as being omnipresent at all times through a real essential connection (*vāstavapratibandha*), therefore the reason called "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) [is present] in sound and so forth.

It certainly establishes impermanence in the subject (*dharmin*) and is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). As they have said: "Otherwise, what necessity would there be for another [property] to be restricted by others? Or, if it were caused by something else, it would be like a dye on a cloth."
Since attachment is not even inferred in the case of clothing, but rather only the *yogyatā* (capacity) for attachment, there is indeed no deviation [in the logical reason].

If this were so, one might argue that some produced thing would not perish; this is not the case, because it is precisely for this reason that the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is established. Furthermore, what is to be proven is its capacity for destruction, not destruction itself; thus it has been stated.
And its non-deviation is indeed certain. For just as when there is an inference regarding the seed's capacity to produce a sprout,

even if the sprout is sometimes not produced due to being eaten by crows or other causes, the inference remains unimpaired— because its purpose is merely to exclude absolute incapacity, just as in the case of a jar or similar objects.

Likewise, here, in order to refute the notion that objects such as a jar are incapable of absolute destruction—just as the self (ātman) and other such entities are held to be—their susceptibility to destruction is inferred. For this very reason, the treatises on political ethics (nītiśāstra) engage in matters such as the protection of property, and experts in statecraft are seen to be skillful; it would not be otherwise. Thus, there is no fault. || 48 ||

Thus, since momentariness is not established even for the nature of the subject (*grāhaka*), the status of being an enjoyer of the fruits of activity— which was introduced by the words of the introductory aphorism and pertains to results in this life— has been explained. Now, [regarding] "the person who..."

To those who, in order to explain these two lines, claim that the mere aggregate of the senses is conscious and that there is no other entity called a "person" (puruṣa), because the notion of "I" is observed only therein— he says in response:
"The cognition 'I am' regarding the body should indeed be understood as being like [the cognition] regarding a beloved woman."
For the man knows indeed that she is the means for his enjoyment. || 49 ||

It has been stated that consciousness is established by experience as being witnessed by itself; however, if it is asserted that this very [consciousness] is the body in the form of an aggregate of sense organs, let it have that other name—it is not a different thing from it, and there is no dispute among the learned regarding a mere name. Now, if...
If it is argued that the collection of the eye and other organs is inferred as an instrument for the conscious self— since the perception of form and so forth would otherwise be impossible— then,
because that collection is established merely as an instrument, it cannot be established as having the nature of a conscious agent.
The status of being the object of the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) previously demonstrated is logical [only for the Self], because of its absolute difference [from the body]. Now, one might argue:

"Just as in the expression 'the self kills itself by means of the self,' a distinction between agent, instrument, and so forth may exist here even though there is no real difference, being merely conceptualized. True, this would be the case if its non-difference from consciousness were established.
However, since difference alone is established by the aforementioned inference, this [claim] is incorrect. Now, one might argue:
"But non-difference will be established here by such scriptural texts as, 'I am the eye, I am the ear, I am the body of all the senses,' and so forth."

Just as in the case of [the statements] "I am the wife," "I am the son," "I am the cow and the horse," or "I am the riches," the scripture can be justified even in a figurative sense because it contradicts direct perception and other means of knowledge; therefore, the position that the sense organs possess consciousness is utterly untenable. (49)
Regarding the position that consciousness is an emergent property of the elements (bhūta-caitanyavāda), he says:
"But the nature of consciousness has a distinct characteristic from earth and the other elements, as well as from that which is non-conscious;

for it is through the perception of this [consciousness] that there is doubt regarding earth and the rest, whereas it remains established within itself even prior to the manifestation of those [elements]. (50)

An object whose nature consists of consciousness—that is, whose form is conscious—is not logically the nature of non-conscious things such as earth and the like, because its characteristic is distinct from theirs. What is meant by this is that, since consciousness and non-consciousness possess stable characteristics that are mutually exclusive, like a jar and its absence, they cannot be one and the same. Furthermore:

Since a doubt regarding the existence of consciousness (cidbhāva)— that is, a doubt concerning its being— is observed in relation to that perception which has earth and so forth as its object, namely, the perceptual cognition of earth and so forth,
therefore there is no identity between the two; for that which is of the nature of one thing is not necessarily determined by the ascertainment of the other.

Just as clay and so forth are [the material cause] in the determination of a jar; whereas that which, in the determination of something, stands in the relation of being the subject of a conflicting opinion, is not of the nature of that thing—just as a *piśāca* is not [of the nature] of the determination of a jar—and likewise, in the determination of earth and so forth in the form of a body, the conscious entity (*cidrūpa*) remains doubtful. Thus.
It is not of that nature. Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), for the nature of another's consciousness is established through inference consisting of the activities of body and speech;
since that very nature of consciousness, by the aforementioned method, exists as the subject (*grāhaka*) of that which is its prior and fresh form.
Manifestation (*vyakti*) is luminosity; therefore, it exists as distinct from one's own body—the earth and so forth—which, by its very nature, is graspable by itself and appears as an external form.
It is distinguished from the form of one's own body, which is characterized by functions such as retention (*dhāraṇā*), and from the elements such as earth.

The meaning is this: since this object, which is of the nature of the grasper and is absolutely distinct from the fivefold graspable self, is established by itself (*svataḥsiddha*), it does not have the elements (*bhūta*) as its intrinsic nature. For this very reason, its meaning is not already covered by the refutation of the Lokāyata school; for in that system, [the mind] is held to be impermanent because it is an effect of the elements.
This has been refuted; here, the distinction is that although there is permanence like that of the primary elements (bhūta), it does not possess the nature of those [elements]. || 50 ||
However, the Sāṅkarṣaṇa-Pāñcarātrikas, who maintain that consciousness belongs to the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), say:

"Even though you [the Naiyāyikas] postulate a person (puruṣa), you have indeed accepted the internal organ as being endowed with the eight attributes such as dharma and knowledge; therefore, it is this very internal organ that is established for both disputants."

Let it be accepted that the nature of the self is knowledge (*jñāna*), because a self consisting of non-knowledge (*ajñāna*) distinct from that is not established; furthermore, if the self were knowledge, there would be the undesirable consequence of experiencing two cognitions, which contradicts direct perception. To those [who hold such views], he says:
Because it is insentient, consciousness does not reside within the internal organ.
This would be the case if we had accepted that the internal organ is sentient;
however, because it is an effect, like a jar and so forth, it is indeed insentient. Nor is its status as an effect unestablished.

For you also accept that [consciousness] as an effect produced by great power (*mahāvibhūti*). If it is then argued that this [consciousness] is something other than that and is eternal, then it follows that this is simply the self (*ātman*) established;
thus, the doctrine of the sentience of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-caitanyavāda*) is not tenable.
To the question, "How then is it that you have stated that knowledge is an attribute (dharma) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)? he says:
"Because it is the ground for the manifestation of consciousness, its modification (vṛtti) is called knowledge. (51)
Since it is by means of this [modification] that a person cognizes an object not present at hand— such as in memory or mental intuition—

the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) only figuratively, and not in its primary sense; for, because the Self whose nature is consciousness is unchanging, the formation of impressions (*saṃskāra*) is impossible for it, and thus at that time, the object—

And because it is impossible for the form being experienced to arise [from anything else], one must admit that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) itself takes on the form of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*); for this reason,
even its nature as merit (*dharma*) and so forth belongs to the internal organ by virtue of its taking the form of those impressions, and not otherwise.

We have already explained at length in the *Svāyambhuvodyota* that [the self] does not consist of dharma and so forth, which are of the nature of ritual acts such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*; this should be understood from that very source. Thus, since knowledge is not admitted to belong to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which possesses dharma and the like, it is established that the Person alone is of the nature of knowledge; hence the phrase "that person" (*yaḥ pumān*).

The two preceding words have been explained. Previously, it was stated that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the non-difference of the person; now, however, he states the means of valid cognition for establishing their difference:
Since pleasure and the other qualities are perceived as distinct within each respective substrate at one and the same time, it is therefore accepted that [the substrate] is composed of atoms.

For by means of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), within each body one's own self is simultaneously perceived as the experiencer of pleasure and so forth, and [the existence of] another self endowed with suffering and so forth is inferred through the movements and other signs of that other body; yet the inferrer is not the object of inference, nor is the inferrer the object of inference.
Thus it has been stated that [the two] can only arise simultaneously because they are absolutely distinct. Therefore, their difference alone is logical.

Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that the state of being an inferer of another's self is either unestablished or non-existent at that time, because it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), just like the manifestation of pleasure and so forth. Nor...
That [self], having that [body] as its object, is real because there is no sublation [of it], just like pleasure and so forth; thus, the distinction of selves is indeed real. || 52 ||
In this regard, the Vedāntins state the intention of the opponent:
"The distinction among pleasure and the other [feelings] does not arise from a difference in their essence, but rather from a difference in their causes;
for if there were a [real] distinction..."
Even though the self is one in each individual body, just as for a person whose body is being scorched by the summer heat,
when the lower part of the body suddenly plunges into very cold water,
there arise simultaneously pleasure and pain in the upper and lower parts respectively, due to the difference in their respective causes such as heat and water.
"It will be that very same consciousness even when the body is divided.
To this, he gives the following reply:
"In that case, there would be a single consciousness for all [experiences of] suffering and so forth. (53)
Just as, because the self is one, a single cognition is experienced as having multiple objects such as pleasure and pain in each individual body, so too, if there were only one self in all bodies,
then there would be only a single cognition having all pleasures, pains, and other objects as its domain.

Because the self (*ātman*) is of that very nature, it follows that everyone would be omniscient, since there is no mutual distinction [between selves]. If it is argued that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is indeed one and that distinction is based on delusion (*bhrānti*), we say no, because that is unproven (*asiddhatvāt*). Is it not the case that in dreams and similar states, a distinction based on that [consciousness] is indeed established?
As it has been said:
"If there were no person in a dream to serve as an illustration for this error,
who could say that [the object] appears truly in a form other than its own?"

No; for even there, because consciousness is free from error regarding its own nature, the distinction between the cognitions of pleasure and so forth in each individual body is indeed real, just as in the waking state. For every erroneous cognition is erroneous only with respect to its objective support (*ālambana*), not with respect to itself. The objective support...

For otherwise, that which exists externally in one way yet is perceived in another way becomes the object of error. However, an entity whose very nature is pure cognition shines forth exactly as it is;
thus, while being self-evident, that which lacks such a nature [is not so], and therefore its own nature resides within itself.
Thus, there is no difference in the experience of pleasure and so forth;

however, because that which resides in another's body— which is established through inference— is perceived as distinct from the inferrer precisely by virtue of being an object of inference, it has been stated that the distinction between selves is indeed real.

But surely, because difference depends upon mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), and because perception has non-existence as its object, difference is not cognizable through the perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*). As it has been said:
"The wise declare that perception is an affirmer, not a negator."

Difference does not depend upon mutual non-existence; rather, it is when difference is established that the establishment of mutual non-existence follows. For if everything were one, there would be no non-existence of anything with respect to anything else;
thus, why would one seeking a jar turn away upon seeing a cloth? Furthermore, the distinction between valid and invalid means of knowledge would not exist.

It might be argued that [the self] is real because it never deviates from mere existence; thus, manifesting through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as non-different from one's own self by way of being the inferrer of another's self, it is indeed real.
For that which is established by self-awareness cannot be a non-entity, because it is not cognizable by another, just like Brahman. Therefore, the selves are indeed distinct.
Success! 53.

Those who have mastered the Vedānta, as well as the followers of the Saṃhitās and Pāñcarātra, say: it is true that the individual souls (jīvātman) are indeed distinct; however, they [arise] from the supreme cause denoted by the term Brahman, which is imperishable, or rather, they are non-pervasive (avyāpaka), like jars and other objects, [originating] from that which is called Nārāyaṇa.
"They arise with the nature of dissolving back into their own causes"—refuting even this by means of inference, he says:
"The person (puruṣa) arises from consciousness alone; he is neither subject to modification nor is he non-omnipresent."
Because it is necessarily non-pervasive, subject to modification, and insentient. || 54 ||

That which is conscious is neither non-pervasive nor of the nature of dissolution, such as the supreme cause; whereas that which is non-pervasive and of the nature of dissolution is not conscious, such as a jar or similar objects; and this self, which is conjoined with the vital breath called *jīva*, is indeed conscious.

Since you yourselves have accepted that [space and time] are established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it is not logical for their nature to be non-pervasive or subject to dissolution; rather, their nature is indeed eternal and pervasive, because they always manifest as delimited by them [space and time] due to their being the perceivers. For indeed...

It has been stated that the apprehender (*grāhaka*) can be delimited by the apprehended (*grāhya*), such as a jar or the like. Furthermore, for space (*dik*) and time (*kāla*) as well, no other connection is possible with an essence consisting solely of being an apprehender, apart from their status as apprehended objects. This is what was said:
"That entity whose existence is not delimited by space or time is held to be eternal and all-pervading; thus, the self is [described as] all-pervading and eternal."

[Objection: In that case, because the Self is all-pervasive, there could be no such cognition as "this object is far away," nor can it be said that [the distance] is relative to the body, since the body is not the knower. This is an understatement;

rather, one must state the consequence that [the Self] would be omniscient with respect to everything. [Reply: No, for [the distance] is like that of the sun's heat and so forth in relation to a cloud.

Because an obscuration of consciousness is possible. If this is so, then since that [obscuration] is removed precisely in its own place by means of the body, the organs, and so forth, its manifestation occurs; thus, with respect to this manifestation, the appearance of distance or non-distance is indeed logical, and there is no fault. || 54 ||

Although you have presented the following inference: "Even though this self is non-pervasive and has the nature of dissolution, it is not omniscient because it lacks the perception of all objects, like a jar," that too is incorrect; thus he says:

In the case of a probans that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatirekin), because you do not perceive all objects, both [the presence of the probans in the subject and its absence from the dissimilar instances] are doubtful for you. (55)
Because there is no perception of all objects even when a correct reason (*samyag-hetu*) possessing positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) exists—

this being your intended position— the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) for another person is unestablished (*asiddhi*), since the supreme cause, namely God and the liberated souls, possesses an eternal and omnipresent nature.
Because [the reason] is not admitted by oneself, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.

And since that [negative concomitance] is doubtful, there is doubt regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) as well—just as in the case of "prior" and "subsequent"—because it consists of a relationship between two related entities.
Consequently, as in the example "He possesses cows because he possesses horses," there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*); thus, it is not a valid reason. This also applies to...

Some have stated the reason [for the non-existence of the self] as follows: "Because the individual selves (*jīvātman*) are not all-pervasive and possess the nature of dissolution, they are endowed with existence (*sattā*) and other qualities, just like a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth. However, this reason is likewise unestablished (*asiddha*), because the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the selves is not established.
For a positive concomitance can only be grasped when the object of apprehension has attained the status of an objective case (*karman*); and the self cannot [be so apprehended] by itself.

In this way, it becomes an object of apprehension within itself, because of the contradiction in an action operating upon its own self; for it has been stated that it always shines forth as the very nature of the subject (*grāhaka*) by virtue of its primordial form.
Now, one might object: "But surely its continuity will also occur through that very same form. No.

Because that [consciousness] is the object of the manifestation of multiple perceivers, and because in the self-awareness of each individual self, the awareness of another perceiver is not possible— since that other would be distinct from it and thus "other" (paratva) like a jar or similar objects; for selves, which consist of nothing but their own self-awareness, do not intermingle with one another.

It has been stated that this would entail the absurd consequence that everyone would be omniscient. Furthermore, if each [consciousness] were aware only of itself, what could be related to what? If it is argued that the omniscient one will grasp all selves, that too is incorrect, because there is a deviation in the case of the omniscient self itself; for that [self] also [knows] only by means of its own self-awareness.

Since it appears as the grasper precisely through its distinction from other selves, and it has been stated that no continuity is possible in the grasper; nor can erroneous apprehension occur on the part of one who is omniscient,
just as he [apprehends] his own self as distinct from other selves.

There is no fault in this: for those other selves, whose nature is absolutely non-concomitant [with one another] and who do not exist [as a single entity], are grasped by perception through error; likewise, being mutually distinct and existing beyond the state of being objects of a unifying synthesis (*samanvaya*), they are directly perceived by that [perception]. Thus, there is no defect.

For this very reason, even the co-presence (*anvaya*) of selves cannot exist within the object of inference (*anumeya*); for at that time, the object of inference appears to the inferrer (*anumātr*) precisely through its dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśya*) to the nature of the inferrer—just like one's own self—and because other selves are inferred only as being absolutely dissimilar to oneself. If that is so, then the self would be non-existent.
Because it is not accompanied by [the universal] existence (*sattā*), like a horse's horn, it does not possess existence through the accompaniment of *sattā*;

rather, it possesses existence by virtue of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpasattva*), like *sattā* itself or the Supreme Cause (*paramakāraṇa*). For even that [Supreme Cause], because it is accompanied by *sattā*, lacks the status of being the Supreme Cause due to its being an effect. How then [is it so]?
In the absence of a positive concomitance (anvaya),
the application of the term "self" to all selves occurs by way of similarity, just as the word "supreme self" is applied to Brahman.
But surely even that cannot be grasped within its own self, which is by nature ungraspable?

True; however, for the sake of conventional usage, setting aside dissimilarity, it is said to exist there in some way through a lack of extreme distance, but not from the perspective of ultimate reality—that which is heard as "no."

"No, such is the nature of the Self"—this has been demonstrated by us in detail in the *Rauravavṛttiviveka* and the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikās*; therefore, it should be understood from those very sources.
Thus, since this reason called "concomitance" (*anvaya*) is unestablished, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpakatva*) regarding the nature of dissolution (*layasvabhāvatva*).

It is logical to infer [the existence of] souls; thus, by the reasoning already stated, they must be accepted as having the nature of being eternal and all-pervasive. If this is so, then because of the presence of all souls in all bodies, there would be a confusion of experiences. No, because [experience] is restricted by karma. But does that [confusion] not apply to them as well?

This is not a fault; for there is a distinction due to the difference in agents. Indeed, agency varies with respect to each individual because of its connection with the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*); it is not possible for one who possesses the desire to act in one thing to possess the desire to act in another.
Furthermore, we shall explain that their agency consists precisely in that desire to act. || 55 ||
Now, in order to establish the agency of the self (ātman) with respect to the Sāṅkhya school, he says:

"Because of the awareness 'It was done by me,' 'I am doing this,' and 'I shall do that,' and because of the authority of the Veda, the atom-like [self] possesses an agency-power that extends across the three periods of time. (56)

First of all, this agency (kartṛtva), characterized by independence as the cause for the engagement and withdrawal of all other causal factors, effects the vibration of the body and senses as well as the effort of the vital breaths and so forth;
it is thus the very agent of every action, whether visible or invisible in its fruit, such as agriculture or the Agnihotra sacrifice.

It cannot be said that the Self, while performing actions, does not exist as something being experienced; for it is experienced as the knower within the self (*adhyātma*) by virtue of its nature as the immediate subject (*pratyagrūpa*) who impels all causal factors from the body downwards. Indeed, if the state of being a knower were not the inherent nature of the inner self, there would be nothing else [to account for it].

It has been stated that there is a cause; for you yourselves accept the authority of the Veda on the grounds that it teaches the duty to be performed by a specific qualified person, as in the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Furthermore, this does not apply to one who is a non-agent, being like a stone.

The teaching regarding agency establishes its own validity as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); furthermore, since that [teaching] would otherwise be inexplicable as a valid cognition, it cannot be asserted that a person lacks the capacity for agency. Moreover, that [agency] exists because it is the very nature of the eternal self, as evidenced by the persistence [of the sense] "I have done this" and so forth at all times.

Because it is the object of apprehension (*parāmarśa*), it must be accepted as eternal, just like the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*). Now, the Sāṃkhyas argue that agency belongs to *prakṛti* alone, and its superimposition upon the self occurs due to non-discrimination (*aviveka*) from it. If this were so, then the state of being a knower would also belong to *prakṛti* alone; thus, the doctrine of a distinct self (*vyatiriktātmavāda*) would be rendered useless. But [it may be objected]: [The text continues: "But..."

Since this *prakṛti*, which consists of effects, causes, and so forth, is established as being always an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), its status as a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is simply not tenable. If that is the case, since it is likewise established as an effect, its status as an agent (*kartṛtva*) is also not tenable. No; for *prakṛti* [is an agent] with respect to its own effects.
Because agency is admitted [for it]. As it has been said: "From primordial matter (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat), and from that, the I-maker (ahaṅkāra).
No; for while it possesses the status of a material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) due to its insentience (jaḍatva), it does not possess agency (kartṛtva) therein; for [agency] is indeed something else.
The state of being a material cause (*upādānakāraṇatva*), which consists in the transformation of one's own nature (*svarūpānyathābhāva*),

is established by direct perception (*adhyakṣasiddha*) in the case of milk, curd, and so forth— due to their very nature as insentient entities— as being invariably concomitant with changeability (*pariṇāmitva*) and other such properties; and furthermore, [it is] otherwise.

Agency consists in independence, characterized by the desire to obtain the beneficial and avoid the harmful as the fruit of action; it is the cause of the engagement and withdrawal of all other causal factors,
is inseparable from the conscious reality, and is established through self-awareness— thus, agency too [is inherent].
In this regard, since [the status of] being a knower is unestablished [in the case of the senses], it is indeed a property of the self (*ātman*). As it has been said:
"That which is the lord over the engagement and withdrawal of the causal factors—whether remaining inactive or active—is called the agent (*kartṛ*), the causal factor."

[Objection: Since agency (*kartṛtva*), being of the nature of non-cognition, cannot be established as self-evident (*svasaṃvedya*), it cannot be a property of the Self (*ātmadharma*), just like a jar or other such objects. [Response: If that were so, then the same consequence would apply to eternality, omnipresence, and so forth, which are likewise established as properties of that [Self]; thus, there would be no-self (*nairātmya*). [Reply: No, because of that...

If it is argued that [agency] is established as non-different from [consciousness], just like the light of the sun, then—just as the power of burning is non-different from the light of the sun—the agency of the conscious self is likewise non-different from consciousness and is established by its own self-awareness; therefore, it does not have a nature other than that [consciousness]. As it has been said in the *Mokṣakārikās*:
"The power of the Wielder of the Trident is one alone, consisting of the nature of all knowledge and action;
yet it is sung as threefold—Vāmā and the others—due to the differentiation of its functions. (56)
Moreover:
if there were a single agent in the form of the seed, there would be the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done;
likewise, if Prakṛti alone—the self-nature that is the material cause of the world—were the sole agent.

Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that, due to the activity of cooking and so forth, there would be an absence of the self-referential awareness of agency— such as "this rice and so forth was made by me"— as residing within the self; furthermore, there would be the arrival of uncreated rice and so forth from some source, like something brought forth by a magician, such that for everyone, at all times, and in every place...
If there were such a practice [of recollection], then even when the fruit of an action has been seen, it would follow that there is an absence of recognition, which contradicts experience.
Here, he states the opponent's intention:
If it is argued that there would be the consequence of transformation for the person (puruṣa) in the case of his being an agent— since agency consists in the nature of movement—
he refutes this as follows:
Not so, because it is not observed in the case of jewels and the like. || 57 ||
Agency is not of the nature of vibration, because vibration is of the nature of action; nor is the agent of the nature of action.
Rather, he possesses the capacity for it, just as a magnet possesses the capacity to produce vibration in iron.
Thus we have stated elsewhere:
"The power that belongs to the movements and actions of inert things is [the power] of the self as agent;
through its pervasiveness, it is established by itself in an immovable form, like a magnet.
Now, one might object: since magnets and the like are inert, how can they possess agency and immutability?

And [the reason] is indeed unestablished. True; however, there is no fault in this objection because agency consists solely in the state of being capable (*śaktatva*), and not in the nature of motion (*spandātmakatva*). Thus, the thesis-statement "and the agent" has also been explained. || 57 ||

Having thus conducted a thorough examination of the Self as it was proposed by refuting other philosophical systems, [the author] now intends to examine the reasoning as well; for those who maintain that the omniscience and other attributes of this Self are established through the necessity of otherwise explaining the scriptural statement regarding its equality with Śiva in liberation— Please note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly, and the translation reflects the incomplete nature of the source. The bracketed section indicates the logical transition of the argument.
To this, he offers a rebuttal:

"Because of the awakening [to the thought], 'I have known,' 'I know,' and 'I shall know,' the power of cognition belonging to the person has that same [nature] even at those times; thus it pertains to all three periods of time. (58)
If something does not exist in a particular place, it might arise there later, as in the case of yellowness appearing later in an *āmalaka* fruit;
however, since qualities such as the person's knowledge of objects belonging to the three times exist even previously, that [knowledge] does not arise at that time.
Rather, that very [knowledge] is omniscience. Furthermore, if it were subject to arising, it would be impermanent like a jar, and thus there would be no liberation from bondage.
[Objection: "Surely, although knowledge of all objects is not being perceived now, it will arise at that time.
To this he says:
"But the power of consciousness is the power of *cit*; when that is manifested, it is called knowledge."
Upon the removal of Rāvaṇa, there was a reunion of the individual manifestation with the two powers of the Supreme Person. || 59 ||
The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is indeed the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*);

and that [power], when it is engaged in the manifestation of objects upon the removal of the veils such as ignorance (*avidyā*) which will be described hereafter, is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*). However, there is no difference between knowledge and its power, as they are always of a single nature.

Since it has been stated that there is no distinction [in the cognition] due to a difference in the object because of the self-cognition of the apprehending subject, it follows that its production does not occur at that time. || 59 ||
What, then, is the distinction between her state of being bound and her state of being unbound? He says:
"In the state of worldly existence (*bhava*), she is colored by the fetters (*pāśa*); in liberation (*mukti*), she overcomes the fetters.
In existence, she has a restricted object; in liberation, she has all things as her object, due to the basis of manifestation. (50)

Just as there is a distinction in the eye caused by the presence or absence of an obscuration characterized by darkness— consisting of the smallness or greatness of its object— even so, in this case, the smallness or greatness [of the scope] of the individual soul (kalādi) in liberation and of the Lord-soul is caused by the smallness or greatness of the manifestor, and not by a difference in their essential nature.
In liberation, there is equality with the Lord due to the manifestation of the capacity of both knowledge and action to have all things as their object, but not because of their production. || 60 ||
Now, if it is intended that the consciousness of the person has as its object all three times, even there he says:

"If the consciousness of the person is not accepted as having the three times as its object, then a distinction [of that consciousness] would follow for it, just as [there is a distinction] in the case of time and so forth. (61)
Since this entire mass of objects of cognition is pervaded by the three times,

and since— just as in the case of "prior" and "posterior"— the time cannot be apprehended if its relatum is not apprehended, this object of cognition which is pervaded by it is likewise unestablished, like the temporalization of time and so forth, which belongs to the realm of māyā.

Since the state of ignorance belongs to the person, his consciousness must necessarily be admitted to exist even prior [to that ignorance], as it pertains to all three periods of time; therefore, in liberation, its manifestation alone is logical, not its origination.
However, the Pāśupatas maintain that for the liberated one, there is equality with the Lord due to the transfer of the Lord's qualities. Others [hold a different view].
Furthermore, [the opponent argues] that it is like a person possessed by a spirit due to the entry of the qualities of Īśvara. To them, he replies:
"The distinction is due to power; there is no other [distinction] than the Lord’s power, since the power of action is observed even in those who possess consciousness. (62)

This position— that this specific excellence characterized by omniscience and so forth belongs to the liberated one [only] through the powers of the Supreme Lord— is also not tenable; for that other Self has already been established as distinct from those powers by virtue of its being a separate consciousness.
It has been stated that he too possesses the power of action; what follows from this? He says:

"For you as well, there exists within an imperishable consciousness of reality (tattva), which would be the antidote to [karmic] refinement, since even [ordinary] cognition is impossible [for you]. (63)

Nevertheless, this [self], which consists of internal consciousness and is characterized by the nature of knowing and acting— known as the reality of the self— is imperishable; yet, due to the cause of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), it would become perishable even while existing in *saṃsāra*, were it not for its counteragent in liberation.

Because of the absence of this consciousness and its activity. This is what is meant: if that which was his own state of being a knower and an agent during the state of transmigratory existence were to still exist in the state of liberation, then he would not be liberated at all.

What is the use of imagining such things as the transfer of the qualities of Īśvara? If it is instead said that [the soul] has perished, then the Puruṣa is not eternal, because of the destruction of his knowledge and agency; furthermore, since no other person is perceived apart from him, this contradicts one’s own scripture. || 63 ||
And he states that there is a contradiction with all the scriptures in this regard:
"In all the great systems of knowledge, consciousness is declared to belong to the eternal atom;
because it would contradict all the scriptures, its instability is not logical. (64)
This position is refuted by scripture, for it is stated: "There is no loss of the seer’s seeing, nor of the thinker’s thinking. As it has been said:
"That which appears to a single person is not distinguished from what is produced [by causes]. (64)
Thinking that this matter might be established by your own scripture, he says:
"In the Śaiva [system] as well, liberation is described as the manifestation of all knowledge and action;
that too is logical for a person only if knowledge and action are eternal. (65)
As it is stated in the venerable *Raurava*:
"The omniscient and omnipotent Śiva, endowed with Śakti," and so forth.
Furthermore, the refutation of the position regarding transmigration (*saṅkrānti*) is treated in detail in the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikā*.
Since it has been shown by the Teacher, it should be understood from that very source. || 65 ||
There is also the view that liberation is the absolute non-existence of the nine qualities of the self: cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression.
The Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas say: "That which is called liberation by the Sāṃkhyas—namely, separation from primordial matter (prakṛti)—is also [thus] explained. He states:
"There can be no engagement in the means to liberation if liberation itself is devoid of knowledge."
For no one who knows the true nature of things engages in activity for the sake of establishing delusion.
For every person acting with foresight, having ascertained the nature of what is beneficial and what is harmful,

engages in specific means for its attainment or avoidance, not out of a sense of addiction. Furthermore, the destruction of one's own consciousness does not result in a state equal to that of a stone or other insentient objects, such as the state of fainting and so forth.

Since it does not appear as something beneficial to anyone who is not insane, no one at all will develop the inclination to engage with the treatises and other means for its attainment; thus, it is indeed useless. [Objection: But surely engagement in sleep is actually observed. [Reply: True, but because that [engagement] takes the form of a dream-cognition, there is no fault.
As they have said: "The fluctuations are of five kinds, both afflicted and unafflicted: valid cognition, error, conceptualization, sleep, and memory."

Even though the state of deep sleep is characterized by insensibility, there is the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, caused by internal tactile sensations such as the nourishment of the body resulting from the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-sāmya*); furthermore, because of the subsequent reflective awareness, "I slept happily," and because of its connection with specific efforts such as the impelling of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), this [state] is [not absolute unconsciousness].
It is precisely the nature of the conditions (pratyaya). As they say:
"How could there be impelling or drawing of the wind without effort? (66)
Now, one might object: "Is it not seen that those tormented by extreme suffering seek death by means of precipices, fire, fasting, or water?
To this he says: "It is not right for us to seek the destruction of suffering; rather, happiness accompanied by suffering is better."

Even for them, the engagement in that austerity is not solely for the sake of destroying suffering; rather, it is because they understand from scripture that one may experience from that austerity a superior fruit consisting of happiness in the hereafter. Therefore, for them, cyclic existence is better than this liberation.

However, this was stated on the assumption that ignorance is not a constituent part of the means to liberation because it is not itself a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), and thus does not prompt activity; it was not stated because the absence of knowledge— which is the very nature of the self— could be produced even by Brahmā, as was previously explained in the case of [the impossibility of producing] eternity and omnipresence.

But the Śākyas, who maintain that [the lamp] is extinguished, hold that all latent impressions of consciousness—whether directly or indirectly—are essentially suffering because they are bound to ignorance and craving; they are never of the nature of happiness. Thus, they apply themselves solely toward severing the latent impressions of all suffering.

By means of the cessation of causes, those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) effectively arrive at the extinction of their own stream of consciousness—which is of the nature of an effect—for the sake of the supreme nirvāṇa; therefore, they say that liberation is indeed emptiness.
To them, he replies:
Latent impressions would result in all suffering, were it not for Your vision.

Apart from your vision, who else possesses such good fortune as this: that all is suffering during the time of existence (*bhava*), while liberation (*mokṣa*) is emptiness, which is absolute non-existence?
This position has already been established as contradicted by direct perception and inference.
This is a mockery, because even through the experience of suffering in many births and the hardship of renouncing them,
all that you attain is merely the fruit of the Lokāyata system. As it was said by the Teacher in the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikā*:
"The Jyeṣṭhamallas are fools, for their own self perishes.
This objection applies equally to the Vedāntins and the Pāñcarātras;
for by them as well, [the self is dissolved] into Brahman, known as Nārāyaṇa, the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti).

Since the dissolution of individual souls (jīvātman) is accepted as liberation, therefore, according to the stated reasoning, liberation— which consists of the manifestation of omniscience and omnipotence— must be accepted as the supreme human goal (parapuruṣārtha), and not anything else, because [any other] is impossible. || 67 ||
If omniscience and other qualities exist in the person even prior to liberation, then why does he not perform all actions? To this, he says:
"Because at all times and regarding all things, there is no activity of either the person or the power."
And another obstruction, called karma, is established as distinct from the bondage of existence. (68)

Just as the non-functionality of an object such as the sun, a jewel, or a sense organ— which has its existence established by another means of valid cognition— is due to an obscuration, so too, by the aforementioned reasoning, the state of being obscured for [qualities] such as omniscience, whose existence is already established, [is likewise explained].
The non-utilization of the *kārya* (the body) implies its cause; thus, the existence of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) is established.
And that [obscuration] is not *karman*, but rather something other than the bondage called *karman*; this was stated by the Teacher in his commentary on the *Svāyambhuva*:
"If impurity did not exist in the person, what would be the cause of attachment to enjoyments?"—this is the internal distinction [between the two].

Therefore, this must be understood from that very source. It is also stated in that same place that there is another impurity called *mala*, which consists of ignorance (*avidyā*) and is distinct even from the bondage of worldly existence (*bhavabandhana*), by means of the passage beginning with "And bodies [arise] from karma," and so forth. (68)
What is that bond of existence? To this he says:
"The bonds ending with the *guṇas* have been taught by the Sāṃkhyas and others;
furthermore, other [bonds] beginning with *pradhāna* have indeed been proclaimed by the Śaivas. (69)

First, those things ending with the elements, the subtle elements, the sense organs, the ego, the intellect, and the [three] qualities—which are well-known in other systems such as Sāṃkhya—are likewise stated by us.
Immediately thereafter, there is the Pradhāna, the cause of the qualities; beginning with that and ending with Rāga, Vidya, and Kalā.
These [categories] are not established in other philosophical systems (darśana) but are taught by the Śaivas alone. As it has been stated regarding the sequence of emanation:
"Then that Supreme Lord, the Vidyeśa, presiding over Māyā and having agitated it with his own rays, created the Taijasa-kalā."
"From the principle of *kalā*, the two principles of *rāga* and *vidyā* came into being;
and from that [the principle of *niyati*], the Lord created the *avyakta* (the unmanifest) and also the *guṇas*.
These, consisting of the principles (*tattva*), elements (*bhūta*), and worlds (*bhuvana*), are the bonds within existence (*bhave*), but not...
The meaning is "in non-existence" or "in excessive existence. || 69 ||
Now, are these [principles], which are not established in other systems, proven for you by scripture alone? No, they are also proven by inference; as he says:
"The reasoning propounded by the followers of Kapila for the sake of establishing the secondary nature of the world..."
For that very logic is sound because it is supported by scripture. 70.

By that very same reasoning through which the Sāṃkhyas established the *guṇas* as the cause— on the grounds that the intellect (*buddhi*) and other principles, being non-conscious and manifold like jars and such, must have a cause— by that same reasoning, since the *guṇas* themselves are also non-conscious...
Since *sattva* is manifold, the cause is called the Unmanifest;
for we have established in the *Bhogamokṣa* that even the Unmanifest, attachment, ignorance, time, and limited agency— which are distinct for each individual soul— are all *māyā*.
The reason that will be stated for establishing the fact that the qualities (guṇas) are effects should be applied to establish the cause of everything from the earth up to the kalās.
Having stated this, [he says]:
"But because they lack consciousness and possess a connection with the number 'many,' their being preceded by a cause is established, like the intellect (buddhi), a jar (ghaṭa), and so forth."

And how this principle is not the invention of the Sāṃkhya alone, but is also observed in our own tradition, has been shown by the Teacher in the *Rauravavṛtti*: "That which arises from passion (*rāga*), ignorance (*avidyā*), limited agency (*kalā*), the manifest qualities (*guṇa*), and the intellect (*buddhi*)."
This should be understood from that very [source] in the commentary on this sūtra. || 70 ||

But is it not the case that others have stated a different logical principle regarding this world’s being produced from other causes, such as the Primordial Spirit (puruṣa), ignorance (avidyā), or atoms (paramāṇu)? Thus, because it appears to be a contradictory deviation (viruddhavyabhicārī) due to the existence of a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva),
he says that this is a fallacious syllogism (nyāsābhāsa):
The reasoning that has been propounded by others regarding the production [of things] from other causes is called a fallacy of reasoning (nyāyābhāsa), because it contradicts all the scriptures.
Just as it is impossible for [the world] to have its cause in persons and the like because they are conscious and thus incapable of transformation,
and because ignorance is not a real entity, and because atoms— being insentient and manifold—
are incapable of being eternal since they must be preceded by other causes, they cannot be the cause of the world.
By this inference: "The one unborn [Self], red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form—
the one unborn [Self] lies beside her, enjoying her, while another unborn [Self] abandons her once her enjoyment has been experienced."

Because this [position] is sublated by the Vedas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other scriptures, this very logic regarding its being produced from another cause is a fallacy of reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*), not the one previously demonstrated. Thus it has been said regarding enjoyment and liberation; therefore, that [matter] should be determined from those [scriptures] alone. Consequently, because this [fallacious argument] lacks a counter-argument, [it is invalid].
In the Sāṃkhya system, this is not a fallacious argument (nyāyābhāsa) like a contradictory or erratic reason; rather, it is indeed a correct logical reason (samyaghetu). || 71 ||
One might object: "Since pleasure and the like are qualities of the self (*ātman*), they cannot possibly be properties of *prakṛti*;

therefore, just as the Sāṃkhya argument that 'this world has pleasure and so forth as its constituent elements' is a fallacy of reasoning because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) regarding the proof of *guṇa* as the cause, so too will this [present] argument be. To this, he says:
Indeed, the existence of the inherence of pleasure and so forth [in the Self] as asserted by Kapila is not unproven;
for, because they are objects of experience, pleasure and so forth are qualities of the Spirit (puṃguṇa), just like color. (72)

That which manifests at some time is not a quality of the Puruṣa, such as form and so forth; and that which is a quality of the Puruṣa never manifests, such as consciousness (*jñatva*) and so forth. Furthermore, pleasure, pain, passion, and the rest manifest only occasionally; therefore, they too [are not qualities of the Puruṣa].

[The opponent argues: "But [these] are merely the inherent nature (*prakṛtisvabhāva*) of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), not qualities of the self (*ātman*); thus, because [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), this reason too is a fallacy of logic (*nyāyābhāsa*). How then could this [reason] of yours be valid? || 72 ||
Now, if you endure suffering without postulating another cause out of aversion to the Sāṃkhya system, then that [cause] certainly exists; thus he says:
"Or, if another cause is postulated, then as much as has been declared in the Śaiva [system applies]."
Indeed, the entire collection of effects beginning with the *kalās* must be established only to that extent.

Even so, we have stated an additional cause called *māyā*—in accordance with the Sāṃkhya admission—for the entire range of effects from *kalā* up to the *guṇas*; therefore, nothing else need be established, as there is a lack of evidence [for it]. || 73 ||
Therefore, he says that this is established by implication: "Know that when this is done, the validation of all scriptures is accomplished;
but if it were done otherwise, there would be mere dry logic. (74)
For once the Self has been established, the entire tradition, beginning with the Vedas, becomes validated;
