for [the scriptures] such as "The Self is to be known" constitute the spiritual form [of knowledge], [just as sacrifice is performed] by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
This is because everything belonging to the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), such as the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," exists for the sake of the Self;

for if that [Self] were not established, one would be resorting to the position of an atheist, whereby the entire meaning of the scriptures would be disregarded, resulting in nothing more than the dry logic of Buddhists, Lokāyatas, and the like— a state of mere sophistry contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
It should be so. || 74 ||
A verse for the conclusion of the examination of the person (*puruṣa*) and the commencement of the examination of the Lord (*īśvara*):
The person has thus been fully described; now I shall speak of Śaṅkara, since that Blessed One is the ordainer of enjoyment and liberation for persons. (75)
It has been stated here that the establishment of Īśvara is preceded by the establishment of the Puruṣa;

for since He alone is the agent of the enjoyment and liberation of beings, His examination follows the examination of the Puruṣa. For this very reason, the examination of Īśvara regarding enjoyment and liberation was also briefly set forth [previously], but here—
"By way of detail" (vistareṇa) [is used] so as not to be redundant. || 75 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Examination of Men," in the *Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa*, the work of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, son of the venerable Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha. 1.
The Nareśvaraparīkṣā, composed by the venerable Ācārya Sadyojyotis, [belonging to] the Yogatantra Granthamālā.
Accompanied by the commentary *Prakāśa* composed by the venerable teacher Rāmakaṇṭha.
Adorned with the foreword of the noble gentleman, Professor Rāmamūrti Śarmā; edited by Ācārya Śrī Rāmajī Mālavīya.
The teacher is likewise the presiding authority over the division of the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Tantra, and Āgama.
The Vice-Chancellor of Sampurnanand Sanskrit University,
Varanasi.
In Vārāṇasī, in the year 2056 of the Vikrama era, in the year 1921 of the Śaka era, and in the year 2000 of the Christian era;
now begins the second book (kāṇḍa).

Now follows the examination of God (Īśvara) immediately after the examination of the person (puruṣa). But surely it is appropriate for those belonging to other systems (tantrāntarīya) to say this; however, here [in our system], since the person has the nature of being a knower and an agent, the limited or extensive scope [of his knowledge] occurs simply through the presence or absence of veils, just as in the case of the sun.

Since the establishment of the Lord as both small and great has already been demonstrated through self-awareness and inference according to the previously stated method, and since the nature of the Lord consists of knowledge and agency, what is the use of any further investigation into Him? This is true.

However, this investigation into the beginningless Lord who is the cause of the world is indeed distinct from that [preceding discussion], and thus there is no contradiction. For instance, He is not established for people like us through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) in the same way as the self (*ātman*), because His nature is different from theirs and He is therefore other than them; for [the selves]...

It has been stated that they are mixed only within self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Nor can they be established through sensory perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*), because by their very nature they transcend the senses;
for even if those bodies were established as not transcending the senses, [the objects themselves would remain unestablished].
This is because neither the Lord nor his opposite is established as possessing the nature of distinguished knowledge and action. As the followers of Jaimini say:
"And this [Lord] can never be known by anyone;
even if his own nature were perceived, his status as a creator would not be understood."
"Nor is their comprehension of this [the self] well-ascertained by his word alone;
for he might speak even without having created [the world], in order to manifest his own sovereignty.
However, like a potter with respect to his effects and activities, he too [is known through them].
In order to show that [the world] is to be inferred from its own effect,
characterized as the universe, by those Jaiminīyas and Lokāyatas who assert that "the world was never otherwise than it is now" and thus accept the eternity of the world— of this [world],...
The unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) of the reason is pointed out; in order to refute those [objections], he says:
"The earth and so forth are considered to be effects because they possess parts, like a jar.
Wherever there is the state of having parts, there is the state of being an effect, as in the case of a pot and the like; however, where...

In that [which is eternal], there is no state of being an effect, nor is there any state of having parts, as in the case of the self (*ātman*) and so forth. On the contrary, everything—including the earth, mountains, and the world with its sky and its wheel—is observed to have arisen; therefore, it is precisely an effect and not eternal, as will be explained hereafter.
The reason is not unestablished; here he demonstrates that, first of all, what is to be proven regarding the world is simply its possession of a material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

If this is so, then since the possession of parts (sāvayavatva) is not established for that portion of the world consisting of sense-faculties, atoms, and so forth, this reason is unestablished with respect to its locus (bhāgāsiddha); to this he replies:
"But because [the senses] are insentient and manifold, their properties as stated are unknown. (1)
That which has the property called "possessing parts" (sāvayavatva) as its stated property is "one whose property is stated" (proktadharma);

and when that [property] is unknown, it is "one whose stated property is unknown" (ajñātaproktadharma). And here, according to the maxim "there is no red cloth," because the negation applies to the qualifying portion, the ignorance has as its object precisely that which has the stated property.
It is understood by implication that [the reason] does not apply even to the subject (*dharmī*); for even in the case of that subject whose properties have been stated but are unknown—

such as the sense organs, atoms, and other portions of the world— the previously mentioned property of being composed of parts (*sāvayavatva*) and so forth is unestablished, because they are non-conscious and exist as many, being distinct for each individual person.

The connection [of the argument] is that "this world is considered an effect, like a tree, a pot, and so forth. Even though it lacks consciousness, because the Sautrāntikas accept this world—consisting of earth and other elements endowed with variegated parts—as a single unity, like a variegated cloth, the previous reason (the reason stated previously) is unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus the former reason was stated.

Consequently, by means of these two reasons, it is established that the entire world—consisting of both parts and partless entities—is endowed with a material cause (*upādāna*); therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (*bhāgāsiddhi*). Thus, the thesis that "the world was never otherwise" is refuted by inference. Nor is it the case that...

There is inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) due to universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, since these too have been made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛta*). Nor is there any purpose for the assertion that "this world was never otherwise than it is now," because even so, the Lord of Beings (*bhūteśvara*) is not established as the controller by means of any other reason. As it has been said:
"This universe, consisting of the elements, though falling away from its accustomed state, reveals the conscious nature as the cause of its stability, just like a living body.
Furthermore, since the establishment of a matter does not result from a mere proposition, a reason must be stated here. Now, [one might ask]: [The text continues: "But surely..."
"The world, consisting of the earth, mountains, and so forth, has never been otherwise than it is now, because neither its production nor its destruction is observed;
or else, there is a lack of evidence for such a state, just as in the case of the Self"—this reason [for the permanence of the world] certainly exists here. No, for it is unestablished (*asiddha*);
for the non-observation of production and destruction occurring at the beginning and end of a kalpa is not currently established for people like us.

Furthermore, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of things such as trees, which possess the nature of being thus [perceived] yet do not constitute a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*).

By this, other reasons such as "because of having a single nature of persistence, like today" and so forth, are also refuted. As for the reason stated—"like the Veda, because there is no recollection of an author"—that too is unestablished (*asiddha*) for us.

Furthermore, the claim that "the one God created heaven and earth" contradicts scripture. Moreover, this example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhanadharma-asiddha*), because the Veda’s being preceded by composition is not established,
unlike the case of a sentence composed by a contemporary poet.

"Since the lack of an agent is unestablished, enough with these refutations of fallacious reasons. [Objection: But by whom can the suspicion that some structured thing might be eternal be prevented? It is like the suspicion that smoke and the like might exist from something other than fire and the like. [Response: We shall explain that this is prevented by the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the relationship [between cause and effect].
And it has been stated by you as well:
"For he who, out of delusion, imagines an obstacle even where none exists, shall meet his end, being full of doubt in all worldly transactions. (1)

But is this reason not unestablished for the proponent, since certain Sāṃkhya sub-sects who maintain the doctrine of the primordial plurality (mūla-pṛthaktva) assert that the principles such as earth and the rest are eternal, and you are included among them? To this he says:

That which extends from the principles (tattva) up to the worlds (bhuvana), and from the limited powers (kalā) down to the earth (kṣmā), is indeed proclaimed by the Śaivas as an effect; for it is produced [from a cause], like a jar, and not by its own nature.
Appropriation and so forth are accepted as his [the Self's] functions, while doubt resides in the agentive factor (kartṛ-kāraka).
Therefore, we establish that Śaṅkara is clearly its agent.

Not only is it the earth and so forth that are established by others, but rather the entire universe— consisting of principles (tattva), elements (bhūta), entities (bhāva), and worlds (bhuvana), extending from the earth down to the *kalā*—
is accepted by us as an effect, just like a tree or a jar; for indeed, because of this.

Its material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) is Māyā; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), its auxiliary cause (sahakāri-kāraṇa) is stated to be Karma. Therefore, unlike those who maintain the doctrine of the plurality of roots (mūla-pṛthaktva-vādins), we do not accept it as being eternal by its own nature; rather, we do so because we maintain the doctrine of the unity of the root (mūla-ekatva-vāda).
Since it is an effect just like a jar and so forth, there is no lack of proof for the proponent;
therefore, by this reason established for both parties, God alone is the probandum according to the method to be explained. || 3 ||
To the question "How so?", he says:
An effect such as the body and so forth, which has an unseen agent, was created by an intelligent being,
just like a pot.

Whatever is an effect is observed to be preceded by an agent endowed with specific knowledge and action, as in the case of a jar and so forth; and it has been established that the entire world, including the body, the sense organs, and the physical universe, is an effect whose agent is unperceived. Therefore, for this reason as well—

It is established that [the world] is preceded by an agent whose nature consists of distinguished knowledge and action; he who is its agent is established as the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). On this point, some say: "Since the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) consists in being preceded by an agent, this reason (*hetu*) is merely a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*). That is incorrect, because [this objection applies only to those who maintain that] the Sāṃkhyas and the Buddhists...

Even if the world is admitted to be an effect, it has been shown that for those who do not accept its being preceded by an agent, "being an effect" is intended here merely as the state of possessing a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). Nor is there a lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because such concomitance is established in the case of effects whose agents are perceived; it is precisely those things whose agents are unperceived that are made the subject (*pakṣa*) here.

As for the one who says: "What is the use of this inference based on an inference (anumitānumāna)? Why is this very reason, 'because of having parts' (sāvayavatvāt), not employed to establish that [the world] is preceded by an agent?"—this is true, it would indeed be employed if it were intended to prove that for the entire world alone.
Since this is intended even for that which is partless, it was not formulated in that manner.

Nor is the reason— by means of the term "unseen agent"— inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the subject (*dharmin*) because of the existence of *trasareṇu*s and the like perceived within sunbeams entering through a window.
He says: "Because it is specified [as such], there is no inconclusiveness due to horses and so forth, because they are not non-opponents. (4)

For a reason that exists in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth. Now, in this case, the counter-examples are not things like mobile creatures (*trasa*)—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including sand, stones, and the like—because even these are made into the subject (*pakṣa*) by the phrase "having an unseen creator. Rather, the counter-examples are only things such as the self (*ātman*). For [in those cases] it is doubtful...
The property (*dharma*) is yet to be proven; it is neither established nor sublated. As you yourselves have stated:
"Because of the statement of a doubtful reason, a pervaded reason lacks a locus.
Furthermore, in all effects whose agent is unperceived, there is indeed the state of being preceded by an agent.
Because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to either establish or refute that [property], it is doubtful for the opponent;

therefore, since they are the objects of the statement of the reason (hetu), even [the cases of] moving beings and so forth possess the status of being the actual subject (pakṣa) and are thus indeed the probandum (sādhya).
Consequently, these too are made the subject of the thesis (pakṣīkṛta), not out of fear of a deviation (vyabhicāra). Nor is it the case that [they are excluded] from the subject itself.

If the object of deviation were [the mere absence of the probandum], then since such a state would obtain even in the inference of fire from smoke and so forth, it would follow that all inference would be non-existent. Furthermore, the real counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is that in which the absence of the probandum is ascertained; and by no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the state of not being preceded by an agent established in the case of things such as grass and the like.

"It is certain. Why? Because how can there be the status of being a counter-example (*vipakṣatā*) when the mere non-perception of an agent is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to ruined monasteries, wells, and the like? If it is argued that, as with wells and such, we have never perceived an agent in the case of [living beings] such as insects, then—

Thus, this [subject], being beyond the range of perception for those such as ourselves, cannot be determined by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to be non-existent when it is possible that it exists there—such as in cases of possession (āveśa) and so forth—just like a piśāca or similar being; therefore, it remains indeed doubtful.

Consequently, it is impossible to eliminate the status of grass, creepers, and the like from the class of negative instances (vipakṣa). If that is so, then [regarding] grass, creepers, and so forth...

Since birth is observed from causes such as earth which are themselves perceptible, the postulation of another unseen agent would lead to an infinite regress; therefore, these [perceptible causes] constitute the counter-example (vipakṣa), and thus [your reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntika). As they say:
When certain things exist, that which necessarily arises from them— if one were to postulate something else as its cause, there would be an infinite regress of causes in all cases.

"When Caitra's wound heals due to his connection with weapons, medicine, and so forth, why is the status of a cause attributed to a post (sthāṇu) which is unconnected [to that process]? [If this is asked, the reply is:
"How is it, then, that those [effects] do not occur at other times? [It is] because of the absence of auxiliary conditions such as rain, sunlight, and so forth."

How can there be an absence even of that? If it is argued, "Indeed, by the power of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), then the existence of grass and so forth is not established even when the perceived causes are present," [we reply: since the unseen is also not rejected, it does not constitute a counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
If it is argued, "We maintain that the unseen is indeed karma," [we reply: no, because there is no proof for such a specific distinction.
This is because one must accept an unseen agent such as a *piśāca*, and in some cases, a deity-soul as the causal agent. As it has been said:
"Even those who are experts in mantras compose certain mantras."
"Their power consists in that [knowledge], established by the logic they themselves have stated.
Since that [power] is possible even here [in the case of the Jaiminīyas], there are no such things as *piśācas* (ghosts) and so forth; thus say the followers of Jaimini.
As they have said:

"Where the five means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are not found with respect to the nature of an object, there the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāva-pramāṇa) exists for the purpose of awakening one to the existence of that object.
This is incorrect, precisely because even when the means of valid cognition have ceased [to function], [the object remains].

Because the existence [of such a person] is established, just like wealth deposited in the earth. Nor is it the case that there is no proof here either, because at that time knowledge is established regarding an object beyond the senses—which is impossible for a mere human being—and which is non-contradictory. If it is argued that even that [knowledge] manifests for the person at that time due to the power of karma:

This would be logical if that [knowledge] were manifest to him at that time; however, due to his forgetfulness, he is established as being merely one whose cognition is then obscured. For in the matter of "this is my knowledge" or "this is not," there is no means of valid cognition other than one's own self-experience, nor is there...
Just as in the case of one walking, the non-perception of grass and such [objects] is logical for that cognition of yours as well, because it is of a determinate nature. As they say:
"And determinate cognition is not absent from its own self."
Therefore, because it enters into human experience— just like the cognition of Devadatta and others—

that cognition must be admitted, on the basis of its effects, to belong at that time to some exceptionally powerful being such as a *piśāca*, who causes the delusion of consciousness and is entirely distinct from [the individual]; it does not arise from the *karmas* [of the individual].
Because of its insentience (*jaḍatva*), there is no absence of an agent there, even for a *piśāca* or similar being that is beyond the range of perception for people like us. [Objection:

Even so, the action itself certainly possesses the status of being the cause there. [Response: What follows from this? Since an unseen agent (*adṛṣṭa*) is also possible, there is a doubt regarding grass and the like as having an unseen agent as their precursor; thus, they do not constitute a counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore—

However, according to the method previously stated, it possesses actual subjecthood (*pakṣatva*) itself. Furthermore, we shall explain that even action, like agriculture and the like, does not produce an effect unless presided over by a conscious agent. This is because, although grass and such things have visible causes, others [the opponents] nevertheless admit that they are effects of the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*).

On the contrary, considering that [the subject] possesses the property of being a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), the Teacher has avoided the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) by means of the very same [beings], such as the *trasa* (mobile beings), on the grounds of the suspicion that they might be dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), and not because they [themselves] are [dissimilar instances].
Now, he states the opponent's intention: "But this reason is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*)."

Since an effect produced by an intelligent being has been observed, it is logical to infer an intelligent agent from that very observation; this does not apply to the body and so forth, as there is no such reversal of the relationship.
For only that which is established as the effect of a specific thing can be its inferential indicator,

not merely any effect— just as smoke is [the indicator] of fire— and it is not established that every specific effect, such as a cart, a jar, a cloth, a palace, or a city, is produced by an agent; therefore, from that alone [no such conclusion follows].

The inference of an agent consisting of distinguished knowledge is logical; however, [the argument] that because it is denoted by the word "effect," it must arise from something of a different genus—such as the body, the world, or instruments—due to its being another effect, is not tenable, for the reason (*hetu*) itself is unestablished (*asiddha*). As the Buddhists have said:
Whatever arrangement and so forth are established as following the presence or absence of a presiding agent,
that [agent] is inferred from them.

It is not logical to infer from a word that is established as distinct in one object that it is non-distinct in another, merely because the word is the same; this would be like inferring fire from a white substance.
Otherwise, because a potter is the cause of some modification of clay such as a jar, he would also be the creator of an anthill.

"It is not logical to establish [a property] well-known in another class of things by the observation of a commonality of words, just as it is not [logical] to [establish] horns for cows and the like on the basis of their being 'go' (cow/goer). (5)
He refutes this as follows:
"Because it is an effect, the body and so forth are not of a different nature from a pot and the like;
and no effect is ever observed to exist without an intelligent cause. (6)

First of all, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is not unestablished for you regarding bodies, instruments, the world, and so forth, which have unseen agents; otherwise, it would be logical to admit that they are of a different genus from those things whose agents are seen, given that the entire universe is impermanent.

Because it is accepted that [the cognition] arises from the appropriation of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). But surely, since its bases (*āśraya*) are distinct, that [cognition] must also be distinct? No; for they too are non-distinct in that form, just as brindled and black cows are non-distinct in their "cowness," or as sound, a jar, and so forth are non-distinct in their "sound-ness" or "jar-ness."

By virtue of being produced (*kṛtakatva*). For otherwise, it would not be possible for you to establish impermanence in sound and the like by means of being produced—as in the case of a jar—or to establish multiplicity in things such as universals (*sāmānya*) by means of their subsisting in many instances (*anekavṛtti*), as in the case of a string of garlands around a person's neck. Therefore, in that form, those [properties]...
It is indeed similarity, as it has been stated:
"A similar instance (sapakṣa) is an object that is similar by virtue of the generality of the property to be proven.
If you argue that this is not so because of [the specific nature of] being an effect, then victory has been won by these upstart seekers of victory!
By denying well-established principles and thereby producing the blindness of unestablishedness (*asiddhatā*) and other fallacies,

how is it that [the existence of a creator] is not [inferred] from the very same properties— such as being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), existence (*sattva*), being an effect (*kāryatva*), emptiness (*śūnyatva*), and lack of self-nature (*anātmatva*)— which belong to all things that possess a specific arrangement?

There is also equality in terms of possessing an arrangement (*sanniveśavat*). Now, it might be argued that what is called "arrangement" is nothing other than the things arranged themselves. This is the talk of a child; for even if something exists, how could its existence be anything other than itself, or its being an effect be anything other than the effect? True; yet, even though those [parts] are distinct, they produce a single cognitive reflection (*ekavimarśa*).
It is accepted as being equal. As it has been said:

"Even though they are distinct, certain things are restricted by their own nature to the accomplishment of a single object through the cognition called 'unified reflection,' just like the sense organs and so forth."

"Just as certain medicinal herbs are observed to cure fever and other ailments either together or individually, while others are not, even though they possess diversity; so too, by virtue of possessing a specific configuration (*sanniveśa*), all things that possess configurations would appear to be identical. Thus [it is argued]. To this, [the reply is: no. For it is not the case that all things possessing configurations are identical. Why? Because there is a difference in their capacities. Just as the medicinal herbs mentioned above, despite being diverse, are seen to have distinct powers—some curing fever and others not—so too, although all things possess configurations, they differ in their respective capacities. Therefore, they are not identical. Furthermore, if one were to argue that "all things possessing configurations must be identical because they share the common property of having a configuration," then one would also have to accept that all things are identical because they share the common property of existence (*sattā*). But that is not accepted. Consequently, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Moreover, the example cited is unestablished (*asiddha*), for it is not proven that all medicinal herbs are identical simply because they are all medicinal herbs. Thus, the argument is refuted. Finally, the opponent’s reason is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite of what is intended. This is because the very fact that things possess configurations implies a distinction between them, just as the fact that medicinal herbs possess distinct potencies implies a distinction among them. Therefore, the claim that all things possessing configurations are identical is untenable.
For some, it would follow that pride (*māna*) is likewise [a distinct category]; thus, their designation as a different genus (*jātyantara*) is indeed improper.

Once it is established that these [Vedic texts] were not preceded by an author, their status as a different genus would follow even if they were denoted by the same word, just as [the status of being a different genus follows] when a difference in material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) is established, as in the case of observed qualities such as paleness (*pāṇḍutva*).

Or rather, it occurs when there is certainty regarding the difference [of the object], as in the case of the nine things such as speech and so forth which are denoted by the word "cow," but not when there is doubt about them. Just as at the very time of grasping the relationship [between smoke and fire],

one infers fire from a different smoke that was not previously seen because of its extreme distance— even though the connection with fire was not perceived— due to the smoke being observed on the mountain range.

It has been stated that [the reason] is unestablished because there is merely a doubt regarding it, and because mere non-perception results in doubt. If that is so, then by virtue of being unestablished, those [entities] would be of a different genus from those whose agents are perceived.
No; for precisely because of this, they are what is to be proven, just as smoke and the like have fire and the like as their material cause, even when [the fire] is at a distance.

On mountains and the like, it has been stated that while the non-establishment of the probans (*sādhana*) is a defect, the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is actually an ornament. Now, if it is argued that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between every effect in general and an agent in general is unestablished, it is replied: since jars and other such things are observed only as having a specific agent, where indeed is there [such a pervasion] for smoke in general?

For you, pervasion is established by fire in general alone. Indeed, even a particular kind of smoke is established as being produced by a particular kind of fire in places such as a kitchen hearth. [Objection: But surely, although there is deviation from particulars—since smoke in general is observed even when grass-fire, leaf-fire, and so forth vary—the smoke at that time is not devoid of its own particularity.

Since the universal (sāmānya) is not established by perception, that same defect remains in that very state. True; for this very reason, through the force of the object or by means of inference—namely, "in all cases, smoke is produced from fire because it possesses the nature of smoke (dhūmatva), like the smoke seen in a kitchen"—there is [the cognition] of mere fire (agnimātra) whose particular distinctions are not established.
In this context, smoke alone, which is the pervaded (vyāpya) and whose specific varieties are not established, is perceived as the mark (liṅga) of the pervader (vyāpaka). As it has been said:
"The mark is declared to have a universal (sāmānya) as its object, because its specific varieties are not established."

If this is so, then here too, since there is deviation regarding specific agents such as potters in the case of effects like jars, cloths, and carts, it is established that mere effectness— whose distinctions are not fixed—
is pervaded by mere agency as its logical reason; thus, there is no lack of proof even for the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
For those who know pervasion (*vyāpti*) maintain that pervasion is rooted in an invariable connection (*pratibandha*). True, provided such a connection existed;

however, in this case, the pervasion is dependent solely upon an example (*dṛṣ� fallacious), just like the inference of the dark complexion of a son and so forth. Therefore, it is not a valid inference. This too—

It is indeed to be trusted, like the instruction of a physician; for here too, the necessary connection—just as between smoke and fire—is established by direct perception. Indeed, the causal relationship between smoke and fire, or between "being produced" and "impermanence," cannot be established without the observation of a connection proven through direct perception.

Identity, or the two states of existing in many and being manifold, is understood from other sources. Even by you, an example is employed in probative statements not merely as an example, but as the objective domain of the means of valid cognition that establishes the relationship;
therefore, even when there is the application of a mere example, [the conclusion does not follow] due to the absence of that [establishing cognition].
The fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāritā*) in such inferential rubbish as "he is dark-skinned because he is his son" is present here as well;

for in this case too, just as with the material cause, the causal relationship between the agent and the effect is established by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the example, and by the force of that very [perception], [the conclusion follows] for everything.
Just as pervasion is established by the inclusion of all jars, so too is it established by the agent; thus, there is no deviation.

If this is so, [one might argue that] the necessary connection (pratibandha) is established only in cases where an agent is observed, and not in cases where no agent is observed, because they are different. This is mere prattle, for the mere fact of being "different" [does not constitute a valid distinction].

Because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the observation of smoke and the like which have a visible agent and are seen to be connected with fire; and if it is argued that "having no visible agent" is what constitutes being "other than those with a visible agent," even that—
[The argument] is indeed inconclusive because of such things as jars and the like.

Now, if it is argued that there is no difference—just as there is non-difference from the nature of a jar and so forth in those cases, so too here [there is non-difference] from the nature of an effect—[we reply:
surely, an inference of something is only proper from that very thing of which its genus has been established; it is not [proper] otherwise.

[The opponent argues: From something of a different genus, just as [the inference of] a potter [does not follow from] an anthill or a mound; and since an effect whose agent is unseen is of a different genus from an effect whose agent is seen, it is not logical to infer an agent from it. [The author replies:
No, because it has already been stated that their difference is not established in that form, just as in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*).

Or rather, [the pervasion] is by means of existence (*sattva*) alone, as in the case of sound, a pot, and so forth, for all categories of things. For it is not possible for you that there is identity (*tādātmya*) between "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), which is distinct from many heterogeneous things, and "impermanence," which is distinct from those same many heterogeneous things; nor is it possible for you that there is identity between "existence" and "momentariness. But surely, by that...
In their form, they possess identity alone, not heterogeneity. But is this not contradictory?
For even though they are indeed heterogeneous, they are not so by way of a difference in properties, just as the *śāvaleyas* and *bāhuleyas* are not heterogeneous in their "cowness.
In that case, this alone is correct: whatever has a relationship with something as it truly is, it is [perceived] as such.

It is only that which is real which causes [the object] to be understood through the force of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). What is the use here of "belonging to the same class" (*sajātīyatva*) or "not belonging to the same class" (*asajātīyatva*)?
As it has been said even by you yourselves: "If this [cognition] is pleasing to objects by its own nature, then who are we in that matter?"

And for this reason, regarding the anthill, a funeral mound, and so forth, even if there is deviation [from the specific artisan], there is indeed no deviation from a conscious agent; thus, in those cases as well, that very same [conscious agent] is the probandum (*sādhya*). Furthermore, what kind of "genus" (*jāti*) is intended here, in relation to which the conventional usage of "belonging to the same genus" (*sajātīyatva*) and "not belonging to the same genus" (*asajātīyatva*) occurs? Is it not [the case that...]?

The similarity is indeed the same as yours. If this is so, then just as all entities are similar by virtue of their existence (*sattva*), all effects are similar by virtue of being effects (*kāryatva*); therefore, that very [similarity] is stated as the reason for establishing the agent (*kartṛ*) due to its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Whatever kind of thing is established from a certain [cause], the agent here must be of that very same kind.

The object of inference has been stated [as that which is] not from a dissimilar class, or not from that which is merely denoted by that word; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddha*).

How then is even the yellowness (*pāṇḍutva*) and so forth produced by fire? For it is observed in lacquer (*makkola*) and other substances even in the absence of that [fire], just as existence (*sattva*) is found in non-products such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth. Nor is there anything without an agent.

No effect has been established such that the deviation of this reason (hetu) for one existing therein could be suspected; for it has already been stated that even mountains, grass, and so forth are established as having an unseen agent (adṛṣṭakartṛka).
Thus, just as yellowness and the like are not unestablished as being produced by fire, the fact that an effect is produced by an agent is likewise not unestablished. 6.

Now, if the connection of a thing is established only with that which exists in its actual state, then it is from that very state that it is inferred; regarding this very point of apprehension, he says here as well: "And it is not the case that the individual which is connected [to the universal] is the same individual that is accepted here [in the inference]."
There would be an inference of that very [object] again from its perception. || 7 ||

If this is so, then since the relation (*pratibandha*) of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) smoke and so forth with the particular fire and so forth— which is excluded from all similar and dissimilar things— is established in places such as a kitchen, and because that [particular] is not pervasive (*ananuyāyin*), there can be no inference regarding another locus (*dharmyantara*).

It is not possible, nor is it established by perception in that very case, because inference is inapplicable; thus, the discussion of inference has ceased. Victory indeed belongs to the Lokāyatas, who maintain that perception is the sole means of valid cognition.

Therefore, since every proponent of inference must accept that inference as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) here has only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, for this reason as well, it is not unestablished (*asiddha*). || 7 ||

Others, however, maintain that because this [reason] proves a quality contrary to the specific property [of the probandum]— namely, that it proves "having a creator endowed with a body" rather than "having a creator"— it is a contradictory reason (*viruddha*), since in the example of a jar and the like, this [reason] is observed only as having a creator endowed with a body.
They say [this is so] because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason is not established.
Furthermore, if the example were as [the opponent] has established it, the reason would become contradictory (*viruddha*),
for it would entail that [the world] has a creator who is non-omniscient, perishable, and so forth.
"And how could he even have a desire for creation without a body and so forth?
If he were to possess a body and so forth, its production would not be caused by him. He refutes this very point as follows:

For those who wish to establish [a thesis], the logical method (nyāya) serves to overturn the opposite of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) for others; indeed, [this] is accomplished by means of perception (dṛṣṭa) itself regarding the body and so forth.

For those opponents who, by means of this very reason— namely "being an effect"— desire to prove the opposite of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), which is "having a bodiless creator as its antecedent," with respect to the subject (dharmin) consisting of the body,
sense organs, and so forth, that logic of proving the contradictory is [refuted] by perception itself.
[The objection] is refuted: because the effect— namely, the vibration that performs its own function—

is established through both internal tactile perception and self-awareness as being preceded by an agent endowed with volition, even without another body, [the opponent's argument regarding] "being an effect" is [invalidated].

Because it is invariably concomitant everywhere, it establishes only that much [i.e., the existence of an agent], but not even "being preceded by an agent endowed with a body," because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). That is not so;
the meaning is that this reason (*hetu*) proves the opposite of a specific attribute (*dharma-viśeṣa-viparīta-sādhana*). Otherwise...

Furthermore, properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) would also lead to the inference of impermanence in sound and the like—just as in the case of a jar—by way of their inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with broad bases, bellies, and so forth; and smoke and the like would likewise lead to the inference of fire on a mountain and other locations—even where no fire exists—just as they do in a kitchen. Thus, for everyone...

If one argues that there is the consequence of the absence of a reason because no specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) is established, [we reply: if it is said that in that case only that property which is non-deviant (*avyabhicārī*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), and nothing else because of its deviation, then this is the same here as well; thus, there is no contradiction. But surely, since things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), here too—

Some maintain that this [reason] is indeed "contrary to the specific" (*viśeṣaviruddha*), because it deviates from the rule that an effect must be preceded by an agent endowed with a body; for they argue that in another location, a different bodily moment arises for the embodied being, aided by the characteristics of the previous body. As Dharmakīrti also said:

"Therefore, those things which are individually incapable, but in whose combination a quality is possible, possess causality when united; this is not the case for [the cause] such as Īśvara, because there is no differentiation.
This is true, provided that this [Īśvara] were momentary; however, that has been refuted in the *Ātmasiddhi*.

Because that [activity] is rooted in the rejection of it. Furthermore, for you who maintain that its very nature is the designation of an ill omen, such a designation everywhere reveals nothing but misfortune; for since activity is impossible given momentariness, agency itself is unestablished. What, then, is this dharma of which [you speak]?

This constitutes the proof of a specific contradiction (*viśeṣaviparyayasādhanatā*). For only when momentariness has been refuted, or when a self, agency, or God have been established or accepted, is it appropriate to introduce an investigation into God; not otherwise. In the interim, however, the alternative based on momentariness is already refuted by its very acceptance. Now, [one might object]:
"Even in the state of stability, because the action of vibration has that [body] as its object, the body must indeed be required by it.

This is the prattle of a child; for it is required as an effect, like a jar or similar object, but not as a body. [Objection: But surely, the immobile state exists for the sake of accomplishing the mobile state?
That [dependence] must indeed be accepted. True; for it has been stated that [the Lord is dependent] because He is an effect, like a jar or other such things.
But surely, for one who is bodiless, both knowledge and action are impossible. As Kumārila has said:
"A bodiless presiding agent would be like a liberated soul."

That is incorrect; for indeed, there is nothing that is impossible when it is actually perceived. Even if the liberated selves possess omniscience through the establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) by means of an example, this is because their equality with the Lord (*īśvara*) is accepted. [Objection: In that case, it will be like the state of isolation of consciousness (*vijñānakaivalya*) and so forth. [Reply: No.
It has been stated elsewhere that their bodilessness is not the cause of their being such [as they are], but rather it is impurity (*mala*) itself.

"This cognizer, because he is bodiless, lacks the established existence of the senses and so forth"—this very point he expresses by means of another term. By this also, the well-known fact that [the Mīmāṃsaka] relies upon logical reasoning (*upapatti*) is established.

It is revealed only for the Buddhists and nothing more than that. As they say: "Intoxicated by those weak arguments put forward by them in their preliminary positions—arguments which are difficult to comprehend—the monks prance about."

Or how can you maintain that the unborn one possesses knowledge of all objects in the absence of a body, sense organs, and so forth? But surely he too has a body! Is that body born of karma or not born of karma? If he were joined with a body born of karma, he would lack omniscience, just like ourselves.

But a body not produced by karma is impossible, because it would have to be generated by specific causes, just as smoke and the like arise from fire and so forth. [Objection: But its body may exist due to compassion. [Reply: True, if its causality in that regard were established through either perception or inference.
Surely it will come from scripture, as it has been said: "Upon transition to the third stage, the acceptance of the treatise is proper.
This is true, provided that its validity is established within the two stages that are the objects of perception and inference.
It might be so; however, it has already been stated in the *Ātmasiddhi* that such [an entity] does not exist.

But surely, because it is bound by duality, it must be a cause of the body, just like craving and so forth. In that case, due to its connection with ignorance (*avidyā*), even a compassionate one would lack omniscience, just like an ordinary person (*pudgala*). [Objection: But surely, by his very power of emanation (*nirmāṇa-śakti*)...
The Buddhists maintain that [the Lord] has a body. In that case, the existence of God is not established.

But surely he must still have a body? If it is argued that he has one as a means for the apprehension of objects, then like us and others, he too would possess a cognition dependent upon sense organs and so forth, and thus he would not be omniscient; for [cognition] derived from the senses...
The capacity for all objects is possible, just as in the case of a lamp and other such things, because it is established that [the cognition] illuminates limited objects.

Now, one might object: even for one who perceives all objects through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), having removed all defects of the mind and thus being independent of the senses, the body is indeed still useful merely as a substratum.
If this were so, then that [power] would not attain the status of being a body, as it is no different from a wall or similar objects. As they say:
"By the mere presence of that Person, like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), teachings emerge at will even from walls and other such things."

His knowledge of all objects exists entirely independent of a body, and his agency regarding the creation of bodies and so forth occurs by mere will; furthermore, you yourselves have indeed accepted that this is the case for others as well, such as Mañjuśrī and those who possess superior qualities.

In the same way, since the Blessed One’s possession of a universal body is established by virtue of being the substratum of the universe, there is no proof of a property contrary to the specific nature [of the subject]. Nor does the potter himself lack lordship (*anīśvaratva*),
for lordship consists in having knowledge, agency, selfhood, and so forth, which exist even in the case of a potter.

Because its own activity has an object; for it is not possible for that [agent] to possess the status of being a potter if there is an absence of knowledge regarding it or a deficiency in its agency, just as in the case of one who is not a potter.
Nor can there be perishability of the self, since its permanence has already been established; therefore, this [objection] does not apply even to the example.

Therefore, even the destruction by a non-Lord (anīśvara) and so forth is established; thus, there is no contradiction with the specific property (*viśeṣaviruddha*) in this way either. By this, [the following is also refuted]:
"In the example as well, the occurrence immediately after a desire is not found.
How can an insentient entity follow that desire?"
This [argument] is also fallacious, because the movement of one's own body and so forth is observed to be exactly like that of a potter and others.

If it is argued that a jar and the like—which are distinct from the body—are observed to function immediately after a desire [is formed], that too is incorrect, because even those [objects] are not established [as such] without a desire; for one who is without desire, or whose desire belongs to another, [does not produce them].

A potter is seen fashioning a jar. But surely, mere will (*icchāmātra*) is not the cause there, since even the body and so forth are required. What follows from this? For the requirement of auxiliary factors does not destroy the causal efficiency of the primary cause; just as in the case of pleasure and so forth, action (*karman*)—such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth—requires the body and other factors, and thus that [action] remains the cause.
It is inferred from its effects that [the power] is non-deviating in all cases. Furthermore, it is not unestablished that there is the production [of effects] by will in things other than the body;
for it is observed that those who possess perfected mantras can alter the nature of snakes, poisons, fire, and so forth, solely through their will.
The Teacher himself will state this later in the Uttara-kāṇḍa. And it has been said by the followers of the Sugata:

"Just as for those whose senses are afflicted by mantras and the like, fragments of clay and other such things appear in a completely different way, even though they are devoid of that [apparent] form."

Alternatively, the Lord, while still possessing a body, accomplishes the work of the world by presiding over another self-created body after having withdrawn his own previous body; for the Master will state in that very same place that his succession of bodies is beginningless, like that of one who enters the bodies of others.
And therefore, as it has been said:
"Your reason would be inconclusive because of his body and so forth;
and that body of his must have an origin, because it is a body, like ours."

This [objection] is also already set aside, because even though that body possesses a specific configuration (*sanniveśavat*), its eternity is not admitted. Furthermore, the sovereignty of the *māyāgarbha* lords is indeed maintained despite their connection with a body. As was stated by the Teacher in the *Mokṣakārikās*:
Even when there is a conjunction of the *kalās*, they are necessarily subject [to the Lord], like a herd of bound souls (*paśu*);
those *kalās* are subject along with the bound souls, and therefore they [the Lords] stand above them.
Thus, there is no contradiction. || 8 ||

But is it not the case that the example here is unestablished regarding the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), because the fact of being produced by God is unestablished in the example, such as a jar? Furthermore, it has been stated that [the reason] is contradictory when used with what is unestablished; for [the nature of the agent] consists of being stainless, omniscient, and possessing the power of creation through mere will.
Mastery is not observed in non-masters such as potters and the like; as it has been said:

"If the superintendence of a potter and others is admitted in the case of a jar and so forth, then there would be no superintendence by God; if [such superintendence] exists [in their case], then [the argument] lacks the probandum."
To show that this too is incorrect, he says:
"Freedom from the bonds of impurity and the like, the possession of qualities such as omniscience, and the capacity to act immediately according to one's own will—these are not seen in a potter. (9)
All this will indeed be established for Maheśa through the power of his inherent purpose;
it does not proceed from inference and the like, and therefore there is no example lacking the probandum.
It has been stated that even for potters and others, the possession of stainless knowledge regarding their own work constitutes omniscience,
and their capacity to act according to their own will constitutes lordship (*īśvaratva*), because otherwise the production of jars and such things would be impossible. Now, as it actually is:

It is argued that the probandum (sādhya), which consists of the connection with a body, instruments, the world, and so forth, is of such a nature that it has not been observed in the example (dṛṣṭānta). Likewise, fire and the like, though connected with a mountain, have not been observed in a kitchen or similar location; therefore, they cannot be established by means of smoke and other such signs.

This would entail the undesirable consequence that all inference would be non-existent. [Objection: But surely it is already established that smoke in general is pervaded by fire in general. [Reply: Where? Not in the example (dṛṣṭānta), for in cases such as a kitchen, we observe that only specific smoke exists because of its existence only from a specific fire. [Objection: But surely...

The pervasion (vyāpti) having the universal as its object is indeed established either by means of the perceptual recognition (pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa) occurring at a later time, or by the inference "because it occurs from that [cause] even once," or by the efficacy of the thing's own power (vastu-śakti-sāmarthya). Let it be so established; however, as for that which resides on the mountain...
How can a specific fire be established? For it cannot be established even by inference or other means that establish pervasion (*vyāpti*), because there is no pervasion with respect to a particular.
If it is argued that the specific fire itself—implied by the general and whose internal distinctions are not fixed—is the object of pervasion, then what [of it]?

[Is the mountain] only that which exists on the mountain? Or is it "that too"? If it is only that which exists on the mountain, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), because its existence was already established at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), and there is also contradiction with one's own experience (*svānubhavabādha*).
If, however, it is said to be "that too," then the restriction (*niyama*) cannot be inferred at all; thus, there is simply the fallacy of proving what is already established. As they have said:

[Otherwise,] there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established regarding the universal (*sāmānya*), and there would be the undesirable consequence of [the inference] applying to fire located in another place. Now,
it might be argued that because smoke is apprehended as restricted by the force of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), fire is cognized as restricted.

"Inference is indeed the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for it is the perception of an object through a mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics; thus there is no contradiction. As Dharmakīrti said:
"The universal (*sāmānya*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), and yet there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*)."

"Because the exclusion of non-connection with that [specific agent] is unestablished. If this is so, then here too, a specific effect whose distinctions are not yet established is proven to be pervaded by a specific agent; for from an object consisting of an effect—such as the body, the instruments, and the world—the specific agent who is its creator is also established by virtue of his capacity.

Since lordship (*īśvaratva*)—consisting of purity, omniscience, and the power of agency through mere will—is established with respect to its own effects, the example [of the potter] is not deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); thus there is no fault. [Objection: In that case, like a potter or others, he would possess ignorance or a lack of lordship regarding anything other than his own effects. [Response: Where else [could this be]?

Because there is nothing else apart from its effects—namely the body, the organs, the world, and so forth. [Objection: But how do you know that it does not exist? [Reply: Let it be; if it is a means for accomplishing the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), then it is indeed an effect. However, if it does not accomplish those goals, then ignorance regarding it—just as in the case of a hare's horn—is truly an ornament. As they say:
What is the use of investigations for those who seek effective action regarding that which is capable of such action?
What is the use of a lustful woman examining whether a eunuch is handsome or ugly?
Thus, there is no contradiction. Now, one might object: "Is not the work of a potter and the like indeed different from his [the Lord's] work? True;

however, because the arrangement by a potter and so forth would otherwise be impossible, ignorance and the like cannot possibly exist in him. For the status of being a potter is certainly not causeless for a potter; rather—
It has been stated that [the world] has God as its cause; however, there is no evidence for the existence of a creator of a pot when the pot itself is not known. || 10 ||
One might object: "Is he not a creator? Then he is not the Lord, nor is he omniscient, just like a potter;

and since you yourselves accept that he is the creator of the body, the senses, and so forth, he too must be non-Lord and non-omniscient. Thus, this position is undermined by a counter-reason (*pratihetu*). To this, he says:
Because of the reason stated, the opponent’s desire for inference regarding the husband’s equality with a potter is indeed contradicted by his own tenet. (11)

If this were so, then where there is smoke, there would be fire unrelated to the mountain, as in the kitchen and so forth; and since there is smoke on the mountain, it follows that the fire there is not located on the mountain. Thus, there would be no cessation of such a mass of counter-arguments anywhere, resulting in the non-existence of all inference.
It may be so for you. || 11 ||
Here the opponent's intention is as follows: "If this contradiction belongs only to you,
then it belongs only to him for whom pervasion (vyāpti) is accessible through repeated observation."

The fault of the "non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) arises from relying on another specific property; this does not apply to us, because for us that [inference] is based upon an essential connection (*pratibandha*).
For reasons such as existence (*sattva*) and smoke (*dhūma*) are indeed [based on such connections].

Since [the reasons] are established as being pervaded by impermanence and fire in general through the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*), and not as being pervaded by their specific particulars— because those particulars may deviate [from the probandum] and because other natures (*rūpāntara*) are possible for real entities— how could there be any possibility of a "non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) among them?
The Teacher says:
If this [position] were correct, it would not be pride;
but since it is obstructed by the power of the actual meaning, from where could its correctness come? (12)

If even this inference were not sound— that is, if it were not rooted in an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*)— then a counter-argument against it would certainly be possible; however, since this [inference] too is pervaded by the capacity of the agent to produce the effect, which is the very nature of the probandum (*sādhya*), [it is indeed sound].

Since the validity of the inference for an agent consists in its being a form of the inference from an effect, how can there be the presentation of a counter-argument against it? For it has been stated that a counter-position is not possible in an inference that proceeds by the force of real entities (*vastubala*). || 12 ||
Now, one might object: "Just as a counter-reason based on a specific qualification is impossible, so too there should be no specific qualification in the probandum (sādhya) either;
consequently, the fault of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā) would apply to the universal. To this he says:
"For the specific qualifications are indeed obtained through the force of the facts (arthaprāpta) regarding the fire that has been inferred."
They can be warded off even with the greatest effort. || 13 ||
For smoke located in a particular place is not produced by fire located in another place;

therefore, by virtue of the capacity to perceive smoke as restricted by place, time, and form, the specific qualities of the fire—delimited from association with other places, times, and forms—are indeed inferred. Thus, there is no fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

The Naiyāyikas maintain that the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is restricted to a specific instance because it is the means of cognition itself that is so restricted; whereas the operation of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is not restricted to a specific instance, as it rests upon a generality by virtue of its dependence on an indefinite variety of particulars. Therefore, they hold that the fallacy consisting in the dependence [of the counter-reason] upon a particular is the sophistical refutation (*jāti*) called "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*). As they say:
When there is a concomitance with the probandum in the effect, even though the means of proof is a generality,
the statement of a fault based on the difference in related entities is considered the fallacy known as *kāryasama*.
Thus, there is no fault. || 13 ||

Others, however, say that this position is untenable because it is a proof of what is already established (siddhasādhyatva), just as in the case of the statement "sound is audible. He shows these [objections]:
"Some here say there is a proving of what is already established by means of the seed, karma, and atoms."

The Sāṃkhyas argue: "Indeed, you are proving that the world has a creator as its antecedent; however, that which is denoted by the term 'seed' as the material cause—namely, that which is called *pradhāna*—is already established. So what is it that remains to be proved? Likewise, the world arises from karma alone; therefore, it is karma itself [that is the cause].
The followers of Jaimini maintain that [the elements] are established as being the agents themselves; as they say:

"If it is claimed that some [element] possesses the status of a mere cause by virtue of being a supervisor, then since that is already established through the actions (karma) of all living beings, you are proving what is already proven."

The Lokāyatikas maintain that only atoms are established as the agents of action whose fruits are perceived; what, then, is to be proven [by an afterlife], since it is impossible for there to be any action other than those with perceived fruits? As they say:
"The person (puruṣa) is the body characterized by consciousness."
He refutes this in sequence:
"Because it is not distinguished from the two preceding [causes], that [cognition] could not be the means of proving the object. (14)
That [objection] regarding the proving of what is already established by means of the two previous [arguments], namely seed and karma, does not apply;

for why? He says: "Because that which is to be proved is qualified by intelligence (*dhī*). For the proving of what is already established is indeed a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*); and we do not prove that the world has merely an agent as its antecedent, but rather—

It has been stated that the distinction [of the subject] is its being preceded by an intelligent agent—that is, "the effects such as mountains and so forth, which have unseen agents, were created by one possessed of wisdom.
Nor is there intelligence in the seed or in karma; therefore, how could this be a case of proving what is already established?

Now, the Buddhists maintain that actions are indeed volitions alone, since they do not admit any other action apart from the volition of giving and so forth. Let it be so in the case of the specific acquisition [of merit]; however, for those [actions] acquired through various states of being, there exist various latent impressions (*vāsanā*), even though they are not perceived as having a distinct form.
This is nothing at all, because [the existence of] sentient beings is admitted. || 14 ||
He has also said regarding the Lokāyatas: "Because the subject (*dharmin*) to be proven, such as the body and so forth, is [already] accepted [by us],
there is no proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) by others, nor even by atoms."

Because the body, the instruments [of perception], the world, and so forth have been acquired [by an agent], and since for you it is not established that atoms are the makers of the body, the instruments, and so on, how can there be the fallacy of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhyatā*)? [Objection: But surely those very [atoms] are established as the makers of jars and such things.
[Reply: True; for that very reason, they have been made the examples here. [Objection: But are not living beings like bubbles in water?

We infer that things endowed with diverse bodies arise from causes that are themselves of diverse natures, because [the effects] conform to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of those [causes].
No, [this is not so], because the cause is unestablished; for when there is a difference in the causes—such as velocity, wind, rain, and so forth—there is a difference in the effects.

The distinction between the large and small size of water bubbles and the like is indeed established; however, no difference in the cause of living beings is established, since there is no distinction in the semen, blood, and so forth.
Furthermore, if a difference in effects were to exist without a difference in causes, it would follow that the entire universe is without a cause.
And it has been stated that there can be no restriction of place, time, or form for that which is causeless. Now, one might object:

"But surely even semen, blood, and so forth possess distinct intrinsic natures. If this were the case, then because they would be as distinct from one another as a jar and a cloth, they would always produce effects of distinct forms; [consequently,] regarding effects—
If it is argued that the identity of form as a living being is untenable because even the causes— such as semen and blood— are not identical [to the effect],
then it would follow that the effects themselves must also be identical [to one another].
There would be no distinction among living beings, such as their being prosperous or otherwise.

Now, one might argue that even though they are similar, some possess a certain unseen nature (*adṛṣṭa*)—like magnets and the like—which attracts wealth and other things. But surely that [nature] too cannot be without a cause.
It has been stated that [this] is possible. If it is thus, it will have an unseen cause (*adṛṣṭa-hetuka*).
In that case, there would be no rejection of an unseen cause; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
Thus it was stated while assuming that seeds and the like possess agency; now, however, he says that such agency is not even possible:
"There can be no activity because of insentience, due to the independence of the actions of seeds. (15)

It has been stated that he who is the Lord of the causal factors (kārakas) regarding both engagement (pravṛtti) and withdrawal (nivṛtti) is the "agent" (kartṛ) by virtue of his sovereignty. Since insentient things possess no such sovereignty therein, they lack agency even if they function as causes. || 15 ||
He states the opponent's intention— that agency is observed even for that which lacks consciousness— as follows:
"If it be said 'like milk,' as the Sāṃkhyas say."
"Just as the flow of milk from the insentient [cow] is for the sake of the growth of the calf,
so too is the activity of the Pradhāna for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa.
To this, he states the following reply:
It is not so, because [the material cause] is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and because clay, the staff, and so forth are not observed [to act independently].
For milk does not establish independence, because it is insentient (*acetana*), like clay, a staff, and so on;
it too is said to be impelled by an agent alone.
Now, it might be argued that since *sattva* and *tamas* are non-active by nature, while *rajas* is admitted to be active in essence,
and because the *guṇas* possess a nature of mutual assistance like lamps and other such things, agency will belong to them. As it has been said:

"The qualities (guṇas) consist of pleasure, pain, and dejection; they serve the purposes of illumination, activity, and restraint; and their functions are mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship.
To refute this, he says:

Furthermore, the relationship of being a constituent part and its possessor (aṅga-aṅgitva) regarding existence and so forth arises from their intrinsic nature, not from the reason already stated. || 16 ||
Precisely because they are insentient, there can be no mutual assistance among them by their own nature;
rather, like a lamp and so forth, they are impelled by a sentient agent. Thus, the agency of that which is insentient is not established.
Furthermore:
the activity of a seed after having remained [latent] does not occur without consciousness.
Whatever proceeds after having remained [latent] is presided over by consciousness, just like a jar and so forth.

Furthermore, having experienced a state of rest during the great dissolution through the withdrawal of all modifications, primordial matter (pradhāna) proceeds again at the beginning of creation; therefore, it too must have a conscious supervisor,
and thus the existence of God is established.

Here, the opponent objects: "But surely knowledge exists in the *pradhāna*, because knowledge is admitted to belong to the intellect (*buddhi*), which is an effect of the *pradhāna*; therefore, the *pradhāna* must also [possess it]."
Since that which consists of knowledge is established, what else remains to be inferred? As it has been said:
"Intellect (buddhi) is determination; its sattvic form consists of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty."
This too he refutes:
"Not so, because of the lack of consciousness, like clay and other [inert materials]. (17)
That is incorrect, because you have stated that both the manifest (vyakta) and the unmanifest (avyakta) are insentient; for it is said:
"The manifest and the Pradhāna are composed of the three guṇas, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive. (SK 11) || 17 ||
How then do you maintain that there is knowledge (*jñāna*) in the intellect (*buddhi*), which is its effect? To this he says:
"Or rather, let it be [unperceived] because it exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*); thus it is equivalent to non-existent.
It is called 'knowledge' (*jñāna*) because by means of it, something is known in the intellect."

We accept that it is of the nature of light (*prakāśātmaka*), but not that it is solely of the nature of cognition (*jñaptirūpa*), because its essential nature is that of the Puruṣa alone. Even though it is of such a nature, it is not manifest within Pradhāna, which is the causal self;
rather, it exists in the form of a potentiality (*śaktyātman*). Thus, [it is distinct] from that which consists of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāyātman*).

Because it does not perform its own function, it is equivalent to a non-existent thing. Consequently, since there is an absence of knowledge—which by nature consists of determinative apprehension—this [cognition] lacks agency; thus, the existence of another agent is established.

As for what was stated— "The activity of a seed [occurs] after it has remained [latent], and there is no consciousness without a conscious being"— the Sāṃkhyas maintain that this is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Because Śambhu also acts while remaining [in that state], he too is subject to being surpassed by others.

Furthermore, even for the seed—or for the *Īśvara* as imagined by you—there exists neither persistence nor activity; nor is there, as in the case of a jar and so forth, the state of being presided over by a conscious agent. Therefore, because this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), it does not [establish] the [existence of] *Pradhāna* either.
The state of being presided over by volition.
He dispels the charge of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) by means of a portion of the *kārikā*: "Because the wise Lord is not equal [to us].
For here, by virtue of the context, the qualification of the reason as "insentience" (acetanya) is understood.
There is no inconclusiveness.

Now, it may be argued that the multiplicity of effects is pervaded by the multiplicity of agents; therefore, since there is a multiplicity of effects—such as the body, the sense organs, and the world, just like a jar or a cloth—it is logical to infer multiple agents, whether for oneself or others, similar to cooks and the like. Consequently, the existence of a single Lord (Īśvara) is not established. As it has been said:
Maṇḍana:
Although it may be established that everything possessing a specific arrangement and so forth has an intelligent cause, how can there be a single cause for such arrangements and the like?
Having thus set forth the opponent's view, he refutes it: "In the world, many things such as Devadatta are seen to be endowed with cognition. (19)

For that which, having remained stationary, proceeds [to act]—such as in cooking and so forth—is not impelled by another; even if it were impelled by another, there would be doubt regarding Maheśvara because of this [same principle]. (20)
This might be so, provided that the mutual relationship of constituent parts among this collection of effects— such as bodies, organs, and the world— is not established; for when that is established,

just as there is a single architect for a collection of effects consisting of parts such as pillars and beams, there must likewise be a single creator endowed with superior knowledge and other qualities.
It is not a fault that many [causes] do not achieve [the effect]; therefore, as for what was also said:
"In this world, even parts such as those of a chariot, though fashioned by various different carpenters, are generally seen to be related as benefactor and beneficiary."

Thus, this [position] is refuted by that very [argument], because even in the case of parts of a chariot and so forth constructed by various makers, the relationship of mutual assistance (upakāryopakārakabhāva) cannot be established without a single cognition. || 20 ||
If it is argued that he too, like an architect or similar figure, must be prompted by another,
the author states the reason to refute this: "Because we shall describe later on the Lord who is marked by transcendence."
Since we shall establish that very [entity] as being endowed with supreme excellence, therefore this fault does not apply.
He shows another pair of objections stated by others:
"But while the world is asleep, does Hara remain waiting? (21)
For he, though indeed independent, creates the world and so forth at all times;
and because he is devoted to compassion, he should create only happiness and the like.

That which causes delusion, suffering, and so forth for human beings is not fitting [for the Creator]. Wise persons act with a purpose in mind; yet we perceive no purpose for the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) in failing to create at the time of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). As they say:
"Even a fool does not engage in action without aiming at a purpose;
nor would there be any purpose for him through such work as that of Prajāpati.
Now, if it is argued that he always engages [in activity] out of compassion alone and not for his own personal purpose, [the response follows:]
Regarding this, they also say:
"Impelled by compassion, he would create only that which is auspicious;
for otherwise, neither creation nor maintenance is possible without the inauspicious."
"For when the means are dependent upon oneself, what indeed could be difficult? And for him who created the world, what desired object could possibly not be accomplished?
Regarding this, he states that it is merely a fallacious objection:
For non-existence is not postulated simply because something is established by valid cognition. || 23 ||

Even when such objections are presented by others in this manner, an object established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot indeed be altered by human fabrications; for those fabrications do not apply to it, as they lack any necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with it. As they have said:
If flawless inference were to exist for the proof of a creator through such fickle conceptualizations as these, then the purpose would be accomplished; yet,
there is no flawless inference for the proof of a creator.
"If the accomplishment of the goal were achieved by such fickle conceptualizations...
To that, he first dispels the objection: "The seed, which produces the sprout, depends upon time, soil, and so forth. (24)
Just as a farmer in this world, so too is the Supreme Lord;
[He observes] the time for the enjoyment of men and the ripening of their karmas. (25)
And the source of the world (jagadyoni) awaits the time for the production of the world,
because Prakṛti’s power is exceedingly diminished by its being the means for the enjoyment of incessant and infinite [objects]; thus,
like effects and causes, or like the field (kṣetra) and so forth, it necessarily [awaits].
We shall explain that, upon the cessation of all activities, a state of rest designated as dissolution (pralaya) must be admitted at some point; and in that state,
