it is the production of the capacity for this [puruṣa] to serve as a means for experience, just as [the capacity for experience is produced] for a farmer and the like.
Just as there is a purpose in waiting for the field, the seed, and so forth, there is no lack of purpose here.
He also refutes the second objection:
"Whatever kind of action has been performed by someone, for him there is a result of that same kind. (26)
The Lord bestows fruit upon a person in dependence upon [that person's] karma.

We do not maintain, like the proponents of non-duality (advaitavādins), that the fruits of pleasure, pain, and so forth for persons come from the Lord alone—which would entail this fault. As it has been said:
"One should not create a disturbance in the minds of those ignorant ones who are attached to action;
rather, the wise man, being disciplined, should cause them to engage in all actions by performing them himself.
However, this refers to one's own actions as real entities, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice or the killing of a Brahmin.

What is this objection—"from the performance of good and evil"? If it is thus [the case] that the fruit arises solely from human activity, then what is the use of God? True, if the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice were seen to follow immediately after the ritual action, as is the case with eating and so forth.

In that case, since the fruit belongs to the next world (*āmuṣmika*) and not to this world (*naihhika*), even though it is something to be accomplished, it would— like the fruit of agriculture and so forth— occur at a later time; and because, according to the method to be explained, it is impossible for a mere person (such as one who performs the preparation or protection) to [attain it] alone, therefore, [it must be] *sātiśaya*...
There is no fault in the establishment of God, even given the existence of karma, because it must be brought about by another who possesses knowledge and so forth.
Now, it might be argued that His activity is improper because He has no purpose in the arrangement of the fruits of the karma of infinite persons; as they say:
"And from such extensive activity, there would be much greater affliction.
To this, he says:
"This alone is compassion—that one should bring about the welfare of others. (27)
Otherwise, the futility of his action would follow, as in the case of Hara’s lack of sentience.

This is not so; for here, his engagement is established through compassion alone, just as the engagement of a king or similar authority is established in the protection of unprotected and helpless beings. Otherwise, since there would be no purpose, one could not admit his engagement in this matter.

Without an agent who performs the arrangement and so forth, actions such as agriculture— which yield results at a later time— would become fruitless, just as in the case of the position that denies the existence of a Lord (Īśvara).

Consequently, because of the non-existence of saṃsāra, [the world] would not evolve through a process of differentiation, according to the principle that "without a mixer, there is no transformation."
Furthermore, because impurity would not undergo transformation, there would be no liberation; thus, the consequence would be the total annihilation of everything.
To this, the opponent replies: "But [if you say the soul acts] depending on karma and so forth, then the consequence would be a lack of independence. (28)
For that which is dependent is incapable [of independent action]. As they say:
"And thus, for one who is dependent, independence is obstructed. He offers this rebuttal:
That which is independent, not to be employed by another, yet itself requires others, employs the causes and so forth, and is never itself employed by them. (29)
This indeed is the independence of the agent, which does not consist in a lack of dependence on action and so forth;
for it is that state of kings and others not being impelled by another's independence,
as well as their own procurement of means such as elephants and horses, and [the management] of those already procured.

The application [of action] according to what is required is called "sovereignty" (svātantrya); however, it is not the performance of acts of restraint or favor while disregarding the objects to be restrained or favored.
For that would be called madness, not sovereignty. It is the same for the Blessed Lord as well.
"There is no loss of independence on the part of [the Lord] because he is dependent upon karma, since there is an absence of being impelled by another.
Regarding this, they say: "Whatever has the nature of being the agent of a certain action necessarily performs that action, just as fire possesses heat;
and since the Lord does not perform any action during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), He does not have the nature of an agent. This...
He refutes [this objection]: "And even when completely withdrawn, he does not remain devoid of all activity. (30)
In the form of the power of the universe (jagacchakti), it sustains the inactive source of the world;
it ripens the karmas of the person and also brings them to rest.
He bestows grace upon those who are to be graced and restrains those who are to be restrained;

indeed, having withdrawn the entire universe— which is characterized by birth, movement, and so forth, and consists of the principles, states of being, elements, and worlds, from *kalā* down to the earth— in its manifest form, he [remains] in the nature of power (*śakti*).

And it has been stated by the Teacher, in his presentation of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), that at that time [Nature] maintains its own primordial state (*prakṛti*) from which the activity of the world has been withdrawn, for the sake of experience and liberation; and at that time, the *karmas*—
having become latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) within Nature due to their diminished momentum— bring them to fruition, as do the persons (*puruṣa*).

It causes rest for those exhausted by wandering through worldly existence; at that time, it also bestows grace upon certain others whose impurities have matured, since scripture declares that grace extends even to the *vijñānakevala* and *pralayakevala* stages; furthermore, it brings about the cessation of those whose impurities have not yet matured, and thus [the reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Thus, by this reasoning, it is not established that Īśvara is a non-agent. It is also stated in the *Śrī Mṛgendra*:
"Even during his sleep, he awakens those fit for awakening, restrains those to be restrained, and causes the karma of those bound by karma to bear its fruit."
Making the power of illusion (māyā-śakti) capable of manifestation, he perceives every category of entity exactly as it is.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Examination of the Lord," in the *Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa*, the work of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, son of the venerable Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha. || 2 ||
The Nareśvaraparīkṣā, composed by the venerable Ācārya Sadyojyotis, [belonging to] the Yogatantra-granthamālā.
Accompanied by the commentary *Prakāśa* composed by the venerable teacher Rāmakaṇṭha.
Adorned with the preface of the noble gentleman, Professor Rāmamūrti Śarmā; edited by Ācārya Śrī Rāmajī Mālavīya.
The teacher is likewise the supervisor of the division of the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Tantra, and Āgama.
The Vice-Chancellor of Sampurnanand Sanskrit University,
Varanasi.
In Vārāṇasī, in the year 2056 of the Vikrama era, in the year 1921 of the Śaka era, and in the year 2000 of the Christian era;
now begins the third book (kāṇḍa).
Having established, by means of valid cognition, the Lord as proven in his own system, he speaks in order to refute the nature of the Lord as established in other systems:
"The Supreme Self is omniscient; from Him, both the conscious and the unconscious arise."

The knowers of the matured Vedānta maintain that you describe the Lord as omniscient and the creator of all; let Him be the Supreme Self alone, who is the material cause of all sentient and insentient things—what need is there for a separate Lord? And thus says the Śruti:

"The Puruṣa alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be. Now, since the eternity of conscious beings has been stated, how can there be their origination from that? True; however, this is said even while granting [the premise], so there is no fault.
He refutes this:
"But when that [seed] is primary, everything that has been stated becomes as if unstated. (1)
This would be reasonable if you did not accept it as a causal basis by way of being a seed; however, since you do accept it as such,
none of this is at all tenable.
Regarding this, he states that the following is not tenable:
"Without a cause, because of its unity, that seed is not considered to be the producer of an effect.
Whatever is a seed does not have the nature of producing an effect by depending on auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*).

It is exclusively [the cause], just like the seed of rice and so forth. Furthermore, you maintain that the Supreme Self is the seed of the world, and it has no other auxiliary cause; for since the doctrine of duality is rejected by the admission that "the Person alone is all this," therefore—
The very impossibility of the world's characteristics as effects [proves this]; as it has been said: "That which is unmixed does not undergo transformation."
And it is not the case that this reason is inconclusive because of the silkworm; for this reason he says:
"Since even the spider-weaver depends upon pillars and the like. (2)
For even he, while constructing a sheath with mere saliva, certainly requires a support such as a pillar. As it has been stated by the followers of Jaimini:
"And no agent ever creates anything without means."
Creation is not held to be possible without a substratum, just as in the case of a spider.
Furthermore, from devouring living beings, his saliva flows forth. Thus [it is said]. (2)
Furthermore, he states that it is not logically possible for two contradictory things to have a single material cause:
"And because [the Self] would produce both the conscious and the unconscious, it would partake of the attributes of both the conscious and the unconscious;
for as the effect is, so indeed must its material cause be."

Just as you maintain that gold and other such materials are the material cause (*upādāna*) of effects such as necklaces and jars—which possess the natures of both sentient and insentient things—so too it would follow that the Supreme Self must possess a nature contradictory to both sentience and insentience. [Objection: No, for [the effect arises] even from that which does not possess such a nature.

This is not so, because [the argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the observation that fire and other effects arise from sun-gems (*sūryakānta*) and the like. No; for precisely this reason, it is the sunlight itself, acting in conjunction with the sun-gem, that serves as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) in that instance. By this same logic, in the production of water from moon-gems (*candrakānta*) and of wind and so forth from fans and the like, it is the moonlight—

One should consider that only air and the like—acting as auxiliary causes such as moonstones, fans, and so forth—are the material causes [of these effects]. This is because even in enclosed spaces and the like, the existence of air is established through the movement of cotton and other such objects. Furthermore, even when scorpions arise from cow dung and similar substances, for us [Buddhists], there is no production of a conscious being.

Since there certainly exists a similarity with respect to the material cause for that body, the charge of inconclusiveness is absent; therefore, the consequence of possessing a contradictory nature—being both conscious and unconscious—remains exactly as it was.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says:
"And because of the contradiction between those two, that [simultaneity] could not exist at one and the same time. (3)

And because those two are contradictory, they cannot possibly exist simultaneously in a single locus, just like existence and non-existence; therefore, it is impossible for that one [entity] to possess the nature of two contradictories. (3)
This was stated on the assumption that consciousness (*cetanā*) is the material cause (*upādāna*); however, now he says that this very [assumption] is untenable:
"For, by virtue of being a material cause, that [consciousness] would be insentient (*acetana*), like clay and so forth."
Therefore, with respect to the task at hand, one requires a person possessed of wisdom.

For a material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) is indeed by nature insentient, such as clay and the like; and since you maintain that the one designated as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the material cause, it too must be insentient. Furthermore, that which is insentient possesses the nature of cause and effect only when presided over by a sentient being.
Since clay and other such materials are determined [to have specific forms], they too must have a conscious presiding agent;
thus, the existence of God (Īśvara) is established. How then is the scriptural statement "All this is indeed the Person" (Puruṣa) to be understood?
Precisely because of that [dependence on the Person], it is a figurative expression (upacāra), like saying "Clarified butter is life," and thus there is no contradiction. || 4 ||
Others, however, [quote]:
"Beyond the Great (mahat) is the Unmanifest (avyakta); beyond the Unmanifest is the Person (puruṣa). There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal."

Since it is established by such scriptural passages as these that the Lord is none other than the Person (puruṣa) himself, they ask: "What need is there for anything else? He refutes them [with the following]:
"The Self is distinct from the unevolved body and so forth, possessing unmanifested power of vision and action."
Because it is like a seed and so forth, it does not know anything, nor does it do anything at all.

The Puruṣa, too, must be either one whose body and organs have not yet arisen and who is thus the cause of his own body and so forth, or one whose body and organs have already arisen. In this regard, he is one for whom the body and so forth have not arisen from the unmanifested seed called *avyakta*, and for whom the powers of vision (*dṛk*) and action (*kriyā*) are undifferentiated, inseparable, and unmanifested. This is why [he is the cause].
Just as one in the state of deep sleep knows nothing nor performs any action, how then can [the Self] be the agent of its own body and so forth? || 5 ||
Nor is the second position tenable, because it contradicts direct perception; thus he says:

"Furthermore, one who has already acquired a body and so forth cannot be the cause of his own body and so forth, since that [body] is seen to be already fully established for him from some other source. (6)

For it is not observed that one who possesses a body can be the creator of another body within himself, as is seen in the case of a yogin entering another's body; rather, that body and so forth are seen to arise from other causes, such as the parents of that [new] being. || 6 ||
Furthermore:

Because there is no cognition of the cause, the fruit, and their respective classes, nor of the body and so forth, and because the seed and other factors lack the capacity for movement, [the effect] does not belong to another. (7)

For indeed, the agent— knowing the price and so forth as the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) of an effect such as a jar, its purpose such as the holding of water and so forth, the clay and so forth as the material cause (*upādāna*), and the body, the potter’s wheel, and so forth as the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*)— is established as possessing the state of agency. And yet, the person [does not possess agency] with respect to his own body.

The cause— previously accumulated karma— is capable of being known as having a fruit consisting of diverse enjoyments, with specific semen and blood as its material cause (*upādāna*) and food and so forth as its auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*);
because of the failure to understand this, it lacks the capacity to impel the seeds and other factors that are the causes of its own body.
Even for another person who has obtained a body, there is a state of non-agency. || 7 ||
The opponent [objects]: "Your argument here is inconclusive because of what is established by yourself;
for just as a person employs the mind even without seeing it, so too will he employ karma and the rest."

Just as you maintain that a person employs the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) without knowing its true nature, so too he would employ seeds, karma, and other causes of his own body without knowing them; thus,
the reason "being a non-knower" is inconclusive for establishing "non-agency."
This objection is refuted by a portion of the verse: "Because it is unestablished, there is no proof. (8)

The reason would be inconclusive only if the invisibility of the internal organ were established for us; however, it has been stated in the *Tattvasaṅgraha* that, in its nature as a mental modification (*vṛtti*), the power of cognition is always indeed cognizable: [The relevant verse from the Tattvasaṅgraha: "Because it is of the nature of a modification, it is always perceived by the self through the cognition of that [modification]; therefore, the internal organ is not unperceived. (TS 198) Thus, since the internal organ is never truly invisible, the reason is not inconclusive.
"Even if the Great One (Mahat) were of a nature as luminous as the sun, nevertheless, because it is an object (*karman*),
it would require another instrument (*karaṇa*) to be able to make itself known.
Since that [Mahat] too, once known, must be impelled, agency is impossible here without knowledge.

Having granted for the sake of argument that the internal organ is not perceived, he avoids the charge of inconclusiveness [of the reason]: "In that case as well, there must be a knowing impeller, because it is an effect, just like a jar or other such things; therefore, it too must have a conscious impeller."
"There must be [a cause]," thus is the proof of Īśvara. And so says the Śruti:
"He who impels our thoughts.
The Naiyāyikas maintain that the initial motion of atoms and the mind is caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
For this very reason, it is taught that the person is dependent upon Īśvara even with respect to experience. || 9 ||
And so they have said:
"The gods do not protect by taking up a staff like a herdsman;
rather, whomsoever they wish to protect, they endow with intelligence."
Regarding this, they raise the following objection: "Surely the parents provide the means of enjoyment for their son and others;
for it is the mother and the father alone who [provide these] for the son or the daughter."
Since they are seen producing a body, how can there be no agency for the person (puṃs) in this matter?
He refutes this [objection]: "There is nothing such as *kalā* and so forth that is distinct from the mere body, which is gross. (10)

In the case of both the eternal and the pervasive [causes], their conjunction and the acquisition of functional activity would not produce an effect that is not born of a womb, for they do not belong to the Supreme.
Those two, while producing only a gross body,
are perfected [in their power], but not a separate set of sense organs, nor the connection of the person with the body and senses;
furthermore, because the self is eternal and all-pervading, even though it is connected to all bodies, [the powers manifest] only through a specific body.

They do not bring about the acquisition of activity for that [body] through knowledge and action; nor is it possible for them to produce a non-womb-born body such as that of a mosquito or a fly. Since this is so, therefore, this [agency] of the supreme person consisting of intellect and so forth, as imagined by you, does not exist here.
The word "agency" (kartṛtva) is to be supplied [as the subject]; from that, the existence of another agent is established. || 11 ||

Having thus accepted the agency of the gross body, [the author] states the following objection in order to show that such agency is untenable: "Why do the parents not create a body for themselves, O wise ones?"

If it is merely a matter of connection with the seed, then just as those two possess agency in the body solely through that connection with the seed, so too will it be in the case of the sense organs and so forth; thus, how can there be the establishment of another agent?
He refutes this with a portion of the verse:
"By that much alone, it is not produced by that. (12)
Because the body and so forth are distinct from their effect, [the self] is not the effect whose nature consists in the presence of the seed that acts as its cause.
For instance: a jar would not be made merely by the application of clay and a wheel;
indeed, when one thing is made, another thing does not thereby become made.
He states their very difference as follows:
"In that regard, a composition must be made capable of accomplishing various purposes. (13)
For the nature of the jar is indeed something other than the clay, since it performs functions such as holding water.
He applies the same principle of distinctness to the case at hand as well:
"Likewise, the structure of the body, which is capable of accomplishing the goals of man, is observed; therefore, it should be understood by the wise as arising from a virtuous agent. (14)

Thus, because it consists of the conjunction of seeds, the effect that accomplishes various enjoyments is indeed other than [the mere] effect; therefore, there must be an agent for it who is distinct and possesses excellence.
In this regard, the intention of the opponent is expressed by a portion of the verse:

if the *bimba* (the original form) consists of the semen and blood, then the state of the *ghana* (solid mass), following the abandonment of the *kalala* (embryonic jelly) stage, is called the *bimba*.
Therefore, that arrangement arises from food and other such factors, not from another agent.
He refutes this as follows:
"For in that very case, something different is also seen;
it is not the case that the construction of everything, such as a son and so forth, is of a single uniform nature, because there is no distinction [in the cause] consisting merely of the reflection."
If it were so, there would be a contradiction with what is perceived.
Furthermore, according to the portion of the verse, the opponent [argues] that if it were wind, then the status of being the creator of the arrangement would be established for wind alone everywhere.
The Teacher says:
Even for that [intellect], there is no independence, because it would entail the loss of consciousness. (15)
In the preceding section, the autonomy of both the seed and action was correctly refuted;
just as in the second chapter agency was denied to the seed as the material cause and to action because of their lack of consciousness, so too must it be denied to the wind.
Furthermore:
"And such a task cannot be accomplished without one of preeminent knowledge. (16)
In those various locations where there is no persistence of skin and so forth, that which remains there would be incapable of performing the function of an atom. (17)

Indeed, an effect such as the body, characterized in this way and endowed with superior knowledge and other qualities, cannot possibly exist without a creator; for [otherwise], how could there be these various [faculties] here in the body—
namely, the ears, eyes, and so forth among the nine gates, including the skin and, by the inclusion of "and so forth," the eyes and others?

Since no abiding [of the self] is observed in the soles of the feet and other such parts, that which were to abide there would be incapable of accomplishing the goals of human endeavor; thus, there is no agency for those two who possess no knowledge.
Here, however, the opponent [objects]:
By a person performing action with heaven and the like as its objective, that [action] is set in motion;
and that [action], moreover, cannot bring about its fruit without the body and other such factors. (18)
Therefore,

we do not claim that the person is the direct agent of everything, such as the body and so forth, which would entail this fault; rather, we maintain that all is done by the person through mere intention (abhisandhi), as established by scriptural injunctions such as "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" regarding actions for heaven and the like.
By performing [the action], it is impelled through the medium of that latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*);
and just as that [impression] produces results such as purgation by bringing about a specific transformation in the *harītakī* fruit and so forth,
it accomplishes its own result— such as heaven— by bringing about the body and so on, through the intention for the result.

When a person performs only the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites, everything performed by him as an imitation of those [original] acts is said to be "done" by them; however, there is no fault here, because unlike in the case of the primary rites themselves, there is no evidence for his being the actual agent in that regard.
He says: "The reason is not inconclusive because it is not pervasive, since it does not exist in places such as the hells. (19)
For men do not perform acts such as the killing of a Brahmin with the aim of experiencing the sufferings of hell and so forth;
rather, they act solely out of desire and the like, pursuing visible results.
Thus, the experience of hellish fruits and the like is logically untenable for them. (19)

Now, it is stated by another scriptural passage that "those who kill a Brahmin shall dwell in the Avīci hell for an eon," meaning that such a state occurs for the perpetrator of that act. Let it be so; however, he is not its producer.

Since agency is not established for a person without intentional purpose (*abhisandhāna*), the Lord must be accepted as distinct from him, just as a king is [distinct] from the punishment of a thief. For it is thus:
even that which is pervaded, such as a jar and the like, is seen to have been made by an intelligent being.
By that much alone, and in that same manner, hell and the other realms will come to be. || 20 ||
It is established that things such as jars, which are pervaded by the state of being an effect, are created by an intelligent agent;
therefore, it is understood that hell and the like are also created by an intelligent agent, precisely because they are effects, just like jars and other such objects. || 20 ||

Nor is it established as a rule that even for those actions performed with a view toward a remote result, the production of that result occurs independently of any further operation on the part of the agent; thus he says:
"Nor can satisfaction arise from plowing and the like by mere intention alone."
Therefore, without another action, it must arise from a different collection of causal conditions. || 21 ||
In the same way, heaven and other such results may arise from the performance of dharma through another action; yet that [result] cannot exist without Īśvara. Thus, the Supreme Lord is established.
For people engage in agriculture and such activities for the sake of results such as food, not out of mere addiction;

nor does that fruit of theirs arise from the act of plowing alone, but rather from subsequent operations by other agents, beginning with its cultivation and protection and ending with its consumption. It is just like that.
Heaven and the like, when performed with those as the intended goal, do not arise from the mere act of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rituals;
rather, they depend on other acts that produce a body and so forth suitable for experiencing them.
Therefore, that [other agent] must also be one who possesses excellence over the performers of those other acts—thus is the proof of God (Īśvara). || 22 ||
But surely he too will be a *puruṣa* (spirit), as they say:
"The Lord (*īśvara*) is a special *puruṣa* untouched by afflictions, actions, their results, and latent dispositions.
To this, he replies:

And because he is sought after by men, and because his vision and action are unobstructed, it is therefore certain that he has cast off his male nature due to its dissimilarity with that [of ordinary men]. (23)
For individuals (puruṣas), because they are veiled by ignorance, are said to be knowers of only a little and doers of only a little.

However, when God (īśvara) is postulated on the grounds that the effects—such as the creation of bodies and instruments—which are impossible for individuals to accomplish, would otherwise be inexplicable, He is established as being distinct from them, possessing unobscured power of vision and action; He is not merely a particular individual.
Since he too is a person, he lacks the capacity for that; or, if he did possess such capacity, he would not be a person. Therefore:

The proponent of the Person (puruṣavādī) says to the proponent of the established tenet (siddhāntavādī): "Those who postulate a Lord (Īśa) on the grounds of masculinity and so forth [as being] devoid of all-knowing cognition and activity, stand refuted because their reason is unestablished, for [masculinity] is observed in the self (ātman). (24)
Because a person lacks omniscience and other such qualities, he possesses no capacity for the creation of bodies and instruments; therefore,

there must necessarily exist another, an omniscient being capable of that creation— thus it is that those who maintain the existence of a distinct Person (puruṣaviśeṣavādins) establish an "other" Lord (īśvara) based on a reason that is unestablished for us.
They too, through the notion of a Lord, are established within the Self alone, which is a particular Puruṣa. || 24 ||
To the question "How so?", he says:
Why indeed is the Person himself not accepted by them as one whose vision and action are unobstructed, even though they postulate a Lord with great effort? (25)
For, since effects such as bodies and instruments would otherwise be inexplicable, some agent endowed with omniscience and other qualities must be postulated by them;
and that [agent] must be postulated as a specific Person (Puruṣa) alone, and nothing else. For in this way, no further distinct category (dharma-antara) is postulated. || 25 ||
But the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says:
"It is not accepted [that there is a creator] because of the absence of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and because of the fault that [otherwise] everyone would be omniscient.
If there were a valid cognition regarding the lordship of a particular person, then the reason (hetu) would be unestablished (asiddha)."

But that [state] does not exist, because you yourselves admit that he, like ourselves and others, is endowed with intellect and the other faculties; for if he were devoid of those, Īśvara would indeed be liberated, and not a distinct type of person (puruṣaviśeṣa)— which is precisely our own position.

Furthermore, because of the connection with intellect (*buddhi*) and the other [faculties], omniscience would exist even in another person; thus, there is the undesirable consequence that everyone would be omniscient.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says:
Consequently, the scriptures as well as the world’s architects and others would not exist. || 26 ||
For it is not logical that one who perceives all objects should be the perpetrator of evil by his own nature, nor is suffering born of various kinds seen to belong to him. (27)
Consequently, because they would be omniscient, it would follow that for all [beings], there is an absence of any teaching regarding things beyond the senses,
as well as an absence of their own engagement with the causes of harm and the experience of various kinds of suffering; for if that were not the case, they would simply not be omniscient.
Therefore, since persons must be admitted [as agents], the reason is not unestablished;

thus, the existence of a Lord distinct from the person is proven. How then are scriptural passages such as "There is nothing higher than the Person" to be understood? There is no fault, for these refer to everything, including the Lord and so forth, because they function solely for the benefit of that Person.

The followers of Jaimini state that the scripture alone— known as the Veda, which is uncreated— is the Lord; for it is this [scripture], by enjoining the fruits of demerit upon a person who transgresses its own commands consisting of injunctions and prohibitions, and no other, [that functions as the Lord].
"The accomplishment of action arises from the scripture, and the fruit arises from the performed action;
and since the scripture is uncreated, what is the use of Hara?"—
this [objection] he refutes with the following portion of the verse:
It is not purposeful. || 28 ||
This is not tenable. || 28 ||
To the question "Why?", he says: "The purpose of Śambhu is said to be the making of karma fruitful;
we shall explain later the supreme [purpose], which is the bringing about of liberation for the person. (29)

This has already been stated; for we shall explain that an action whose fruit is remote, such as agriculture and the like, is not capable of producing its effect if it is not presided over by consciousness. || 29 ||
"Is it not the case that when something is already perceived, it is not proper to postulate an unperceived entity? To this he replies:

"Just as stability is postulated for an action in order to establish [the attainment of] heaven and so forth, so too should Maheśvara be postulated; for without him, that [stability] does not exist. (30)

If this were so, then because human actions such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice—which consist of the casting of Soma into the fire and so forth—are rendered exhausted by the mere sight of the deity, the attainment of otherworldly fruits such as heaven would be impossible. [Objection: But surely, it must be admitted on the grounds that the scriptural declarations regarding fruits such as heaven would otherwise be inexplicable.

If it is postulated that [the action] remains unextinguished in the form of an unseen impression (*saṃskāra*), then since the postulation of an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is likewise possible, God (*īśvara*) must also be postulated; for it has already been stated that without Him, even that [unseen force] cannot be established as a producer of results. || 30 ||
Now, since this treatise takes the form of a composition, its uncreatedness is impossible;

therefore, to demonstrate that you must necessarily accept God as its author because the validity [of the treatise] would otherwise be inexplicable, [the author first addresses] the eternality of sound.
To refute this, he says:
"If color-form were eternal, why is it not perceived at all times?
For if that which has a perceptible nature were eternal, its nature would never perish."
There would follow the undesirable consequence that it must be perceived at all times.

By the portion of the verse beginning with "but because of its unmanifested state," the phrase "it is not perceived" is understood to carry over. For that which is manifested has a nature that is always perceptible.
Because it is unmanifest, it is not perceived due to that very state of being unmanifest.
The Teacher says: If that manifestation were eternal, then the defect would be eternal. (31)
If the manifestation of sound were also eternal, then the very same fault—that it would be perceived at all times—would result from its being eternal. || 31 ||
The opponent's intention, expressed by a portion of the verse, is as follows:
"If [the manifestation] were impermanent,
then, out of fear of this fault, it might be said that the manifestation of the word is impermanent."
The Teacher said:
"For what reason and by what means of valid cognition has impermanence been understood by you?"
The opponent states the proof:
"Because it exists only at certain times.
Since it occurs only occasionally, that manifestation is impermanent, like lightning and the like.
To this, he replies: "Even in the case of sound, its impermanence cannot be avoided, because it is the same [in that respect]. (32)

If, in this way, sound were perceived only when its own causes—such as the impact of the place of articulation and the organs of speech—are present, and was not perceived when they were absent, then let it be non-eternal like lightning and the like; what is the use of postulating this other [theory] of its manifestation? || 32 ||

[Objection: But surely, in the absence of that [sound], its non-perception is established otherwise (anyathāsiddha), because the person's auditory faculty is obstructed by stagnant air—just as for a deaf person regarding the object that is sound; therefore, it is not sufficient to prove the impermanence of the phonemes (varṇa). [Reply: That is incorrect, because:
The Maruti wind possesses no pride that would ever conceal the phonemes (varṇas).

There is simply no evidence for the claim that even though the phonemes exist at a time when there is no impact from the vocal organs and articulatory positions, they are not perceived by the auditory organ because they are obstructed by the stagnant air.

For if the air were excessive there, pain and other such symptoms would arise; hence the mention of "stagnant" (stimita). Furthermore, since the obstruction of the auditory organ would be no different [at that time], the phonemes would not be heard even at the moment of the impact of the place and the articulator.
[Objection: But surely they are heard because they are manifested at that time by the air produced from that [effort]. [Reply: No, because that is unestablished; thus he says:
"Nor is the air the manifester of the phonemes, because it does not grasp the phonemes situated behind it. (33)

For that which manifests [a sound] must be illuminating, not obstructing, because the two are contradictory; and air is observed to be an obstructor of phonemes (varṇas), since there is no perception of those phonemes situated behind it and followed by air, as is the case in a windless place.
Therefore, because sound is apprehended [from it], it is not established that air is the manifestor [of sound]. || 33 ||

Now, it might be argued that there is no perception of phonemes by means of the air produced through the impact of the articulatory places and organs— by which [you claim] this fault would arise— but rather, having reached the vicinity of the ear, it removes the dullness of the auditory faculty, and from that, the perception of the phoneme occurs. To this, he replies:
It is understood that this [wind] has not arrived because there is an absence of trembling and so forth;
for wind is characterized by touch, sound, support, and trembling, and in the absence of these characteristics,
how could it be known that it comes from the mouth of the speaker to the vicinity of the listener's ears?
Moreover, when the ear-cavity is completely filled, there would be the apprehension of all phonemes. (34)
When that manifestor pervades the cavity of the ear, because the obstruction has been removed, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving all sounds. || 34 ||
In this regard, the opponent’s capacity of the manifestor is understood from its effect as follows:
"Indeed, [the manifestor] does not manifest the phonemes even when they are closely joined, because we observe [the cognition] of only one. (35)

For if sound were eternal, just as its manifesting agency is postulated— namely, that the wind produced by the impact of the articulatory places and organs acts as a manifester through the medium of assisting the auditory organ because otherwise its perception would be impossible—
in the same way, from the perception of each individual phoneme, [the manifesting agency] must be postulated through the assistance of the specific power of the respective auditory organs.

Because one may postulate that the air produced by the impact of specific locations and articulatory organs possesses a specific power to manifest particular phonemes, this undesirable consequence does not arise. || 35 ||
He refutes this:
"If its status as a creator of manifestation were established, then this [argument] of his would be logical;
that is, if its being a creator of manifestation—its being a manifestor—were ever established for that air."
It might seem plausible to claim that a specific [quality] manifests a particular color; however, it has already been stated that this very point is unestablished.
Even granting this, he says: "Furthermore, this property of being a manifestor is not observed in the case of lamps and the like. (36)

It is logical that there is a difference in capacity among manifestors such as the eye and ear with respect to their respective manifested objects, such as form and sound, due to the difference in those objects; however, in the case of this [manifestor] such as a lamp, since its object—like form—is a single thing, namely sound, it is entirely improper to postulate a difference in capacity based on its internal subdivisions. || 36 ||
Furthermore:
If the permanence of phonemes were established, then a manifestor could be postulated;
but from what cause is their permanence established?

For in deep darkness, once the existence of jars and other objects is established through touch and so forth, a lamp or similar object is established as their manifestor; indeed, it is only when that [existence] is established that clay, the wheel, the staff, and so forth are said to be their producers.
Therefore, in this case as well, even in the absence of the impact of the articulatory places and organs (*sthāna-karaṇa-abhighāta*), the class of phonemes [is already established].
If there were a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the establishment of the existence of [manifesters], then they would indeed be manifesters;
however, in the absence of such a means, it is logical that they are merely producers (kāraka).
The opponent states the proof here with a portion of the verse:
"But because of recognition" (pratyabhijñānatastu). || 37 ||
"The very same color is this"—from this very perception called recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), which has a stable entity as its object, their stability [is established]. || 37 ||
He refutes this as follows: "Recognition is doubtful because one observes both that state and its opposite;
therefore, the claim that it is valid with respect to sound cannot be established without another reason. (38)

"That" refers to stability, and "not that" refers to instability; since that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is observed to exist even when both of these are present, we do not know whether it has stability as its object— like [the cognition of] a mountain and so forth— or whether it has instability as its object— like [the cognition of] a continuous stream of flames and so forth.

Because it is doubted whether [the cognition] is erroneous, it is not a means of valid proof (*sādhana*). Therefore, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) must indeed be stated in order to establish its stability. || 38 ||

Now, even if there is error in some instances of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), it is not erroneous in all cases, because its object is a thing being experienced, just like perceptual awareness (*ālocanajñāna*). As it has been said:
"The validity of all means of knowledge should be understood as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*)."
"For a capacity that does not exist by itself cannot be produced by another.
But rather, it is because of the existence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*). Here too, he states the subverting proof:
"The multiplicity of the phoneme [is] understood, like *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and so forth."
For it is uttered simultaneously by many men. || 39 ||

The phonemes, beginning with *a* and so forth, are distinct for each person because they are uttered simultaneously by many individuals, like the phonemes *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and so on. [Objection:
But surely, because these are manifestors (*vyañjaka*), their status as producers (*kāraka*) is unestablished. [Response: True, if...

Even in the absence of those [manifesters], there would be proof for the existence of the phoneme; however, since its non-existence is established in their absence, these [manifesters] do not possess the nature of manifestors, but rather the nature of producers—thus it has been stated, and therefore [the reason] is not unestablished.

Having thus accepted that recognition is not a valid means of proof because it is sublated, he now states that such recognition itself is not even possible: "Recognition is not perception, because the senses have ceased [to function] by that time."
Among the castes, it is understood through the manifestation of latent impressions and recollection. || 40 ||

In this case, recognition is not direct perception, but rather a mere semblance thereof; for it is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only because it determines its object immediately following a non-conceptual [perception].
As it has been said:
For there exists an initial non-conceptualizing cognition of mere observation,
which arises from the pure object itself and is similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and others.

"Beyond that, it is further determined by the intellect through the properties of the object, such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth; that [intellection] also is accepted as being of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This is because [the word] is perceived as perishing immediately upon being uttered.

When the activity of the senses has ceased for all classes of beings, recognition occurs in the form "this is that," arising from the perception of an object situated before one; it does not have a perceptible object as its domain,
but rather arises solely from memory, which consists in the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from prior experience, in the form "that very same thing."
Because it consists essentially of conceptual determination (*parāmarśa*), it is indeed a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). As it has been said:

"If, however, having perceived [an object], someone were to close their eyes and form a conceptualization, there would be no status as perception therein, because it does not follow from the [sensory] connection. (40)
It might be argued that, because recognition cannot otherwise be explained, sound must persist for some period of time; to this he says:
"Nor could stability of sound be possible for such a length of time."
Or, if stability [is admitted], then everything must be eternal, because recognition is observed. || 41 ||
In this way, there would be the undesirable consequence of imagining stability for everything, including a stream of water or a flame; thus, nothing at all would be impermanent. || 41 ||

To provide a summary, he says: "In this way, the eternity of the collection of phonemes is not tenable; that [eternity] is even more utterly discarded in the case of words, their combinations, and sentences. (42)

Thus, since it is impossible for a speaker to be the manifestor [of sounds], the impermanence of phonemes (*varṇa*) is established by virtue of their being produced causes; consequently, the impermanence of words (*pada*) composed of those phonemes, as well as the collection of sentences (*vākya-vrāta*) consisting of their conjunction, is also established. Therefore, [the same applies] to the Veda.

By the principle that validity cannot otherwise be accounted for (*prāmāṇyānyathānupapatti*), a Lord (*īśvara*) must be accepted as the creator— one whom you Buddhists do not rely upon because omniscience is difficult to establish, but certainly not because of a perception of faults.
As it has been said:
If, however, someone were to first create the world, along with dharma and adharma together with their means,
as well as the relationship between words and their meanings and the Vedas, [then there would be no fault].
"For the benefit of the world, no fault whatsoever attaches to the Veda;
yet, because it is as difficult to establish as the omniscience [of a Buddha], they have not relied upon it. (42)
Here, the opponent [objects]:
"If words are unstable, then once a word whose conventional meaning has been understood has perished, how could there be knowledge of the meaning from another [word] at this time? (43)

Since words and sentences—which consist of the conjunction of those words—are unstable, the conventional agreement (*saṃketa*) known for a particular word, such as a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix, has perished; that word has ceased to exist and another entirely new one, composed by a contemporary poet, has arisen. Therefore, because the convention has not been established for it, [the meaning cannot be understood].
Therefore, it follows that there would be an absence of knowledge of the meaning. || 43 ||
He states the reply:
"Surely, non-difference does not result from similarity; [the identity] is established through conformity.
What can we do? For there is indeed no means of valid cognition for the eternity of words. (44)

For when the impermanence of sounds is established by valid means of knowledge, their function—such as the communication of meaning—is indeed possible through a basis in a universal (sāmānya), just as it is for objects.
There is no contradiction here, as our notion of similarity as a universal is not like that of the Sāṃkhyas. || 44 ||
Here the opponent's intention is as follows: "Now, let the eternity of words be postulated precisely on this basis;
that is, the eternity of words is asserted because the communication of meaning would otherwise be impossible."
To show that this is incorrect, he says:
"In that case, [the cognition] would arise from the closing of the eyes and so forth; because it is similar to those, there is no permanence. (45)
Because even impermanent things—such as the winking of an eye, a hook, or a blow—are observed to convey meaning, this [reason] is inconclusive. || 45 ||
Even so, the opponent maintains that the proof for God being the creator does not hold here:
"There is no time devoid of scripture, nor is dissolution possible;
therefore, even at dawn, there is no such thing as an unauthored scripture. (46)
"A Brāhmaṇa should study the Veda with its six ancillaries; one born of a Brāhmaṇa father from a Brāhmaṇī mother, consecrated by the Vedic sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*,
is a Brāhmaṇa"— thus, because of this lack of distinction from the Āryan tradition, the Veda possesses authority precisely through its association with such qualified persons (*adhikārin*).

Because of the established nature of the continuum— like that of seeds and sprouts— even though it is impermanent, it possesses the quality of having no beginning (anidamprathamatva). For this very reason, since a time designated as "dissolution" (pralaya) devoid of scripture and its objects is impossible, and likewise the commencement of a day (aharmukha) for its creation and so forth is impossible, the Veda cannot have the Lord as its author.
As it has been said:
"There is no means of valid cognition for you regarding even the dissolution, since that dissolution consists in the total annihilation of everything. (46)
To this, he replies:
Having observed the deaths of living beings by the millions, it is concluded that there must indeed exist such a time wherein the destruction of all people occurs. (47)
Since the simultaneous creation and destruction of countless creatures, such as mosquitoes and flies, is observed, it follows that because all living beings are likewise creatures,
there must at some time be a simultaneous creation and destruction of all breath-bearing beings.
There is no fault, because the establishment of creation and dissolution [is possible]. || 47 ||
Regarding this, he states the opponent's intention through a portion of the verse:
"If such an action [is the cause], for the aggregation of the body and so forth is indeed dependent upon action and is not without a cause; nor is it..."
Since no karma is heard of as having the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) as its cause, [the claim] is untenable due to the absence of a reason.
As it has been said:
"Nor is this [dissolution] the fruit of any karma that has not been experienced."
To this, he gives the following answer by means of a portion of that very [work]:
"Death does not result from karma alone; rather, it results from its exhaustion."

Even the withdrawal of the body is not itself the fruit of karma, because it consists in the absence of experience; rather, it is merely projected by the exhaustion of the karma that produces experience. In the same way, the withdrawal of everything [the universe] is also so; thus there is no fault.
How then [do we explain such injunctions as]: "One desiring long life should sacrifice with a sacrificial fee of gold," or "One desiring death [should sacrifice]"?

The scriptural injunctions regarding longevity and non-longevity, such as "One should sacrifice with the Sarvasvāra," are intended solely for the purpose of implying other actions that bestow enjoyment and for their subsequent withdrawal; for indeed, mere longevity is not possible without enjoyment, nor does death occur when there exist actions that grant enjoyment.
[Objection: Even so, a great dissolution (mahāpralaya) remains untenable because other karmas that yield their fruits still exist. [The author] says:
"Even sleep [occurs] due to the non-ripening of others. (48)

Because another karma has not yet ripened and the previous one has already been experienced, this sleep called deep slumber (suṣupti)—which is projected by the requirement for the ripening of karma over some period of time—is established as such; however, it is not itself the fruit of karma. For even the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) is a form of sleep, and thus it too is projected solely by the ripening of karma.
Regarding the phrase "the fruit of karma": as for what was stated—"Nor is this non-experience the fruit of any karma"—that is merely proving what is already established. || 48 ||
Now, how is it that at that time there is no ripening of karmas?
He says: "Because of the incapacity of the cause of ripening"—for it is determined by seeing the exhaustion of karmas in the millions.
And the maturation of all [karmas] can indeed occur simultaneously. || 49 ||

For the occasional creation and dissolution of innumerable mosquitoes, flies, and the like— which are observed— is due to their extremely minute nature; because they experience only such limited enjoyment, their power is diminished, just as in the case of very delicate women and others.
The inability of another karma to bestow enjoyment upon one who is resting, and the capacity for such bestowal, are inferred as being caused by the ripening of karma;
otherwise, why would there not be the existence of mosquitoes and the like even at other times, just as there is for birds? Now, [one might object]:
A specific time alone is their cause. What follows from this?

Even that [time] exists only through the manifestation of the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*). Similarly, although the other *prakṛtis* are great, their power is exceedingly diminished because they serve as the means for the enjoyment of endless individuals without interruption.

Because [the atoms] lack the capacity to bestow enjoyments in accordance with karma, they lack the agency to produce the maturation of karma; yet, because they eventually rest, their capacity for that maturation is inferred, and thus the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is established.
As it has been said:
Nor is it logical for those possessing karma to remain in a state devoid of its experience;
indeed, for all [beings], a state free from fruit is impossible.
Furthermore, what would then be the cause for the manifestation of karmas?
Thus, that [position] has already been refuted. || 49 ||
Here the opponent's intention is as follows:
"If all karma were destroyed, from what source would there be a subsequent creation?
Even so, the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) ultimately results in nothing but the destruction of karma; therefore..."
It would follow that cyclic existence does not exist. As it has been said:
"Or, if all karma were destroyed, further creation would not be possible."
He refutes this as follows: "Karma that has its fruit in another body is certainly not destroyed by death. (50)

According to the rule that "karma not yet experienced does not perish," the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is not the cause for the exhaustion of those karmas that are to be experienced in other bodies; rather, as stated above, because it is governed by their ripening, it is only the cause of their ripening. Thus, this undesirable consequence does not arise. || 50 ||
For this reason as well, the proof of dissolution is established; thus he says:
"The fact that earth and the other elements possess form was declared to be due to their prior birth;
therefore, the sleep of the world is understood to follow from that, and the destruction of the world occurs before it. (51)

Whatever effect possesses a specific form has the nature of arising from a material cause that does not possess that same form, just as a banyan tree and the like arise from a banyan seed and so forth. And since the world, consisting of earth and other elements, is an effect possessing a specific form, therefore— regarding its birth— its...
Furthermore, the proof of dissolution is established by the fact that previously [the world] must exist in a nature consisting of the undifferentiated form of that [Supreme Principle]. || 51 ||
Moreover—the future dissolution is also understood precisely because it is an effect;
indeed, the total destruction of effects such as the body and so forth is clearly observed. (52)
Since the world and its contents are produced, they must, like bodies and the like, undergo destruction in their entirety;

thus, the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) which is yet to come is established. Since there exists a time not accounted for by the scriptures, there must necessarily be an agent for that [dissolution], and thus the existence of God (Īśvara) is proven. How so?

In that case, there is a conjunction with the qualified person (*adhikārin*). For this very reason, it is preceded by that [qualification], like the continuous succession of seed and sprout; thus, there is no fault. || 52 ||
To refute the claim that the Lord is the author of the scripture, he states another reason cited by the opponent:
"The Lord's sovereignty arises from merit; the knowledge of dharma arises from scripture;
therefore, if the scripture were established prior [to the Lord], [the objection would hold]."
Whatever sovereignty there is, that arises solely from dharma consisting in the performance of the meaning of the scriptures,

as is the case with the sovereignty of yogins; and since you yourselves accept that the world-creator possesses sovereignty, that too must arise from dharma— therefore, the scripture is also the means for the comprehension of dharma.
Because [the world] was established previously, it cannot have God as its creator.
To this, he gives the answer with a portion of the verse:
"It is accepted that [He existed] in the past kalpa. (53)

If it is merely the priority of the scripture (*śāstra*) [to the world] that is being proven here, then that is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because the scripture exists at every creation just as the world does. If, however, its priority to God (*īśvara*) is being proven, then the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus he says:
However, it will be explained that the sovereignty of Maheśvara does not arise from dharma;
for if that sovereignty were established as being achievable through dharma, then the scripture would indeed have been established even prior to the Lord. But it is not achieved by dharma; rather—
He will state later that [the world] is beginningless.
Even granting [the opponent's position], he says with the intention of one who asserts a Lord (Īśvara) as eternally continuous in its stream:
"Or let it be that, by way of its nature (dharmatā), what is impermanent from that [state] attains permanence. (54)

Therefore, that scripture is indeed different, since from it there arises a cognition of those [worldly] dharmas; for that reason, he has now composed this other work for the welfare of the world. (55)
For those who maintain that God is eternal through a continuous succession (*pravāhanitya*), God, being omnipresent, creates the world only after composing the scripture and ordaining it,
until another God is established through the performance of the duties prescribed by that very scripture. But in that case...

Upon his arrival, like a servant, he performs his own duty; having withdrawn all scriptures, he becomes one who delights solely in his own self. Then, the Lord of Siddhas, perceiving that the work of the world had been concluded by him through this very state of non-existence, awaits the time of night, being omnipresent.

Having composed a scripture, He performs the work of the world for as long as another Lord is not established through the sequence of practice based on that very scripture He has ordained; thus, like creation and dissolution, the scripture— though non-eternal— is eternal by way of its continuous flow.
Because it is eternal, it must have God alone as its creator. || 55 ||
Furthermore, another [opponent], unable to tolerate the view that the scripture has God as its author, says:
"Knowledge regarding objects arises from the scripture; therefore, it is not something produced.
For from a produced word, one's intention (*vivakṣā*) is understood. (56)

As the author of the Śābarabhāṣya has said: "For from a worldly sentence there arises the cognition, 'This person knows thus,' whereas from a Vedic sentence there arises the cognition, 'The meaning is thus. (1.1.2)

Therefore, since the understanding of the meaning arises from the treatise itself, setting aside the speaker's intention, it is not made [arbitrary] as in worldly usage; "no" is used here in the sense of negation. || 56 ||
This too he refutes:
"From this [reasoning], non-artificiality would not follow, because perception and the other means of knowledge are impossible.
For the non-artificiality of the word is refuted by perception according to the method already stated; therefore, it cannot be established by inference."
It is possible to establish this.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that intention (*vivakṣā*) is understood from worldly speech—that too is unproven; thus he says:
And because the cognition of the object arises prior to the sentence in every case, without distinction. (57)

Just as from a Vedic sentence, so too from a worldly sentence, for one who has understood the relationship between words and their meanings, there arises first of all a comprehension of the meaning immediately upon the utterance [of the sentence];
for in that very case, its power of denotation is established through either an innate or a conventional relationship.
For there is no difference between those two in their capacity as denoters, as you yourselves have stated:
"Those very words that are worldly are the same as the Vedic ones, and their meanings are the same" (Śābara-bhāṣya 1.1.30).
However, subsequently, due to the impossibility of the primary meaning, [the word] is taken in a secondary or figurative sense.
This very point has been stated by you as well:
"A word, when examined in its preceding and succeeding context, produces a different understanding. (57)
But for one who maintains that even figurative and indicative words may deviate [from their primary meaning], it must now be explained how such a word conveys the specific cognition of the speaker;
thus he says: "How could that which is used for another purpose not be subject to deviation?"

A worldly statement such as "a herd of hundreds of elephants resides on the tip of a finger" and so forth— which is contradicted in every respect regarding its own object by perception and other means of valid cognition— indicates either a speaker's intention to deceive or the presence of erroneous knowledge regarding an object other than that [which is being stated].
It causes [the cognition] to pass away, as you yourselves have said: "In this case, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is sublated, but not a herd of hundreds of elephants"—
provided that it was not uttered by one who is insane, nor by one desiring practice, nor with the intention of conveying a different meaning.

It would be so employed. But when it is employed by them, it is not even that [external object], but rather merely the intention to speak (*vivakṣāmātra*); thus it has been said. However, a statement for which there is no deviation from perception and the other means of valid cognition does not express the speaker’s intention, nor even merely the intention to speak, but rather the actual object itself.
Regarding the phrase "he establishes":
here, by means of a portion of the verse, the opponent [argues] that doubt arises because [the object] has already been produced within the tantra.

If this were so, since there would be no distinction [between it and ordinary speech] in terms of its being produced and its conveying meaning, there would likewise be doubt regarding the object of the meaning in the treatise (*śāstra*) just as in worldly sentences; yet such doubt does not arise,
therefore that [knowledge] is indeed unproduced.
He refutes this with another alternative:
"In that case, what could it be that is unarisen? (58)
If even a scripture consisting of a composition were not impermanent, then objects such as jars would likewise be so;
consequently, it has been stated that this would entail the absurdity of everything being eternal. How, then, does doubt not arise from that?
Because there is an absence of the quality of being deceptive, which is the cause of doubt; and that absence [of deception] exists because the scripture was produced by a reliable person (*āpta*).
We shall explain this in the section on the words "like those of a father" and so forth. || 58 ||
To those who say that in this grammar there is no actual meaning of a word, but rather only what is intended by the speaker, he replies:
"And a sentence-meaning devoid of the connection between word-meanings would be non-worldly."
For there exists no word that can express what one intends to say. (59)
For the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) is not the meaning of a sentence, because the meaning of a word cannot logically constitute the meaning of a sentence;

since a sentence is nothing other than words joined together, and the meaning of a word is not the speaker’s intention but rather the external object itself, it follows that the meaning of a sentence must likewise be that same external object. Therefore, the non-artificiality (*akṛtakatva*) of the Veda is not established on this basis. || 59 ||
Furthermore, in order to refute the doctrine that the Lord is the creator, he states another further reason regarding the Veda:
"Surely the meaning of the scripture is imperceptible, because it is specific and thus not inferable.
An inferential mark (liṅga) is held to be that which is pervaded by and makes known the generality of the object to be inferred (liṅgin). (60)

And without knowing that, how could anyone compose a treatise? Dharma is an object characterized by injunction (*codanā*), and it consists of something to be accomplished (*kārya*), not an already established nature; thus, it is not based on perception. As the author of the Sūtras, Jaimini, has said:
"When there is contact of a person's sense organs with existing objects, the arising of cognition is perception;
that [Dharma] is not its cause, because perception is the apprehension of what is presently existing.
And because it is preceded by perception—just like inference and the other means of knowledge—it does not currently possess the status of being a cause [for the knowledge of Dharma].

And the author of the Bhāṣya [states]: "Because it is specified, it is not inferable; for the Dharma, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, is indeed one and the same, yet it is perceived by all students of the three Vedas through the distinctions of the duties of the Hotṛ, Udgātṛ, and Adhvaryu priests. For there is no difference in the three Vedas or in their subject matter for every student or performer."

There is no difference between the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices even when they appear in different recensions (*śākhā*), because their essential nature (*svarūpa*) remains identical. As it has been stated:
"The ritual act is one and the same as cognized through all recensions.

Since [the subject] is thus qualified by its oneness, there is no established pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) based merely on the commonality of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
For this very reason, since [the Lord] is not an object of the inferential mark (liṅga) for one who infers the generality of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma),

even if the Lord were accepted, he could not be taught because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) other than the Vedic injunction (codanā) that makes dharma known, and because it is impossible to teach what has not been known.

The establishment of its status as the author of the injunction [is thus set forth]. This [objection] he refutes: "O wise ones, this may rightly be said once its validity has been fully established. (61)

Since it is already established that one should direct the mind toward objects such as dice and the like [only when they serve a purpose], for the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in its capacity to determine what is to be avoided, what is to be adopted, and the means to those ends. As they say:
"That which makes known the reality of what is to be avoided and what is to be adopted, along with the means to achieve them..."
"He who is established as an authority" (pramāṇa)—
once that authority of Īśvara is established, he shows by means of an interrogative intonation (*kāku*) that it is not proper to say [the opposite].
And that authority is established precisely through the proof of his omniscience (*sarvajñatva*), which is about to be explained.

Just as an injunction is authoritative, so too that knowledge— transcending the senses and the like— is capable of making known every object of this kind: past, future, subtle, concealed, remote, and so forth.

How could that which is "capable" not also have *dharma* as its object? But was it not said that because *dharma* is something to be accomplished (*kārya*), it cannot be its object? No, for that would be inconclusive due to [the case of] the fruit (*phala*) and so forth; moreover, no other "thing to be accomplished" is established apart from the fruit and the action (*karman*). But surely [it is] of the nature of an injunction (*niyoga*) itself...

[Objection: But then, since even that [intention] consists of forms such as commanding or requesting, and because it is essentially a particular state of mind belonging to a master or similar authority, it falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, this [Vedic intention], which has an authorless (*apauruṣeya*) subject matter and is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition, must be something entirely different. [Response: No; for [the same applies] to that which is of such a nature.

It has been stated that because there is no apprehension of a relationship [between word and meaning], there is no cognition from the word; for a non-worldly (alaukika) meaning of a word is not possible. If it is argued that there is indeed an acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) here by means of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as instigation (*preṣaṇā*), we say no; for in that case, this [meaning] would not be non-worldly, since it would be mediated by those limiting conditions.

"Because it is the object of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)"; for this very reason, since an injunction (niyoga) consists in the activity of an instigator (niyoktṛ), just as in worldly sentences, there must also be an instigator in the Veda—thus, the fact that God is the author [of the Veda] is established.
He says this very thing:
And there is no sublation by which its validity could be precluded. || 62 ||
Nor is there any subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*) by which the invalidity of the Lord's cognition regarding that dharma could be established, thereby proving his lack of omniscience.
[The opponent objects: "But surely there is also no establishing evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*. To this he says:
In this way, therefore, that [knowledge] arises from a valid cause; for that very reason,

since there is an absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), it is established that the knowledge of the Omniscient One, being of such a nature, is also a communicator of the Dharma, and consequently, it arises from a valid cause.
He states that very fact—that such knowledge arises from a valid cause—[in the following]:
"And it will be declared that the Lord's knowledge is non-contradictory regarding objects of the three times. (63)
For one who knows [reality] unstained by the three times, a defect in the cause cannot exist regarding the non-arising of knowledge.

[Objection: In that case, since the injunction (*niyoga*) is perceived as being unconditioned by the three times, its status as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is not established. [Reply: True; if it were so perceived, but it is [perceived] through such sentences as "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice."
By setting aside its existence in the past and present, it is perceived as a mere future universal.
As the author of the Śābarabhāṣya stated: "And this object is future; it does not exist at the time of cognition," thus there is no contradiction.
For this very reason, he says that this [other point] is also established:
Nor does anyone who is not omniscient and has a short lifespan compose it;
for its internal parts are not mutually contradictory and it is free from great contradictions. (64)
Once the author of the Veda is established through inference, its comprehension is achieved through its internal consistency and non-contradiction;
furthermore, because of its extreme vastness due to the various auxiliary branches such as the Śākhās, Nirukta, and Prātiśākhyas,
it is established that those portions which set forth already established facts are but parts of that [Veda].

Even if there were a possibility of contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, since [the scripture] can be justified through explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like, and because there is no sublation by other means of valid cognition, it is established that its author likewise possesses such extraordinary qualities as knowledge; thus, his omniscience, beginninglessness, and so forth are proven. || 64 ||
Now, one might object: "Many people could somehow compose such a Veda by means of various parts and sub-parts. To this he replies:
"In the case of its composition by many, there would be no conformity with the characteristics previously stated."
For in that case, there would be no continuity between the stated Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, nor among all the Śākhās characterized by their primary and secondary limbs,
because they would have different authors, just like the scriptures of the Buddhists and the Ārhats.
Now, if it is argued that although there are many who subsist [on the sacrifice], there will be only one agent therein, to that he says:
"If the capacity [for agency] were attributed to a single one, O Hari, there would be nothing but hostility. (65)
For in this way, since He alone is established as the Lord who ordains the Veda characterized by the previously mentioned qualifications, there is no dispute. || 65 ||
To further strengthen this very point, he says:
"The sign of a great being from the past, created by Īśvara, would have fulfilled its purpose; therefore, it is only Īśvara who is appropriate here. (66)

Since the proof for the existence of a vast multitude of authors of various kinds in the past is established by that very mark which, indeed, finds its fulfillment in a single creator— namely, God— it is not logical to postulate many. As they say:
"The conceptualized destroys the conceptualizing itself, precisely because of the accomplishment of its object. || 66 ||
For this reason as well, he states that such knowledge arises from correct practice:
"And Śarva is not a deceiver, because he is the Lord of the entire world;
having deceived living beings, what unprecedented gain would he obtain from them? (67)
For street-charlatans are deceivers because they deceive others for some purpose of their own;
but since he whose conduct is directed toward the welfare of others lacks any personal motive, how could there be any possibility of his being a deceiver? 67.
Furthermore:
How could he who, being omniscient, composed the mantra teachings for the sake of others—teachings that all possess every form of excellence—ever deceive anyone? (68)

Since he has composed many treatises on spells, elixirs, and subterranean pills for the sole purpose of benefiting others— serving as means to accomplish every desired good— it is simply impossible that he could be a deceiver. || 68 ||
Nor, moreover, is there agency for persons in this matter; thus he says:

"The meaning of the mantra-injunctions is beyond the senses and, because it is specific, it is not inferable by men, even when accompanied by its procedural details, just like the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites. (69)

For the status of being a teacher would belong to those things established through direct perception for people— such as the purgative effect of *harītakī* and the like— or established through inference, such as the removal of cataracts from the eyes and so forth; but it does not belong to that which transcends the senses, according to the reasoning already stated.

Furthermore, because of its distinctiveness, the subject matter of the collection of scriptures consisting of mantras and injunctions— such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice— is not established by direct perception, even though it serves as a means to achieve results like heaven, just as in the case of that which is not an object of inference; for it is conjoined with a multitude of auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), including meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and so forth.
And because he is unique, he cannot be inferred; thus, the status of being a teacher is not possible for ordinary persons—it belongs properly to the Lord (Īśvara). || 69 ||

Furthermore, he states that the authorship of the mantra declarations is not established merely by the establishment of an author for the Vedas— as is the case with the Vedāṅgas— because such an author is impossible within the Veda:
"Moreover, because their existence is impossible, Garuḍa and the others do not exist in the Veda."
Since these [beings] are all-knowing creators, it is understood that their sole intent is [to bestow] grace.
