For it is by well-established, beginningless tradition that the status of being a Veda belongs only to the three [Vedas], and that specific branches are specific branches of the Veda—not by any other means of knowledge. Nor is there a traditional consensus among the proponents of Mantras regarding the Vedas as such; therefore, they are distinct as separate treatises.
An effort has been made to establish a specific agent for them. || 70 ||
In this regard, the opponent states the following to establish that the Lord’s knowledge arises from the performance of non-virtuous actions:
"If Śaṅkara were devoid of all cognitive and creative activity because he possesses the faculty of speech,
then like us and others, the Lord would be devoid of omniscience and other such qualities, simply because he speaks."
To this he replies: "That is incorrect because it is unestablished (asiddha):
'The state of being a speaker and the state of being an author of a treatise do not entail the aforementioned defect. (71)
In this context, "being a speaker" is not established as merely being an author of words like those of ourselves and others;
rather, it is something quite different—namely, being the author of a treatise—and its pervasion by non-omniscience is not established.
And he states that this reason is contradictory:
"On the contrary, from this very [work], the Lord is understood to be omniscient;
for by composing this scripture, everything indeed would have been accomplished by him. (72)
Since all the fruits attained by men are accomplished through the scripture,
this has been stated:
"Furthermore, no one who is not omniscient and short-lived can compose such a work."
Thus [ends the verse]. 72.
Therefore, he says:
"How could one who knows all that was previously stated make such an objection? (73)

This objection applies only to the ignorant, but not to one who has been refined by the aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, because it is produced by the performance of virtuous acts, the knowledge of the Lord is possible even with respect to objects such as *dharma* and so forth.
Since the scripture deals with matters that are beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition, there is no failure to establish that the Lord is its author. || 73 ||
In this matter, one of our own school indeed exerts every effort to establish the validity of his own position alone;
why then has he laboriously expended such effort in vain over the validity of the Veda as well? (74)
For every discerning person must exert effort specifically to refute the suspicion of invalidity regarding their own philosophical system,
and not because other systems are useless; for there is no distinction [in this regard].

Furthermore, because it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress by attempting to justify the authority of all scriptures, this attempt of yours to establish the authority of the Veda through the agency of God is indeed untenable.
That is incorrect; for it is that [Veda] alone which must be relied upon here, and not other scriptures. Thus he says:

"Without the Veda there is no ritual action (karman), and without that [Veda] there is no Kalā and so forth. It has been declared that all karma and the rest are to be severed by initiation (dīkṣā). (75)
The castes, stages of life, and other such categories mentioned in the Vedas are authorized within the Śaiva tradition;
therefore, we have made this effort regarding the authority of the Veda as well. (76)
For it has been stated here that the karma— consisting of merit and demerit accumulated over many births—

which serves as the cause of the entire cycle of existence (saṃsāra) comprising the principles (tattva), states of being (bhāva), elements (bhūta), and worlds (bhuvana), beginning from Kalā and ending with Earth, is to be severed by initiation; and [this applies] to that which is not unknown.
Thus, its status as something to be cut off is established; and without this [Veda], the knowledge of that [Dharma] in its entirety is not possible,
because even the Dharma taught by the Buddhists— such as sleeping in a *caitya*— and that taught by the Ārhats— such as the plucking out of hair— is in some way a part thereof, as it has been said:

For every affliction ultimately results in the exhaustion of evil; moreover, even that which is conceived as "dharma" by barbarians—such as the taking of another's life—is pervaded by unrighteousness (*adharma*) because it is of that nature. Furthermore, in this context, the system of castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramasthiti*) prescribed in the Vedas is heard of as something to be protected.
Thus, one should not transgress the conduct of the castes and stages of life even in thought;
whoever, having been initiated into the teaching of Śiva, should abide in whichever stage of life he occupies.
"He should remain established in that very state and protect the dharma of Śiva. Thus,
since the abandonment of all ritual actions would otherwise be untenable as an instruction,
and because of the Vedic revelation establishing the various systems of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), we maintain the authority of the Veda.
An effort has been made regarding other scriptural traditions. || 76 ||
One might object: "Since its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is already established, this effort is nonetheless fruitless. To this he says:
"Because the Veda has been rejected by those seeking liberation and by others.
For the Buddhists, the Jains, and so forth, have indeed rejected the authority of the Veda.
Therefore, this effort is indeed fruitful;
and since it cannot be rejected, he says:
"Without the Veda, how can there be liberation for living beings, just as [there is no liberation] without cyclic existence? (77)

For liberation is not possible without fully understanding that which is to be abandoned and the means for its abandonment; and it has been stated that without the Veda, knowledge of that [reality] in its entirety is not possible. Therefore, because the teaching of liberation would otherwise be inexplicable, the Veda must also be accepted by them.
It must indeed be accepted as a valid means of knowledge. || 77 ||
If this is so, the opponent argues that this is like raising a Vetāla while performing a rite for peace;
since liberation is already established in the Veda, what is the purpose of Śaivism?
For in this way, liberation would be [established] just like the system of castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-vyavasthā*) and so forth.
Since it would merely be a restatement based on what is already understood from the Vedas alone, the treatise (śāstra) would lack authority as a source of knowledge.

Now, [the author] says that even if these two [texts] convey a single meaning independently of one another, their authority will be optional (vikalpa), just as in the case of two different Vedic recensions (śākhā): "Because the person situated in that [other text] is not qualified for this [text], an option between them is not appropriate here. (78)

It is appropriate that two branches [of the Veda] possess authority through optionality, because they are equally enjoined. Here, however, since the eligibility of Brahmins and others is established by the consciousness of the Veda as it was originally enjoined, the comprehension of that [eligibility] must necessarily first arise from the Veda itself; thus, there is an inequality of injunction.
Because conceptual construction is untenable, it lacks validity altogether. || 78 ||

Now, although the two scriptural passages— "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"— have the single fruit of heaven, [the former] possesses a greater result due to the greater frequency of its performance;
thus, even though these two scriptures have a single fruit, [they differ in their results].
He says that validity will arise from the abundance of the fruit due to the abundance of the practice:
"The performance of the methods taught by the two views does not result in an abundance of fruit;
this is not tenable, because, unlike the fruit of heaven and so forth, no excellence [or superiority] is possible in the case of liberation."
For this reason as well, he states that this [view] lacks authority: "And the destruction of karma through action has been declared to be devoid of logical justification. (79)

Since liberation is established solely through the cessation of ignorance by means of knowledge, this scripture—which asserts that ritual action in the form of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the cause of liberation—is indeed invalid, like the Vedic text "one should sprinkle with fire. As it has been said: "The fire of knowledge [consumes] all karmas..."

"He reduces to ashes" means that, since the Mīmāṃsaka here maintains the position of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), it is stated that liberation consists solely in the exhaustion of karma. || 79 ||
To refute such an opposing argument, he says:
"In the teaching of Śiva, the state of Śiva as proclaimed in the Gītā is the supreme liberation;
it should be understood as superior even to all other fruits. (80)

This fault would indeed arise if liberation here were limited solely to the principle of the individual soul (puruṣatattva); however, in this system, it is heard that liberation is the attainment of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), which is entirely unprecedented compared to other philosophical systems and consists of omniscience and omnipotence.

Since the liberation taught by the Buddhists, Vaiśeṣikas, Ārhats, Sāṃkhyas, Pāñcarātras, Vedāntins, and others is progressively superior, how could the previously mentioned defect apply to this [knowledge], which is even more superior than those forms of liberation? As it is heard:
The Buddhists are established in the principle of intellect (buddhi); the Ārhats are established in the qualities (guṇas);
the Sāṃkhyas are established at the summit of the qualities; and the Pāñcarātrikas are established in the unmanifest (avyakta).
"The knowers of the Vedas abide in the Person," and so forth. || 80 ||
He states this very point:
"From the excellence of the performance, there is an excellence of the fruit for the wise man;
even that which is not explicitly stated should be inferred therein, as otherwise there would be a lack of authority due to its impossibility. (81)

Because it is the cause of practice, knowledge is called "practice" (*anuṣṭhāna*); since this very [knowledge] proceeds according to the stated sequence by demonstrating other points attainable through all other scriptures, its excellence is established as being superior to all scriptures due to its freedom from all contradictions.
O wise ones, since it is established by logical proof, one must conceive of the fruit consisting of liberation as being the most excellent, even if it has not been explicitly stated;
why then is it said that it is not possible? Thus, the previously mentioned fault of lack of authority does not apply here. || 81 ||
Nor is the second [alternative] valid; thus he says:
"Everything is attained through initiation alone, even that which is proclaimed in some places regarding the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika);
therefore, one desists from what is taught in the Vedas and other [texts] because of its fruitlessness in that regard. (82)
Even in your own tradition, it is heard in the Upaniṣads that there is a destruction of karma prescribed by the Vedas and other sources through its performance:
"When one who has been initiated into this supreme qualification becomes a knower of the Vedas..."
All his karma, both good and evil, is constantly exhausted.
Thus [ends the verse]. 82.
He states that this is prescribed not only in the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa), but even in the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa):
"In the Veda, the destruction of evil through auspicious action is enjoined."
Since there is scriptural testimony that evil deeds are destroyed through expiatory rites such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*,
the destruction of karma through ritual action is not without justification; thus, there is no fault, for this is established by scripture just as it is for you.

Is it not the case that "reasoning" (yukti) here refers to inference (anumāna), because the fact that the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such practices are causes of purification is ascertained through a divine cognition (pratyaya), such as [the perception of] a jar or similar object? As it has been said:
"From unrighteousness comes darkness; from that comes heaviness in the body; but when this [darkness] is diminished..."
"Because it arises from a light [substance] according to its nature, it is perceived as a jar.
To this he replies:
"And its destruction is observed in the Śaiva system through action alone, such as by means of a scale and so forth. (83)

In this case as well, such reasoning certainly exists even regarding the initiation of the jar (*ghaṭadīkṣā*); therefore, it is not stated that the destruction of karma through ritual action is devoid of logical justification. || 83 ||
Moreover— if [the authority of the Veda] were not accepted on account of initiation (dīkṣā), how could there be an absence of ritual action (karma) from any other source?
For those who maintain the doctrine of ritual action (karmavādin) admit that the Veda possesses authority regarding matters that are to be accomplished.

Because there would otherwise follow the consequence that the Upaniṣadic portion, which teaches knowledge and so forth, lacks authority due to its having an already established object as its content, its authority is established by its connection with the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) as an explanatory passage (arthavāda) intended for praise.

Since no self other than that consisting of the yoga of knowledge is established through any specific action, if [the Veda] were not accepted as such for some reason, it would follow that the Veda lacks the status of being a scripture on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*); consequently, it would follow that the Buddhists and others possess authority in this matter. Therefore, by the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) regarding its status as a scripture on liberation, it must necessarily [be accepted].

The absence of karma must be accepted as resulting from some specific ritual action; and since that very [action] is accepted as initiation (*dīkṣā*), the destruction of karma through ritual action is not without logical justification.

Regarding this, the opponent states otherwise concerning the absence of karma: "There would be [no karma] for subsequent actions due to non-performance, and for prior ones due to their enjoyment. (84)
Thus it has been said:

"One who desires liberation should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with the intent to avoid transgression; one should not engage in those rites that are performed for specific desires or those that are prohibited."
Thus [ends verse] 84.
He refutes this [view]:
"One performs in a single birth alone those karmas that are to be experienced over many births; therefore, this has been stated out of rashness. (85)
This might be so if a person performed only such actions as are to be experienced in a single birth; however,

since one is seen performing various actions with diverse fruits— such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and the killing of a Brahmin— that are to be experienced over many births, it is unproven that [karma] is exhausted through experience in previous lives.
For it is not possible for the fruits of hell, heaven, and so forth to be experienced within a single lifetime;
thus, this was stated by you without due consideration of the nature of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 85 ||
And therefore, even if no action has been performed here in this life, nevertheless there will be another birth resulting from that very same previous karma. (86)

Since it is not established that all previous [karmas] are exhausted through experience, even if one does not perform actions that result in the fruit of transgression in this life, there will certainly be other births due to earlier karmas; therefore, one should perform the obligatory and occasional rites— thus it has been stated.
The logic regarding the means to liberation would be untenable precisely because of its inconclusiveness. || 86 ||

Thus, when there is the possibility of karma to be experienced over many births, that very karma which possesses an intense momentum, by suppressing the experience of other karmas with weak momentum, brings about its own effect and becomes the cause for a single birth alone; this is the case regarding other karmas.
He states that because the non-existence [of karma] is established precisely through its sublation, there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) of this reason:
"A person performs actions to be experienced throughout many births;
even then, there is no destruction of all those actions merely through the experience of one. (87)

In that regard, among those various karmas to be experienced over many births, the exhaustion of all karmas does not occur through the experience of even one, because—just like that—one has not yet been experienced; as it is heard:
"Karma that has not been experienced does not perish."

Rather, like seeds obstructed by frost and the like, they remain for a time in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as the givers of fruit after an interval; since the destruction of actions with non-intense momentum is not established, there are indeed future births from them, and not merely within a single lifetime.

That liberation results merely from the non-performance [of rites] due to the cause of the fruit of transgression—this is not tenable. If it is argued that this refers to every birth, that is incorrect; for it is impossible to perform those obligatory rites in births such as those of barbarians (*mleccha*), since they lack the requisite qualification (*anadhikāra*).
And because [acts such as] the killing of living beings are prohibited, they are, on the contrary, contradictory [to the goal], since they serve as causes for future births.
Now, it may be argued that as long as there is no exhaustion of all karma, there can be no human birth; for it has been said:
"Indeed, the first body is rooted in the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*); other bodies that follow are rooted in karma."

Thus, since the destruction of all karmas that are to be experienced over many births is established through the impossibility of [otherwise] accounting for human birth, liberation indeed occurs in this very life through the non-performance of actions that cause the fruit of transgression. To this, he says:
Since not all karma is experienced in one's final birth, this distinction of pleasure, pain, and so forth is observed even in this present life. (88)
If this were so, then since human birth would not be the fruit of karma,
it would follow that there is an absence of diversity; for it has been stated that the diversity of pleasure and so forth among persons is indeed based upon karma.
In this world, you shall consider only the ripening of your own actions;
as for what will happen to you in the next world, reflect upon that which is wholesome or unwholesome.
Thus,
because the statement "the first body is rooted in the human goal" would be sublated, this [opposing view] would be declared unauthoritative, like the injunction "one should sprinkle with fire."

All the auspicious and inauspicious karma performed during this life and up until death— blended together in the relationship of primary and secondary factors— will produce only a single birth simultaneously; thus,
there is no possibility of postulating that karmas to be experienced over many births [could be exhausted in one].
He states that the aforementioned fault will apply here:
"The fruit of Indra-hood and so forth is declared in the Veda as being distinct for each [birth];
therefore, not even a single birth occurs from those produced over a lifetime. (89)
"One desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the *vājapeya*": here, "self-sovereignty" is indeed Indra-hood, which is its fruit;

by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), actions such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* resulting in fruits like heaven, and [actions] such as the killing of a Brahmin resulting in hell, are also included. The ellipsis to be supplied is that "each of those produces a separate birth."

Furthermore, because the Vedic texts have mutually contradictory results precisely when they are independent of one another, it is not tenable to conceive of all [the texts] as forming a single ritual procedure (*prayoga*) through the relationship of primary and subordinate elements, due to the contradiction with the Vedic texts. To conclude this, he says:
And that [karma] is accepted by many; for those who possess such karma, it results in multiple births.
Therefore, one must accept that karma which has multiple births as its cause or which is to be experienced in multiple births.
Those who possess this [karma] continue to exist in saṃsāra even when they do not perform actions that would cause transgression in this life.

Since the Veda cannot be established as a scripture for liberation even by this method— namely, the injunction "one should perform the obligatory and occasional rites"— it is well said that, in order to justify that [status], you must necessarily accept some specific action for the purpose of exhausting karma.
"If one who has been initiated were not to lead [the sacrificial horse], how could there be an absence of ritual action? Thus it is said.

However, some—citing the scriptural statement that "no unexperienced karma perishes"—maintain that for the knower (*jñānin*), there is the experience of all karma through the power of yoga; thus, they hold that liberation results from the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*) and not from initiation (*dīkṣā*). Having set forth this view, [the author] refutes it.
It is not meaningful to say that the knower enjoys all karma through the power of yoga.
Why is this so? He says:
Because enjoyment in pleasures and the like is never seen to occur without ignorance and the rest;
for dispassion consists of a lack of thirst for sense objects, whereas knowledge arises from the cessation of the persistence of attachment.

Experience arises from karma; because knowledge and action possess mutually contradictory consequences—just as right and wrong knowledge cannot be combined—there is no possibility of their coexistence.
Therefore, by the force of the scriptural statement that "karma which has not been experienced does not perish," even for the knower, karma must necessarily be exhausted through experience alone.
"It must be destroyed because it cannot otherwise be accounted for; therefore, it can only be destroyed by initiation (*dīkṣā*).

This statement—that the destruction of karma occurs through ritual action—is irrational and thus refuted. [Objection: But even in that case, since experience (*bhoga*) is possible, the same defect remains as before. [Reply: No.

There is no fault, for even for those whose delusion and so forth have been removed by the power of mantras employed through theft, it is possible at that time— even for the knower— just like the experience in a dream.
Having thus spoken while accepting liberation through the destruction of karma, [the author now states] that very same [liberation]:
He says that this is not tenable:
"Even when the collection of karma has been exhausted, there would be no destruction of [impurity] such as the *mala*s. (91)
"Let the means taught by Śiva for the severing of the bonds be adopted;
let there be the exhaustion of karma through knowledge, yoga, renunciation, or through experience."
Even when that [karma] is exhausted, because of the inclusion of the word "beginning" (ādi), there is no exhaustion of impurity (mala) nor of being impelled by Īśvara;

thus, their state remains that of a *vijñānakevalin*, not liberation (*mokṣa*). And just as ignorance, memory, and so forth, must be admitted as distinct from the bondage consisting of primordial matter (*prākṛta-bandha*) and from karma, so too must impurity be admitted as something other [than those].

Thus it was stated by the Teacher in his *Svāyambhūvavṛtti* in the passage beginning "If there is no impurity of the person," and it has been explained therein by our father, the venerable Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇakaṇṭha, in his commentary (*ṭīppaka*); therefore, this should be understood from that very source. And because that [impurity] is a substance (*dravya*), it...
Liberation does not arise from knowledge alone; rather, we shall explain that it occurs through a specific action, just as [the removal of] cataracts and the like [is achieved by medical treatment].
Therefore, it has been stated: "The destruction of karma through action is devoid of logical justification."
Since this [scripture] is also defective, it is not appropriate to say that it is non-authoritative merely because it is sublated by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, he states that the existence of God is established not only through inference and one's own scripture, but even from your own scripture as well: "He is understood from scripture, whether it be eternal or non-eternal. (92)

Let it be that the authority of the Veda is established by its having God as its author; or rather, he shows by way of an alternative that there is no lack of authority even if God is established in every respect through its being uncreated—a position accepted by the opponent. And thus: "The *raudra* oblation..."

In such passages as "One desiring offspring should offer [an oblation]," and "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a *caru* to Sūrya," Rudra and others are enjoined as deities by means of the *taddhita* suffix expressing deityhood, according to the scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Now, an objection is raised: the Veda possesses authority regarding matters that are to be accomplished (*kārya*), but not regarding established entities (*siddha*) such as deities.

How, then, are injunctions of qualities such as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) or "one offers with milk" (*payasā juhoti*) to be understood? For in those cases, since the injunction "one desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra" already establishes the verbal action (*bhāvārtha*), it is impossible to enjoin that same action again as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*); therefore, the substances such as curd and the like must be established as having an already-accomplished nature.

Since they are enjoined as the means for accomplishing that [result], by what could their validity regarding that object be refuted? Now, it might be argued that because an injunction necessarily concerns an action (bhāvārtha) due to the very nature of things, it cannot be connected with an already established entity; therefore, even here, there is only an injunction concerning an action to be accomplished through curd and so forth, and not [an injunction regarding an existing substance].

Therefore, the injunction regarding curds and the like does not have as its object something already established. From what, then, is the understanding of curds and so forth as being the means to that [result] derived? Just as in the case of the "task" (kārya), here too, because no other means of knowledge is possible, it is derived from the power of the injunction of the "action-entity" (bhāvārtha) which is colored by that [task].

[The deity] is subordinate to the material, just as the singularity [of the animal] is subordinate to the animal itself. Let it be so; enough with this difficulty regarding the ritual procedure (*prakriyā*).

Here too, by the power of enjoining a purposeful action (*bhāvārtha*) qualified by a deity, the deity—being a constituent factor (*kāraka*)—is likewise subordinate to the material, just as curd and the like are.
"Success" (siddhi) does not mean the non-existence of Īśvara, because he exists in the form of a specific deity. || 92 ||
Regarding this, the opponent states by way of a verse-quarter: "If the deity were merely a word,
then it would be logical for words such as 'curd' (dadhi) and so forth to apply here."

The status of being a *codanā* belongs to those [words] which, by having as their object a matter established through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), convey a meaning capable of serving as a subordinate element (*śeṣabhāva*) for an injunction; however, since the words denoting deities do not establish a matter already established by other means of valid cognition, they do not possess that status.

Because it would be purposeless; for if, like the *stobha* syllables and so forth in the *sāmans*, the connection with the ritual action were through its own form alone and not by way of meaning, then the status of being an injunction (*codanā*) would not be established, and thus the deity would not be established.
This is rejected by another section [of the text]:
"The object would not exist through cognition.
It is logical that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that *stobha* and other such elements convey meaning.

In the case of the utterance of the word's own form (*svarūpa*), there is no syntactic connection with an action (*kārya*). However, in the case of scriptural mentions of deities (*devatā-śruti*), we observe connections with various case-meanings through such passages as "The animal dedicated to Rudra is to be immolated," "We worship Tryambaka," "A Brahmin should sacrifice a Brahmin," and "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed in a low voice."

Since the capacity to convey meaning is established for [words such as] *dadhi* (curd) and so forth, just like [the words] *śruti*, and since the application [of the injunction] occurs precisely to that meaning, the connection is established by means of that very meaning; thus, there is indeed the status of being an injunction whose purpose is to indicate the deity.
Now, it was argued that these [mantras] are purposeless because they do not convey a meaning established by other means of knowledge; to this, he states a further supporting argument:
"And because we do not [accept] them as being causal agents, the scriptural mention of them as causal agents is meaningless. (93)

To begin with, the object denoted by the term "deity," being heard as the recipient (*sampradāna*) factor of the sacrifice, necessarily enters into a connection with the ritual action as a subordinate element for the purpose of its performance— just like curds and other such materials. Therefore, if that [deity] is not established by any other means of knowledge as a specific entity (*idantayā*), then...

According to the principle that "one who strives for the establishment of what is heard must exert effort to perceive what has not been heard, and must not practice laxity regarding the scripture," it follows here— since the scriptural mention of the *kārakas* would otherwise be inexplicable—
that they must be accepted as established by the scriptures, just like the referents of terms such as *yūpa* (sacrificial post) and *āhavanīya* (sacrificial fire).

Furthermore, since it is established that the scriptural passages concerning deities are not purposeless because they serve to convey that [meditation], they must indeed have the deity as their object;
moreover,
she is understood from the word to be distinct from the scriptural passage concerning meditation, otherwise [there would be no distinction].
If sound were directly perceptible, the injunction to meditate upon it would be purposeless.

According to the Vedic scripture, "One should meditate mentally upon whichever deity for whom the oblation has been set aside," since the deity is already perceptible through the word [of the mantra], the injunction to meditate would otherwise be purposeless; therefore, it is understood from the word that the deity consists of a form other than [the mere verbal expression]. || 94 ||
Furthermore:
Since praise here consists in the form of the object, this deity is [known] through the hymn;
for the glorification of specific qualities is directed toward a specific object. (95)

Because of the Vedic scripture stating, "Having sacrificed with the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, one should praise the deity," and because it is accepted that praise consists in the naming of the qualities of the possessor of those qualities, the deity is indeed the object itself, not the word whose nature is the naming of it. || 95 ||
Nor can its corporeal form be denied, because it is established by scripture; thus he says:
"And she, possessing distinct forms, is enjoined as being separate and separate;
one should indeed meditate upon her with the mind within one's own body, according to the scripture. (96)

Since another scriptural passage enjoins that one should meditate upon the deity as distinct from other deities by means of form, appearance, splendor, and power, it follows that the meaning of the preceding scriptural passage is that one should meditate upon that [deity] with the mind within one's own body; thus it becomes [the case for] the deity.
The accomplishment of the body. || 96 ||

Therefore, when there arises a specific desire to know what kind of form it has and to whom it belongs, its form is to be understood as that which is presented by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
For instance, from the Vedic revelation, "He lays down the sugar-lumps smeared with ghee," [the question arises]: "Smeared with what? [The answer is provided by an explanatory passage.]

When there is a desire for a specific [substance], the understanding of that specific substance arises from the explanatory passage (arthavāda), "Ghee is indeed light. Likewise, here too, when there is a desire for a specific form,
the understanding of that specific form arises from the explanatory passage, "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads."
Therefore, by describing them in that way, their status as objects of praise is not lost. || 97 ||
For explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are called such because they praise a specific purpose in this manner;

otherwise, being devoid of meaning, they could not function as *arthavādas*, just like musical fillers (*stobha*) and the like. Furthermore, because they are required by the injunctive sentences (*vidhi-vākya*), the confusion of mind among these people is caused by the *arthavādas*.
Thus, even this is proclaimed by you as being illogical. || 97 ||

Even for those injunctions where no distinction is found through the explanatory passages (arthavāda), the true nature of the deities must be clearly understood from the concluding portions of the Vedas (vedānta) and in cases such as death, for the sake of the non-deficiency of ritual actions. (98)

And thus, although the Vedāntas, Itihāsas, and so forth establish already-accomplished matters (siddhārtha), they possess authority as being syntactically unified with the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) by virtue of establishing the specific forms of the deities required therein; hence, there is no contradiction.
And therefore, it has been stated: "Indeed,
the operation of the *Mahābhārata* and other such works regarding dharma and so forth occurs in the form of narratives (*upākhyāna*) and the like, just like the Veda."
Thus, this is indeed appropriate for them, because error is impossible for them.
And so, he states that the authority of this scripture is established even by its inclusion within the Vedas:
"In those very [Vedas], one should know the form of the Supreme Lord, both supreme and non-supreme."
And that which is his supreme form is proclaimed in the Śaiva [tradition]. || 99 ||
As stated in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* and other texts:
"The Lord is said to be twofold—the supreme and the non-supreme;
yet there is another who is higher than those two, who cannot be described."

Furthermore, since this [text] establishes the nature of the Supreme Lord who is required by that [Veda], you must also admit its authority as being part of a single coherent statement with it. || 99 ||

Now, one might object: since the Vedāntas are understood to culminate in the duty of realizing the Self as their subject matter, it is impossible for them to have the Lord as their subject matter; how, then, can this [text] possess authority by virtue of being a single syntactical unit with them? To this, he says:
Indeed, the injunction such as "the Self is to be seen" refers to the Lord alone;
for everything that constitutes the nature of the scripture is heard immediately thereafter. (100)

In that context as well, in passages such as "the Self is to be seen, it is to be meditated upon," the word "Self" (ātman) refers specifically to the Lord (Īśvara) as the object to be known; for immediately thereafter,
[the text describes] Him as the Lord of All and the benefactor of all, thus establishing that the subject matter is the Lord.
His entire nature, as established in the scriptures of the Lord, is heard [in these accounts]. || 100 ||
Furthermore:
"The scripture is purposeless with respect to the agent (aṇu), because [the agent] is directly perceived.
If, in that case, the self alone were intended, and not the Lord, then [the scripture would be useless] with respect to Him."

In the case of the Self, which is the qualified candidate for the knowledge of Vedānta and is established by its own self-awareness as the knower through the aforementioned process, the scripture stating "it is to be known" is indeed useless because it would be something already accomplished.
As it is heard:
"He who does not know that, what will he do with the Ṛg-veda? But those who know this sit here together.
Therefore, it must be accepted that by the word "Self" (ātman) in this context, the Lord (Īśvara) alone is taught as the object to be known.
Moreover:
"In some Manu [text], 'Manu' and 'Rudra' are indeed seen as designations for the same entity. (101)
Just as in the *Atharvaśiras* among the Rudra-hymns, in the passage "He alone is the Self, He alone is the Lord," the use of the word "Self" (*ātman*) for the Lord is indeed observed. 101.
To the question "What is the purpose of this?", he says:
An instrument is seen to have action as its purpose, and that which reveals its own nature [serves the same end].
Therefore, because [injunctions] such as "the Self is to be known" are intent upon the necessity of attaining God (Īśvara), [they do not aim at producing a new result].
Since it forms a single coherent statement with the exposition of the nature of the Lord as impelled by that [Veda], its authority must be accepted by you as well.
Here, the opponent [objects]: "Surely, because the gods possess embodied forms, that [agency] would belong to them. (102)
As they say:
"If it were like a hide, it would be impermanent; if it were like space, it would be equivalent to a non-entity.
Therefore, the previously mentioned agency of this [self] is untenable. || 102 ||
But the Teacher, even while conceding that [the Lord] possesses a corporeal form, rejects this [position]:
"It would not establish that essential nature [of the Lord] as being present in things such as *śāla* trees;
for this is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatvāt*), since, for example, although *śāla*, *khadira*, and other such trees are impermanent,"

In this regard, since the status of being a *kāraka* (instrumental factor) is established for the *khadira* wood by such scriptural injunctions as "he binds [the animal] to the *khadira* tree," and likewise for the deities by the aforementioned scriptures, what contradiction is there?
Furthermore, if these [deities] do not have the purpose of [accomplishing] an action, that is equally true for the deities as well. (103)

Now, if it is accepted that, like the eternal genus (*jāti*), [the deity] possesses the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the praise, while the non-eternal particulars such as *khadira* wood possess the status of being a causal factor (*kāraka*), then in this case, it must be maintained that only the eternal self of the deity is the subordinate element, and not its bodies, which would be like entering another's body.
Thus, everything is the same in that impermanent things are characterized by being either to be accepted or rejected. For this very reason,

since it would otherwise be impossible for [the deity] to be the means of accomplishing the sacrifice, the deity must simultaneously serve as the instrument for multiple sacrifices performed by numerous qualified agents situated in different locations.
The perfection of sovereignty (aiśvaryasiddhi) is so called because it is fashioned by the creation of multiple emanation-bodies through the power of irresistible will (prākāmya). || 103 ||

Now, one might object that because many deities such as Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra are heard of here as being divine, a divergence of opinion could arise, resulting in the non-establishment of the Lord (Īśvara).
To this he says: "But this distinction regarding the Lord is understood only through the knowledge of Him."
This specific distinction regarding the Lord is understood from scripture alone; for it is heard in the Śruti:
"They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, and he is the divine, beautiful-winged Garuḍa.
That which is one, the sages call by many names; they call it Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan."
The Lord is indeed one, yet he is designated as manifold due to the diversity of those over whom he presides, just as a king is designated by the diversity of his royal commands;
and he is none other than Rudra. As it is heard in scripture: "Rudra alone existed, not a second;
hundreds upon hundreds of thousands."

In the passage beginning "Those Rudras who are upon the earth," the universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*) of that very same Blessed Lord is established among the Rudras. Now, one might object: since the deity is heard of as being subordinate (*guṇatva*), like curds and other such offerings, it cannot be the Supreme Lord. This is not so, because she [the deity] functions as the recipient (*sampradāna-kāraka*).

Because of its primary importance, that which one intends through the object (karman)— the most desired by the agent— is the recipient (sampradāna). If this is so, then since every ritual action such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa has for its purpose deities such as Indra— established by scriptural injunctions such as "The curd for Indra on the new moon day"— [it would follow that all such actions have a recipient].
It is not the case that [the substance] is the object of an injunction by virtue of being a subordinate action (guṇakarma); as it has been said:

"In those cases where a substance is intended to be prepared, a quality is understood [as the primary element]. This is because [the status of the substance] is established through its being taught as an end in itself, like the Self and like the guest-offering (ātithya). For just as it is said, "The Self is to be known," [so too is the substance].

Thus, even though the meaning of the verbal root has the self as its object, just as in the case of the injunction, "One should sacrifice a great bull or a large animal for a guest who has arrived," which is accepted by you all as being within the scope of an injunction because it must be performed since it is enjoined for the sake of the guest, so too is this [the case here].

There is no contradiction in [the result] being "about to come into being. From where, then, does the fruit arise? It arises from the deity itself, or else by virtue of the *niyoga* (injunction), just as in the case of those who hold [the view] that you [Mīmāṃsakas] accept: for instance, when it is said, "One desiring a village should serve the prince," the fruit arises from the prince's injunction regarding the act of serving the prince; so too here.

The fruit arises necessarily from the very act of propitiating the deity. Now, one might object that in the case of a prince and the like, the success of the propitiation is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Let it be so; however, in this context, it is established by the scripture (*śāstra*) through the performance of the ritual acts in their entirety, or by the authority of faith (*śraddhā*).

It has been stated by those of great intelligence in the *Devatākāṇḍa* that [the deity] is understood. Indeed, the investigation of the Veda was undertaken by the authors of the Sūtras, such as the sage Jaimini and others, through the division into three sections: the section on ritual action (*kriyākāṇḍa*), the section on deities (*devatākāṇḍa*), and the section on the Upaniṣads (*upaniṣatkāṇḍa*). And that—
It has been interpreted as having exclusively karma for its subject matter through ignorance by the Mīmāṃsakas, who perceive only the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*). For this very reason, they say:
"One should not create a division of intellect in the ignorant who are attached to action."

The Teacher (Ācārya), in order to apply the authority of the deities to the *karmakāṇḍa* as well— despite the contradiction with the established meaning of the sentences in the *devatākāṇḍa*— has stated here:
"But this distinction regarding the Lord is understood from that very knowledge [of Him]."
For this very reason, even from the perspective of the Upaniṣadic section, he says: "Indeed, that which is the supreme purification for a person in the treatise on Dharma... (104).
And it is also recited in the Yogaśāstra that [liberation comes] from devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna).

For in Vedānta, among the categories of the Lord, the inner self, form, the vital breath, Virāj, the elements, and the senses, liberation is heard to result specifically from the worship of the Lord; this is likewise stated in the Smṛtis and other texts as being like the Agnihotra and other sacrificial rites.
The merit consisting of the worship of the Lord is fulfilled by one who properly constructs a temple of Śiva built of baked bricks;
thus it is heard in scripture:
"One should point out liberation [only] after [the completion of] *pūrta* works.
And in the *Vāyupurāṇa* and other texts:
"How can there be liberation for one who has not worshipped the Lord, just as there is none for one who is bound?"
Thus, it is stated in the *Mahābhārata* and other *itihāsas*, such as the *Kuṇḍadhāra-upākhyāna*, and in the *Gītā*:
"He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds—
he, undeluded among mortals, is liberated from all sins."

Since liberation is attained even through the worship of Īśvara according to the Pātañjala [Yoga-sūtras], one must not maintain that such a being does not exist, as that would contradict all the scriptures.
Now, one might object: "In the Yoga treatises, it is taught that the attainment of *samādhi* results from devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*), not liberation. To this he says:
"The attenuation of the entire mass of afflictions (*kleśa*) is *samādhi*; its fruit is [liberation]. (105)
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the afflictions (*kleśas*).
The attenuation of their aggregate is indeed tranquility (*upaśama*), because it is the cause of *samādhi*.
Since *samādhi-yoga* consists in the mastery of the mind, [the practice] of devotion to the Lord (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*) is that [cause].
There is no contradiction, for the characteristic fruit of meditative absorption (samādhi) is indeed the fruit of liberation; it is nothing other than that. || 105 ||

Now, it might be argued that if this were so, the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas would lack authority because they would be non-eternal due to having a corporeal nature consisting of parts; to this he says:
"In that regard, the deity exists in the form of a continuous stream, and there is its formal manifestation."
The non-eternality of sound and meaning is sublated by their corporeality. || 106 ||

Since it has been stated that the deity, who constitutes the meaning of the Veda, exists as the continuum of bodies— both those to be accepted and those to be rejected— just like a person entering another's body; and since the universal (jāti) is established therein, both in the word and in the object, therefore...

The claim that words and their referents are impermanent because they possess a formal manifestation (*mūrtimat*)—an argument advanced here to prove invalidity—is refuted, since it is established that only the eternal universal (*jāti*) is the object of valid cognition in this context.
As the Mīmāṃsakas say: "The universal alone is the constituent element [of meaning]. (106)
To provide a summary, he says: "And if it were conceived in this way, what fault would there be, by which [the dependent] is so designated?"
Even by those who are learned, there is atheism when they speak of the non-existence of deities.

Thus, since the authority of the Veda is established even when the deity is the primary referent, the Teacher [Śabara] maintains that the Mīmāṃsakas have merely adopted the position of the nihilists by pointlessly asserting the non-existence of the deity.
Generally, due to ignorance, the Mīmāṃsā has been turned into a Lokāyata system in the world;
this effort has been made by me to place it on the path of those who believe in the existence of the hereafter.
This also demonstrates that very point. || 107 ||

If this is so, then because the Veda is authoritative by virtue of being composed by God, and God is established through the Veda, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). As they say: "In this way, even the Veda, being preceded by Him, would not be authoritative regarding His existence and other matters, as it would be subject to doubt. This [is the objection].
He objects:
"Even if [the Veda] were spoken by God, its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) cannot be established on the grounds of being created by Him;
for that would involve mutual dependence (anyonyāśrayatā). Therefore, this fault does not apply to those who do not maintain that [the Veda] is eternal. (108)

For we do not accept that the Veda is authoritative *because* it was created by God, since [the reason] would be inconclusive due to [the existence of things like] bodies and sense organs; rather, [we hold that] it is authoritative and happens to have been created by God.
Thus, even if the scripture were created by God, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). || 108 ||
How, then, is its authority established? He says:

"The authority of the scripture is established by reasoning as previously stated, precisely because it generates valid cognition through its distinctness from the body, the senses, the world, and so forth."

It has been stated that its validity is derived from perception and other means, as in the passage beginning, "For from the sentence, first of all, there is cognition of the object in every case. And it has also been asserted by you yourselves:
"The validity of all means of knowledge is intrinsic (*svataḥ*)."
Both eternality and non-eternality are entirely irrelevant to the validity [of a means of knowledge].

Is it then the case that even being prompted by God (īśvara) is of no assistance here regarding the word? No; he says: "Because it was spoken by God, its lack of authority can never be established. (109)
Because it is a product [of human effort], there arises a suspicion of its lack of authority, similar to the speech of a man on the street;

this suspicion is dispelled solely by the fact that it was composed by Īśvara. For in the case of men on the street, contrary statements are observed due to their connection with desire, anger, and so forth, whereas in the case of Īśvara...

Since that [self-interest] is absent, and because [the Lord] acts for the sake of benefiting everyone—just as a father and others act for the sake of their son and so forth—it is not the case that He is like them; thus there is no fault. || 109 ||
Now, one might object: "Is there not no purpose here in proving that the Veda has God as its author? To this he says:
"Since [the Veda] is equal [to other scriptures] in its effect, [the proponent] proceeds, satisfied by that;
for he who, out of delusion, fails to understand the authority of the Veda through its eternity..."

One does not act by superimposing invalidity upon this [Veda] because it is a product; nor, even if one were to act, is one deterred by another. Rather, its status as a product is demonstrated for the sake of establishing the equality of all treatises, so that those who have been initiated may engage with it.
Thus, it is not without purpose.
Furthermore, due to the confusion regarding another application [of the verse], the opponent asks: "How can one who is not all-knowing know the Lord?"
As it has been said:
"An omniscient being is not apprehended by people such as us at present; therefore, he does not exist because of his non-apprehension, like the horns of a horse."
He says that this too is incorrect:
"Because it has been stated according to the means of valid cognition" (110).

Therefore, yoga must be practiced directly with devotion; thus, one whose eyes have been refined by means such as collyrium through the attainment of skills like mineralogy (khanyavāda) [should proceed]. 111.
Just as one perceives even subtle objects and other things beyond the senses, so too does the yogi, whose self is refined through yoga, perceive [all things]. 112.
By means of the supreme Māheśvara yoga—

which arises from the repeated practice of the sequence of realities established in the Āgamas— the yogin, possessing a preeminent knowledge manifested through that supreme yoga, perceives all supersensuous objects, such as Īśvara and the rest.

He perceives objects just as a person whose eyes have been refined by means such as *siddhāñjana* perceives treasures and the like— which are utterly concealed and beyond the range of ordinary persons; thus,
regarding the Lord established through yogic perception, our non-perception of Him is unproven (*asiddha*).
"It is not a proof of non-existence. [Objection:
But surely yoga itself is not established; how then can there be a vision of God through it? [Response: There is no such lack of establishment here. Thus he says:
And it is observed here that through intuitive insight (*prātibha*), there is an engagement with the meaning of a sentence even in the absence [of prior knowledge]. (113)
In all three times, there is no cognition without signs;
likewise for intuitive knowledge, and for the yogi, it is entirely through excellence.
The impulsion toward yoga is for the sake of accomplishing that [knowledge] which simultaneously measures everything;

just as [one knows] "your brother will come tomorrow," through intuition alone— without recourse to scripture or inference— the intuitive person possesses a knowledge that is non-contradictory regarding the three times.
Just as cognition directed toward objects such as Īśvara will likewise arise for a yogin through yoga itself—
since this is established by the inference of possibility— the rejection of yoga is first of all improper; furthermore,
it is established by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), for in the Vedāntas...
Making the self the lower fire-drill and the syllable Om the upper fire-drill,
one shall behold [the Self] like a hidden treasure through the practice of churning with meditation.

Since such injunctions regarding yoga exist in the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, the knowledge of the yogis is certainly not to be rejected. Nor is there any lack of authority in those injunctive statements; thus he says:
For how could that which is free from deviation (vyabhicāra) not be a valid means of knowledge (apramāṇa)? || 115 ||
"How could one who performs an action impelled by that [injunction] not obtain its fruit?"—

this has been stated because worldly sentences are seen to be non-authoritative due to the observation of deviation, as in the case of "A herd of hundreds of elephants stands on the tip of a finger. However, there is no such deviation in the case of an injunctive sentence (*codanāvākya*).
The very fact that "something exists for someone" is the proof itself;

for the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) establishes its own denotation as a specific state of yoga— the soul characterized by liberation— which is the agent of the act of cognizing established entities such as God.
Otherwise, even the Veda, being equal to that [in its nature], would be neither a means of valid knowledge nor a producer of experience. (116)

Because there would be no distinction [between them], it would follow as a consequence that even those portions of the Veda which set forth the ritual section— such as "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"— would lack authority, and that there would be an absence of agency regarding results such as heaven. || 116 ||
Here the opponent's intention is as follows: "If both of those are accepted here,
then in this portion there would be both validity (*prāmāṇya*) and agency regarding results such as heaven."
And both [of these] are accepted.
The Teacher says: "In the case of yoga as well, let this be accepted in the same way."

Since the same logic applies, the authority of the Vedānta and other texts that expound Yoga, as well as their status as producing the fruit of liberation, are established. Thus, because the practitioner of Yoga is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the activity directed toward the Lord based on his knowledge is established; therefore, our own non-perception [of such a practitioner] is unproven.
"Thus, the proof of its non-existence [is established].
He concludes:
"In this way, Hara is declared to be the object of all means of valid cognition. (117)
Thus, since Īśvara is established by means of inference, scripture, and the direct perception of yogis, your denial of his existence is nothing but ignorance on your part. || 117 ||
Now he establishes the nature of the Lord by removing misconceptions:
"And He, due to the purity of His own nature, is free from the *kārmamāyīya* [karmic and illusory bonds];
for since their effects—the *kārmamāyīya*—are beginningless through their continuous flow, He too [is beginningless]."

Precisely because he is the agent of that [creation], he is declared to be established from the beginningless past by virtue of his natural purity; for in the case of a liberated soul established from the beginning, natural purity would be impossible due to the prior existence of bondage.
And therefore, those who [worship] the Lord through the performance of specific rituals, like Indra (Śatakratu), and those who...

The followers of Patañjali [claim] that [cognition occurs] through the capacity of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth; the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas say it is due to the conjunction with the mind (*manas*). These [views] are rejected, because such a being—like the individual soul (*puruṣa*)—would be subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*), and thus could not possibly be the Lord (*īśvara*).
"Surely, like a liberated Śiva, his sovereignty also comes from another Lord," say those who maintain the doctrine of an eternally successive succession of Lords. He refutes them:
"If his stainlessness [arises] from another, then he is a liberated soul; and from that, he [is a liberated soul]. (118)
But that by which [the world] is made pure is indeed pure by nature;
for this would only be the case if there were a destruction of lordship (īśvaratā), yet we shall explain that such does not exist.
Consequently, because both the produced and the producer are lords (īśvara) in their proximity, the former—
Or rather, one must admit that the primordial state is inherently pure; how then can there be a doctrine of a Lord who is eternal by way of a continuous stream?
For this very reason—
Because of its stainlessness, it has no karma; for one who is stainless is not a doer of karma.
Because he is devoid of impurity (*mala*) and karma, the [principles] beginning with *kalā* belonging to *māyā* do not exist for him.

Due to the absence of the bond of *āṇava*, there is also an absence of *kārmika*; and because of the absence of those two, there is also an absence of *māyīya*. Thus, the Lord is established as being free from all bonds. Even in the absence of karma—

Because the body is maintained through the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), like the whirling of a potter’s wheel, some who possess impurity (*mala*) alone still have a bond consisting of *māyā*. Thus, both [impurities] are mentioned here. As it is stated in the commentary on the *Svāyambhuva*: "Grace (*anugraha*) is possible even for those joined with the two called *mala* and *māyā*."
And for this very reason:
"Because He is partless (niṣkala), how could attachment, aversion, and the like arise from the emergence of parts (kalā) and so forth? (120)

Since the bondage of *māyā* is absent, the non-existence of those [qualities] consisting of it— namely, attachment, aversion, and so forth— is established; thus, it is stated that the bestowal of pleasure, pain, and the like occurs according to the karma performed by the *puruṣa*, and not through attachment, aversion, and so forth.
"By which [agent], of what kind of karma," and so forth. || 120 ||
How, then, is it that in passages such as "He who knows the Sakala and Sadāśiva," Īśvara is said to be *sakala*? To this, he says:
For Maheśāna is described as "sakala" (with parts), being endowed with the portions of Śakti.
Indeed, he who possesses a body is called "sakala," and it has been stated that his very body consists of the Śaktis—thus it is said:
"Śiva is declared to be knowledge and action, pure and supreme in all matters."
Furthermore:
"And even in its entirety, it knows and acts toward everything solely by means of its power. (121)

Even for the entire self, power alone is the body, because it is through that [power] alone that it functions everywhere and because it is of assistance to it; this external [body] is called "body" only figuratively. || 121 ||
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"Therefore, Śakti is the aggregate of the kalās, and Maheśvara is the Sakala.
Therefore, Śakti alone, because she is employed for manifold effects, is the aggregate of the kalās—that is, the body.
Since he is described from the perspective of ultimate reality, Īśvara is said to be "sakala" (with parts).
But he alone, because he possesses the power of the mass of energies (śaktipiṇḍakalā), is known as the possessor of power (śaktimān) and the partless (niṣkala). || 122 ||
Precisely because his body is *śakti*, he has no body composed of external *kalās* and so forth; thus, he is "without parts" (*niṣkala*). As it is said in the *Mokṣakārikās*:
"He is not bound by the aggregate of *kalās* beginning with *kalā*, as is the case with the bound soul (*paśu*)."
"Even at any time, O Lord of Gods, singing [the name] from that [source] is indeed fruitless. Thus [it is said].
And thus, it is stated that there is no ultimate difference between the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala). As it is said in the *Tattvasaṅgraha*:
"In this context, the pair of principles has been taught for the sake of accomplishing awakening, meditation, and so forth."
The statement that "it is formless" and "it possesses that [form]" is a figurative expression regarding power and the possessor of power.
Thus [ends the verse]. 122.
Right here, he states another opinion: "According to some, the *sakala* possesses activity, whereas that which is devoid of it is fruitless.
When it performs actions such as remaining stationary and so forth, then it is *sakala*; but when its activity has been withdrawn..."
Some maintain that the distinction between the *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts) is due to a difference in state (*avasthābheda*) and not in reality.
Regarding this, it has been said: "The Lord, Sadāśiva, and Śānta are distinguished only by the difference in their functions."

If this is so, since the same possibility of being both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*) applies to the Person (*puruṣa*) as well, what then is the difference between him [and Śiva]? To this he says:
"And because of his purity, his power of knowledge and action are connected to all objects" (123).

Because the impurity that veils perception and action is also absent, his knowledge and action are simultaneously connected to all objects; whereas, because the person (puruṣa) is veiled by impurity, they occur sequentially—this is the distinction. || 123 ||
Moreover:
He is understood to be omniscient not only because of his purity, as previously shown, but also because of his being the creator of all.
The Lord is established as omniscient.
To this he says:
"Just as a potter knows everything along with its effective result. (124)

The creator of all knows everything along with its causal factors; just as a potter or similar agent, being omniscient regarding his own task, thinks, "I shall fashion a jar from clay and other materials in order to purify the price previously received. Thus, the agent is observed to be all-knowing in relation to his own work.
In the same way, the Blessed One also, because he is the creator of all, is established as being cognizant of everything in his own activity; thus, he is proclaimed "omniscient."
If it is argued that because agency is observed to occur sequentially, consciousness is also established as sequential, and therefore he lacks omniscience simultaneously, [the author] says:
"In the case of objects to be released, produced, withdrawn, ceased, or impelled... (125)
In these [entities] existing at a single time, simultaneous agency is maintained;

for while action (*kriyā*) is indeed sequential, agency (*kārakatva*) is not, since even in the case of a potter and others, agency is established in respect to multiple actions such as eating and going simultaneously. This applies to these [entities], such as the liberated ones (*mukta*).

Since the Lord's agency regarding the objects of existence occurs simultaneously when those objects serve as the causal conditions for his actions, his knowledge is likewise established as being simultaneous; thus, there is no contradiction.
For this very reason, he states that his stainless knowledge of the three periods of time is established:
And that [knowledge] pertains to the three times; by means of it, Śaṅkara knows thus.
"By this [agent] this action was performed, and such a fruit must be given to him";
for in all activities, it indeed concerns the three periods of time.
O Śambhu, the state of having accomplished all that was to be done cannot arise from anything other than this realization;
this is what has been stated in the passage beginning with "just as a potter knows [his own work]," and so forth.
Therefore—
And that authority known as Śaiva is distinct from both the bound soul (paśu) and the human.
The function [of the means of knowledge] is mediated through the door [of the object], whereas its fruit is the direct apprehension of that [object].
Therefore, by this [means of knowledge], every object is cognized exactly as it exists;
thus, that means of knowledge is distinct from the cognition of animals and humans. As for the purpose of that divine knowledge:
The accomplishment of the fivefold activities of the world through the mediation of the Vidyēśvaras and others, as well as the direct bestowal of grace upon Vidyās, Vidyēśvaras, and so forth—
this is the nature of the means of knowledge for the bound soul (paśu), which he describes as being distinct from that [of ordinary perception].
Furthermore, knowledge derived from the words of the *sad-akṣa-liṅga* is clearly of a personal nature (*paudgala*). || 129 ||
Perception, inference, and verbal testimony have been declared in sequence;
due to the distinction between the three means consisting of the senses and so forth, they are of three kinds— namely perception, inference, and scripture— and their objects are limited.
Now, as to why that very [knowledge] depends on means (upāya) yet is not supreme (pārameśa), he says:
"Śaiva knowledge does not depend on manifestors, because of the removal of obscurations. (130)
The Gurus have declared that [the cognition] of those who consider themselves bound souls (paśus) is contrary to the Dharma;

therefore, because it is not enveloped by the fetters of the garland and so forth, the supreme Lord’s [cognition] does not proceed toward objects in dependence upon the senses and other means— thus it is said to be distinct from the means of knowledge belonging to the bound soul.
For this very reason:
"It does not consist of doubt or error, because it is independent of those. (131)

Since this knowledge is seen in a bound soul (paśu) due to the defects of its manifesting causes, it is like the knowledge of a bound soul; because it does not depend on means such as the senses, it is not subject to falsity, ignorance, or doubt arising from the defects of contact— thus it is distinct from that [ordinary knowledge].
Nor does it have the nature of memory because it apprehends what has already been apprehended; thus he says: "And because it is always arisen, that too cannot be of the nature of memory. (132)

Since the cognition whose nature is that of the grasper has already been established as eternal and unitary in the very first section, it is only of this determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya-jñāna*) that distinctions such as memory and so forth are possible;
for this reason as well, [the object] is distinct from that [cognition]. || 132 ||
He asks, "What follows from this? and replies:
"In this way, that which is devoid of the form of [ordinary] cognition is indeed valid cognition itself.
And therefore, because it consists in the direct perception of the object while being free from doubt and the like,"
Like sensory perception, that divine perception (*īśvarapratyakṣa*) is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Here, the opponent objects:
"But surely, for one who is bodiless, consciousness and agency are not logically possible. (133)
Since for Śaṅkara, consciousness is observed to exist only when there is a body and so forth in persons,
the inseparable connection of consciousness with the body and its dependence upon the body are established in cases such as our own;
thus, by implication, since a contradiction with the absence of a body is established, there is the state of being an all-knowing one who is bodiless (*adehasarvajñatvam*).
There is no tautology here, as it is refuted by means of a different argument; as Maṇḍana stated in the *Vidhiviveka*:
"The mind is dependent on external [objects]."
Thus [it is said].
This he refutes:
"No means of valid cognition has been stated for the negation of the body and so forth that is consistent with reason. (134)
Furthermore, since the omniscience and other attributes of Maheśvara are clearly established [by us],

this [objection] is not tenable; for in the *Madhyamakāṇḍa*, his possession of a body and so forth was refuted through such statements as "the Lord is equal to a potter," while here [in this work] his omniscience has been demonstrated.

Since there is no contradiction between bodilessness and omniscience, their coexistence is not impossible; therefore, this "perception of the contradictory" does not establish the absence of omniscience.
[The opponent objects: But surely dependence is established by the example of the external mind; to this he says:
And because it is obstructed, that [consciousness] of men requires the body and so forth for its manifestation. (135)

If, in this context, "mind" (*manas*) is intended to mean the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then the reason is unestablished due to a difference in locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*). Since that [internal organ] is dependent, what inconsistency is there in [the Lord's] omniscience? For it has been stated that omniscience does not arise there through conjunction with the mind, as it does in the case of an ordinary person. And as for those yogins who possess intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-yogin*):

Furthermore, according to the previous reasoning, since the mind's engagement with external objects is established as independent and not contingent upon the sense organs, the reason [you have provided] is inconclusive (anaikāntika). If, on the other hand, you intend for the mind to be of the very nature of the apprehending subject, then its dependence on the sense organs and so forth would be unobserved in your own system regarding the Supreme Self (paramātman) and other such entities.
Since [agency] is established as being obstructed by ignorance, and since that [ignorance] is absent in the Lord (Īśvara), his [agency] is also non-existent; thus there is no fault.
In this way, he states that He alone is the creator of all: "In the Great Lord (Maheśa), there is a greater power of action even than that of the Mantras and Mantreśvaras. (139)

Although the Mantras and Mantreśas possess omniscience, because they lack the capacity for agency regarding the pure path (śuddhādhvan) due to their connection with the agency of all things within the sphere of Māyā, they do not possess universal agency like Īśvara; thus, [the Lord] is indeed superior even to them. || 139 ||
Furthermore:
He is even more distinguished than those who are liberated, because of the natural purity of his own nature,
just as [he is distinguished] from liberated Śivas by virtue of his omniscience.
Even though he possesses the capacity for universal agency equal to that of Īśvara, he does not possess equality with Him because he lacks beginningless omniscience and universal agency.
Not only is He beginningless,
but He is also all-pervasive, because His attribute is characterized by vision and action.
If the locus of qualities (*guṇasannidhi*) belonging to one who possesses qualities (*guṇin*) were not present wherever all objects go,
then because we observe the persistence and other states of the effects of those powers (*śakti*) everywhere,
that [locus] must also be all-pervasive, just like the powers themselves; for a power cannot exist without that which possesses the power.
For:
Furthermore:
Nor can any eternal time be conceived that exists apart from that [moment]. (141)

Indeed, not even a fraction of a moment can be conceived as being devoid of a Lord, because the existence of His effects, such as the stability [of the world], would otherwise be untenable, leading to the consequence of the total incoherence of saṃsāra; thus, the existence of an imperishable Lord is established. || 141 ||
He refutes those who maintain that God is eternal by way of a continuous stream (pravāha-nitya), on the grounds that another [God] would simply come into being at that time:

"And because He possesses the qualities of vision and action, and because of the absence of a cause, He is eternal"—the word "eternal" carries over from the previous context. That which is endowed with the qualities of vision and action is eternal, just like the Self (ātman).

If the Lord is endowed with the qualities of vision and action, He is therefore imperishable. Furthermore, that which is without cause is eternal, such as the self (ātman) and so forth; since the Lord is declared to be without cause, He is likewise imperishable.
Thus, this is not a doctrine of a Lord who is eternal only by way of a continuous stream (pravāha-nitya).
As for what they also say: "Tell me, what is the purpose of him who creates the world?
For not even a fool acts without aiming at a purpose."

"In the same way, if there were activity [of the self], what would it have to do with consciousness? To this, he replies: "Because of the absence of impurities and so forth, its activity does not lead to its own self-realization. (142)
Nor is it joined for the sake of its own enjoyment, because of its connection with omniscience and other qualities.

Since he has attained all that is to be attained through his stainlessness, the activity of that [Buddha] is neither for the sake of liberation—as in the case of an ordinary person—nor for the sake of enjoyment, because of his omniscience. This is not tenable.
For it has already been stated that enjoyment is impossible in one who is omniscient, because it is invariably connected with ignorance.
Nor is it for the sake of play; as he says: "Playful activity is not tenable, because there is no exclusion from that [which has already been stated]. (143)
It exists by means of its negation, because of the negation of that [agency] belonging to it;

even for the sake of play and so forth, activity is not appropriate for him, because the causes of such activity— namely impurity (*mala*) and the rest— have been stated to be absent due to their exclusion, for play and the like are observed among persons to have impurity and the like as their cause.
Since impurity and the like are negated therein, that [agency] is also negated. As it has been stated by you as well:
"But if activity were for the sake of play, then the state of having accomplished one's purpose would be frustrated."
For this reason as well, his activity is neither for his own sake nor for the sake of play and so forth; thus he says:
"Moreover, when the Lord is active, the enjoyment and liberation of the person are seen. (144)
From his activity, it is understood that [the Lord] acts for the sake of the fruit of human beings due to his very nature;
and because liberation is impossible without the operation of the Lord according to the sequence previously stated,
his activity is perceived as being solely for the sake of others, precisely because his nature is to assist others, and not from any other cause.

In order to establish that liberation has God as its agent, he states its essential nature: "Liberation is equality with the Supreme Lord; it is the supreme state of being a Mantra and a Mantreśa. (145)
It has been stated that the innate nature (*svabhāva*) of the person (*puruṣa*) consists in being the agent of omniscience;

therefore, the attainment of that essential nature is supreme liberation (*parā mukti*), which is equality with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). The non-supreme liberation (*aparā*), however, is equality with the Mantras and Mantreśas, as will be described hereafter. || 145 ||

If it is created by Īśvara and not by the person (puruṣa) as is held by those who advocate for knowledge and liberation, he says: "The atom does not perform this [action] itself, because its power is obstructed by bonds."

Now, one might argue that just as the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices results in the enjoyment of heaven and so forth, so too the person (puruṣa) himself will bring about liberation through the performance of such injunctions as "the Self is to be known. Since there is no established contradiction between the state of having one's strength bound by fetters and being the agent of liberation, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika). But what, then, [is the case here]?
The "bond" (pāśa) is what you accept [as the cause of bondage]. But is it indeed ignorance? If so, is that a real entity (vastu) or a non-entity (avastu)?

If it is a non-entity, then—since it is eternally ceased like the horn of a hare—this injunction for the practice of knowledge intended to remove it would be entirely useless. If, on the other hand, it is a real entity, is it the very nature of the person (puruṣasvabhāva)?

Therefore, because it is non-removable—just like its eternality and pervasiveness—there would be no liberation.
