However, if there is a distinction [from the self], then that other substance must be accepted as being denoted by the word "ignorance" (ajñāna), because it has the nature of an obscuration of the eye like a cataract (paṭala) and so forth, and because it is the cause of ignorance. This is because [it is] a substance.
Since it is established that [the soul] possesses a nature to be removed by knowledge— just as a window, darkness, or a film of cataracts is removed by knowledge—
and since there is a proven contradiction between having one's power obstructed by fetters and being the agent of liberation,
there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) in this case.
In that case, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the bonds release the person of their own accord because their purpose has been fulfilled, as they say:
"Just as a dancer ceases from her dance after having exhibited herself to the audience."
"Having thus revealed herself to the Puruṣa, Prakṛti desists.
Regarding this, he says: "Even the bonds do not act [independently], because they are the restrictors of that [Puruṣa]. (146)
Furthermore, it is not observed that the bond releases that which is bound;
for even when the eye-veiling film (*paṭala*) and so forth have reached ultimate maturity and their purpose has been fulfilled, they do not become devoid of thought (*niścitta*),
nor is it established that they possess an inherent nature of cessation as an obscuring agent such that this [bond] would persist even in liberation.
When it is being conceptualized, it is logically tenable.
Therefore, for this reason: Hara is more powerful than the bonds of the individual soul (paśu), because he is their liberator. || 147 ||
He alone is the liberator from all those bonds of existence;
just as when cataracts and the like are removed from the eyes and so forth, the Lord alone is the cause for the removal of the fetters,
and no other.
[Objection: Is it not established that in illusions such as [the perception of] silver in mother-of-pearl, human beings possess the capacity to remove ignorance?
Therefore, liberation too will occur in the same manner. To this, he says:
"For humans whose powers are dependent [on other factors], [the Lord] is one whose power is always unobstructed. (148)
Just as the sun manifests its power for those who have eyes, it is logical [that knowledge acts] here;

for, as stated in the first section (kāṇḍa), ignorance too is of two kinds, and that which consists of determination is indeed characterized by a lack of discrimination regarding the similarity to the object.

In cases such as mother-of-pearl appearing as silver, a cognition consisting of error arises; therefore, its cessation through correct knowledge, which serves as its antidote, is entirely logical. However, that which consists of non-determination arises from other substances, such as darkness and the like.

Its nature as an exclusion from its own cause’s opposite—such as the sun—is established as being due to a distinct substance, not from the cognition of a counter-positive. Furthermore, it was previously demonstrated here that human ignorance, which is non-determinative in nature, exists during states such as deep sleep; whereas [knowledge] is of the nature of determination.

Because it is Buddhist [in nature], therefore that [non-existence] too is inferred to have as its very nature the exclusion from a real entity other than God—namely, from His opposite cause; thus, He alone is established as the cause of liberation, and not the self (*ātman*), since the capacity for such knowledge is not established in relation to it. Therefore, there is no fault.
To the question, "How then are the scriptural passages such as 'the Self is to be known' to be understood? he says:
"Such a reality must be accepted; otherwise, liberation is not possible. (149)
It has already been stated that these [scriptures] must also be accepted as culminating solely in the necessity of attaining the Lord, for otherwise liberation would be impossible.
Indeed, those who maintain that there is no liberation argue that it would be better not to have liberation at all than to have a Lord (Īśvara). As they say:
"Because existence for persons is beginningless, it never ceases;
therefore, the attainment of pleasure and pain and their cessation are recorded in the scriptures."
Regarding this, it is said:
"It must certainly be that men who possess the nature of the cessation of all obscurations are destined for the attainment of everything,
according to the increase or decrease of those obscurations."

Because its own nature is perceived as being either inferior or superior during states such as delusion and so forth—just like the sun obscured by clouds—it is not logical to maintain that there is no liberation;
thus, the non-existence of the Lord (Īśvara) is not established. Nor is existence beginningless, because it has karma as its cause. As it has been said:
"And from karma arise bodies, objects, and organs."
And he states that this position is not contradicted by scripture: "Liberation for persons [comes] from the Lord, and not otherwise; this has been established. (150)
And so it is said in the Śrī Pauṣkara:
"A person never attains liberation through his own power alone.
Also in the venerable Dīkṣottara:
Liberation for souls occurs through Śiva alone;
and since initiation consists of the activity of the Lord, this has also been established in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"Initiation alone liberates; it leads one upward to the abode of Śiva. || 150 ||
Now, even if this were so, one might suspect that passion and hatred exist in the Lord because some are seen not to be liberated; to this he says:
"Neither passion nor hatred belongs to him," and this is established through reasoning.
It has already been established in the Middle Section itself that the Lord is devoid of attachment, aversion, and so forth;
therefore, this too is not a fault.
Nor can it be argued that this liberation is not resorted to by anyone because it does not constitute a human goal, as is the case with the liberation of the Vaiśeṣikas and others; thus he says:
"And the desire for the supreme state always exists in everyone, even in the most wretched. (151)
Therefore, that which is being sung is never not accepted;
for when all bonds have ceased and universal sovereignty has been attained, it is impossible for anyone to be devoid of desire.
If this is so, since the Lord is independent, why is there not the simultaneous liberation of all? To this he says:
"The capacity for favoring the individual souls exists in Śaṅkara in every way. (152)
Nevertheless, the simultaneous liberation of atoms is not observed by him.
Why? He says:
"In the act of creation, Maheśāna awaits the proper time for the womb. (153)
In the same way, He awaits the time for the removal of impurity;
for it was stated previously that, because He depends upon the ripening of karma as the cause for creation from Māyā, the Lord does not bestow all enjoyments simultaneously. Thus...
Because liberation depends upon the ripening of impurities, there is no consequence of everyone attaining liberation simultaneously, since the very absence of such dependence is unestablished.
In this regard, he states the opinion of others: "Others also hold that this [self] is independent, according to how and when it pleases them. (154)
For that Supreme Lord, the men [are devoted], and their liberation occurs then in that manner;

for the Supreme Lord is indeed independent because He does not depend on others due to His omnipotence. But if there were dependence on another, that which depends would be incapable; thus, the Lord would be rendered incapable.
It may be so. Therefore, whatever [object] pleases someone according to its relationship with the higher or lower [levels], he joins it to him in that very way;
he does not depend on the ripening of impurities or other such factors.
He refutes this [objection]:
"Because [we hold] that there would be the consequence of a new existence due to independence; therefore, it is not so. (155)
This is not so, because if this [agency] were independent even in the case of worldly existence— as it is held to be in the case of liberation—

then it would cause even a liberated person to undergo worldly existence again; furthermore, it would lead to the absurdity of the wicked going to heaven and the virtuous to hell, thereby rendering the scriptures on liberation and the performance of good deeds purposeless.
Only the Lokāyata system is to be venerated by you. || 155 ||

Now, if it is argued that this undesirable consequence does not apply there because it depends upon the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*), then— since the nature of Śaṅkara is not established as being such [i.e., dependent on karma]—
it follows that he is not established as having an independent nature (*anapekṣasvabhāva*) even with respect to experience (*bhoga*).

Just as one expects the ripening of karma in liberation, so too will one expect the ripening of impurities; what contradiction is there in this? Furthermore, independence does not consist merely in not depending on karma and the like, but rather in not being dependent upon another Lord.
And that [dependence] does not exist for him precisely because he is the Supreme Lord, as has been stated in the *Madhyamakakāṇḍa*.
Furthermore, he states that this position contradicts scripture:
"And it has been said by him: 'One who is equal to that [state] does not attain another existence. (156)
Nor can it be said that such a statement is false;
for it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva* and other scriptures:
"Because it is devoid of beginningless impurity, one does not attain another state of existence."

Thus, what has been stated—that [the doctrine] is untenable under the view of an independent descent of power (*svatantra-śaktipāta*) because the possibility of rebirth (*punarbhava*) necessarily follows therefrom—has already been addressed; for it was previously stated that the word of the Supreme Lord is not unauthoritative. Therefore, since the possibility of rebirth is established, [the objection stands].

Furthermore, since the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is independent yet depends precisely upon the ripening of impurity (*malaparipāka*), there is no consequence of the simultaneous liberation of all beings. And just as this consequence does not follow even from the transformation of impurity, so it has been stated by the Teacher in the *Tattvatrayanirṇaya*; that alone should be kept in mind.
In order to establish the independence of the descent of power (śaktipāta) through another form, he invokes the meaning of the scripture:
"Mantras, together with their presiding deities, were created by the Lord for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human beings. (157)
Even one among them is capable of performing that; what need is there for many?

There are seven crores of mantras, and eight lords of mantras (mantreśas), beginning with Ananteśa, who were created by the Lord for the attainment of human goals; such is the meaning of the Āgama, [established] by a single [authority].
Because that [proof] is established, it is incorrect.
This [view] he refutes: "Even their arising would be a favor, and there would be a concern for favoring them. (158)
The appointment to a task as taught by Śiva is for the sake of accomplishing that task, not for the sake of [the soul's] birth.

For at that time, because many possess equal fitness, there is simultaneous grace toward them in the form of being recipients of grace as mantras and mantreśvaras; it is not, however, [for the sake of their birth].

"Arising occurs precisely for the sake of qualification"—thus, there is no fault regarding arising. [Objection: But qualification will still take place. [Response: No; for this very reason, there is no fault here, since the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is established as being independent.
Here, the opponent says:
Indeed, having been born through the grace of Śiva, they are all equal in power. || 159 ||
Therefore, the relationship of the impelled and the impeller is not appropriate for them;
for, through the grace of the Supreme Lord, the Mantras and Mantreśvaras possess equality with Śiva, just like liberated souls (muktātman).
"Impelled by the ordinance of Śiva’s will, they exercise authority.
To remove the contradiction with such scriptural passages [as these], he says: "The arising of all-knowledge is equal, but sovereignty is distinguished. (160)
For that [nature] of theirs is not manifested in the same way as it is in Maheśvara; therefore,
because the scriptural statement regarding their being impelled by the ordinance of Śiva’s will would otherwise be untenable,

it is understood that their equality with Śiva— even in terms of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*)— is not manifested in the same manner as it is for liberated Śivas (*mukta-śiva*), but rather [only partially].
Since the scripture states that they are "endowed with all knowledge," there is no contradiction in [the Lord's omniscience] being due solely to the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
Moreover:
for their qualification consists in purification, and that very [purification] is enjoined for them. (161)

For they, having fulfilled their office, attain equality with Śiva; for this consecration consisting of office was ordained by the Supreme Lord as being limited in duration. As it is heard in scripture:
When those great universal monarchs have passed away into infinity,
their status as the creator of all things is established as the supreme cause and the ultimate state.
Thus, even for that reason, there is no equality with Śiva.
Regarding this, he states another opinion: "Others have declared that even when [the two means] are equal, the accomplishment of the object occurs [through one and] not through the other. (162)
Some maintain that,

although the Mantras and Mantreśvaras are equal to Śiva, they will exercise authority under him just as disciples do under their guru; however, they should consider the similarity here only in terms of the illustrative example.
For even though disciples are equal to their guru, they are subject to the possibility of transgression due to their failure to carry out his commands;
it is not, however, because they possess equality with Śiva.
Previously, the Lord's status as an agent was established on the basis of his assuming a body;
now, by refuting that [position], he says:
"The Lord of Gods performs his duties by mere will, not through exertion. (163)
And His will encounters no obstruction in its operations.

The inclusion of the word "only" (mātra) is for the purpose of restriction; that is, the Lord’s agency consists solely in His unimpeded will, and not through exertion such as the creation of a body or instruments.
Their non-existence [is established] because they are of no use.

Now, one might object: "Whosoever is an agent is not independent of exertion such as that of a body, nor is his will unimpeded, as is the case with Devadatta and others; and since God is an agent, He must likewise be of such a nature. To this, he replies:
"Because men perform exertions, their will is subject to obstruction. (164)
And that [dependence] is prohibited for the Lord by the path of logic because of His being the Supreme Being (paśutva).

Even though omniscience and omnipotence exist, it has been stated that for individual souls (puṃsām), due to being veiled by impurity (mala), there is a dependence on the body and so forth for action, as well as a lack of lordship (anīśvaratva); however, for the Lord (īśvara), that [impurity] does not exist.
There is also the non-existence of those two.
Now, one might object that the agency of persons is not seen to arise from mere will alone; to this he says:
"The successful accomplishment of rites such as *stobha* is seen to occur through mere will. (165)
Indeed, for men whose minds are pierced by the nature of superior mantras and the like,
and who have mastered those mantras, effects such as the paralysis of poison and so forth are seen to occur even through mere will.
He demonstrates this very point: "For that [bond] binds the bound animal by means of its extraordinary power. (166)
The Lord acts solely by His will; what wonder is there that He might not act?

That which was previously described as bondage—such as the binding by poisons and the like, or the paralysis of powers and so forth—is present in him who is a bound soul (paśu); he is the very person previously mentioned, endowed with cause and effect.
It is marvelous that one performs such acts as paralyzing [an opponent] by mere will through the extraordinary power of a mantra, whereas Īśvara does not possess such extraordinary power.
As for what some have said:
"It is not logical that [the world] should arise through the will of Īśvara without a cause;
or else, whatever is its cause must be the [cause] of the elements."
Regarding that, it is said:
"Some declare that [volition] is touched by the collection of causal factors. (167)
The object to be liberated, such as the soul, is the *nimitta* (efficient cause), while the knowledge thereof is the *karaṇa* (instrumental cause).

Indeed, it is the very capacity of the object to be liberated, produced, and so forth, that serves as the cause for the arising of the will; this is established in the same way for people like us. However, the instrumental cause is that which has that [object] as its domain.
Since it is likewise possible for God as well that His knowledge is [produced] by a creator, this argument amounts to nothing.
He states that even its division into one and many is not without a cause:
"In the case of objects that are produced at the same time and possess a single form... (168).
The single will is likewise manifold among those differentiated by time and form;

its differentiation and non-differentiation arise from the distinctions and non-distinctions in the forms of its objects, such as maintenance and preservation, and even within maintenance and so forth,
from the distinctions and non-distinctions of time— thus, these two are not without cause.
And he says that this [power] is not other than the power of action:
"That differentiation of the power of action, beginning with the left [channel], is also understood. (169)
Since the Lord performs all actions by means of desire alone—
because, as stated in the *Madhyamakakāṇḍa*, desire is established as the indispensable causal factor even for ourselves in all undertakings— it is that very [desire] which [acts].

It should be understood that the power of action (kriyāśakti) is presented in the scripture as being divided into the categories of Vāmā and so forth; it is nothing other than that, for no such [separate] power is established.

And because it is non-different from the nature of the partless Self, that power of knowledge—which is of the nature of the Self—is also non-distinct [from it]; this he demonstrates by means of an illustration:
"Just as the rays of the sun are embraced by the lotus by the teachers. (170)
It is described in two ways: as that which effects illumination and as that which effects expansion;
likewise, the single Śakti appears as if it were manifold among objects due to their mutual conjunction. (171)
It is said to be twofold because it performs both manifestation (*vijñapti*) and its activity (*tatkriyā*).

For just as the ray of the sun, when it touches lotuses, is said to be twofold because it effects both awakening and illumination, so too the power of the Blessed One effects both illumination and expansion in relation to objects.
"Performing [its function] in two ways"— it is designated as distinct due to the difference in its effects, but in the ultimate sense, there would be no distinction in it.
In that very same way—
Though it is one, it appears as diverse due to the distinctions between the object of knowledge, the object of empowerment, and the object to be accomplished. || 172 ||
Śakti is not primarily divided by various distinctions such as Vāmā and the rest;

rather, as stated in the *Puruṣaparīkṣā*, the distinction of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) arises solely from the distinction of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), and the distinction of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) arises from the distinction of effects (*kārya*). Consequently, even the division into Vāmā and so forth belongs to that [power of action].

It is not primary [in this sense], being conditioned by the distinction of effects. For this reason, it is proclaimed that the Lord, through His will alone, is the performer of actions without exertion. || 173 ||

For that reason, just like a potter and others, Īśvara is declared to be the agent in the world with respect to the movement of his own body and so forth, without depending on the exertion of another body; it is not otherwise. || 173 ||
Regarding this, the opponent says: "He acts from mere desire. But surely, no desire exists for him.
It would be appropriate to say this if desire were possible for him; however, that [desire] is a modification of the mind, and he [the Lord] is devoid of mind.
And because the mind is impossible due to the non-acceptance of [independent] causes and instruments, it does not occur.
He refutes this:
"The activity of power toward its functions is specified as having the aforementioned definition. (174)

The activity of the cause is said to be its will (*icchā*) for the sake of directing [the effect]; however, this will is not merely a modification of the mind (*manovṛtti*), but rather the engagement of the agent’s power of action (*kriyāśakti*) toward the effect. This is because it has been stated that will is established as being antecedent to all activities.
For even in the scriptures, it is stated that the Lord acts through the Vidyeśvaras for the sake of enjoining their activities; as it is said:
"Impelled by the injunction of Śiva’s will, they exercise their authority."

How then is it that desire is described by the Sāṃkhyas and others as a function of the mind? To this he says: "In some [systems], desire is considered to be a power (śakti) designated by such an activity. (175)

For just as the power of cognition itself is called "intellectual awareness" because it is reinforced by intellectual operations such as determination (*adhyavasāya*), and since awareness is not possible in reality due to the insentience (*jaḍatā*) of the intellect, so too the power of action itself, consisting of will, [is called volition] through the operation of the mind.

In certain systems such as Sāṃkhya, it is said that [the self] is a "mental modification" because it is manifested by a perfected being through the creation of something unprecedented during states such as daydreaming; however, in ultimate reality, its power to create something unprecedented is not tenable.
Because an emanation, by virtue of having the nature of Īśvara, is impossible in that which is insentient. || 175 ||
In this treatise,
it is proclaimed that [the will] performs its function without a distinct object; likewise,
the will of God performs its function without a distinct object characterized as the mind.
It is said that [the word] "but" (*tu*) signifies that it refers to the entire [power] in relation to a different object characterized as the mind.
He concludes: "The single power that pervades all objects is never divided from the will. (176)
And thus it is established that power, consisting of knowledge and action, is indeed one alone; it is not the case that will is something other than that. || 176 ||
Now, one might object: "Since there is a difference in their effects, desire must therefore be a distinct power;

or rather, because those things desired possess the nature of manifestation, like the manifestations of pleasure and so forth, they consist of consciousness itself and thus have the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), not the nature of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Since this [power] exists as that which is capable and unspoken, there is no assumption of anything further.

Because the very means that was described for the sake of establishing the power of action (kriyā-śakti) exists also in the case of will (icchā), for that reason there is no will distinct from that, nor is it of the nature of knowledge (jñāna).

This is what is meant: by virtue of being the cause of actions such as the movement of one's own body, the power of action (kriyāśakti)—which is established as a means consisting of self-awareness—is indeed will (icchā) itself; and in reality, it is this [will] that thinks, "May this belong to me," with respect to a son or other objects manifested through the power of cognition (jñānaśakti).

Because its nature consists in the manifestation of things related to the Self, it is not of the form of cognition, but rather is indeed the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). This very point has been stated in the *Mantravārttika*:
"For that mind which belongs to the Power (*Śākta*), this [will] is indeed the power of action."
Thus,
it is established that the Lord of Gods performs his duties by mere will, not through exertion.
To the objection that "this is merely proving what is already established," he replies:
"Nor is there no disagreement, because this [notion] is unestablished for everyone. (177)
For this is not established for the Mīmāṃsakas, Buddhists, and Lokāyatikas; therefore, there is no proving of what is already proven. || 177 ||

"In that case, this position is indeed unestablished," [the opponent] says: "Nevertheless, the position should be accepted according to the tradition, even though this position has been reduced by you to the status of an object. That is to say, even if this position has been brought by you to the state of being an object, it should nevertheless be accepted with patience.

Having rendered [the opponent] unable to endure [the argument], one should accept the reason demonstrated by me here after conducting an exhaustive investigation, and not out of constraint. As it has been said:
"One should accept my words after investigation and not because of respect for me, if they are found to be untenable."

The Sāṃkhyas object: "Is this not a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*)? For they admit that yogis possess a mastery born of karma over the self consisting of *sattva*. As it has been said:
"By merit there is ascent; by demerit there is descent."
"The creation is vast with *sattva* at the top, vast with *tamas* at the root, and vast with *rajas* in the middle, extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. Thus [it is said].
Regarding this, it is also said:
Sovereignty, which is supreme mastery, does not arise from dharma because of the absence of karma. (178)
Because Śambhu has cast aside all excellence, He is the one who acts according to His own will;

whereas the limited sovereignty of yogis is of a different nature altogether, for it is born of karma and is held by them to be subject to both decay and excess. This [sovereignty of Śiva], however, is indeed different.
Because it is established as having all things as its object by virtue of being devoid of beginning and end, it is not born of action;
and because it is established as being produced by mere will, there is no proof of what is already proven (*siddhasādhanatā*).
[The opponent objects: "But surely there might be another who possesses even more exalted sovereignty than that? To this he says:
"By the power of his own sovereign majesty, there is none by whom he could be surpassed. (179)
He alone would be Maheśvara; if he were not the Lord (Īśvara), then that very one is accepted by us as the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), so there is no fault.
And he says that there will not be another beyond even that, lest there be an infinite regress:
"Sovereignty, like dimension, is accompanied by excellence everywhere. (180)
In some cases, that [limit] is cast aside by an excellence, as is the case with Maheśvara.

Whatever is endowed with excellence must exist somewhere at the ultimate limit of its progression; it cannot be characterized by infinite regress, just as the excellence of magnitude—starting from the atom—is found only in some particular thing.
It possesses a dimension that culminates in supreme magnitude;

furthermore, this particular excellence of sovereignty is endowed with a progressive intensification, such that it is possible for it to reach a state of ultimate perfection, and that very point where it exists in such a state is [the Lord].
The term "Supreme Lord" (parameśvara) does not entail an infinite regress.
To conclude the section, he states its purpose at the outset: "Having thus known Śambhu, the supreme of all and the bestower of all fruits... (181).
For one who always perceives [the truth], the highest good is immediate and everything [is attained] from nowhere else.

Thus, having first ascertained the existence or non-existence of the proving and subverting means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) presented here, according to the aforementioned method, [one distinguishes] from those [entities] such as *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* well-known in other systems of philosophy.

Having understood that among lords there is a supreme Lord who, for that very reason, bestows all fruits, one should meditate upon Him alone; from Him alone, through the process of initiation and without delay, the supreme good—liberation and spiritual perfection—arises. Thus, the accomplishment of the purpose is stated by us elsewhere: [The passage continues with verses: "By knowing the Lord, who is the cause of all causes, who is the master of all masters, and who is the giver of all fruits, one attains the supreme state. "Through the grace of Him who is the Lord of lords, the supreme liberation and all perfections are attained without effort. "By worshipping Him who is the source of all sources and the sovereign of all sovereigns, one quickly attains the highest goal. "From Him alone, through the sequence of initiation, the supreme good, which is both liberation and perfection, arises; thus the purpose is established. "By knowing the Lord, who is the cause of all causes, who is the master of all masters, and who is the giver of all fruits, one attains the supreme state. "Through the grace of Him who is the Lord of lords, the supreme liberation and all perfections are attained without effort. "By worshipping Him who is the source of all sources and the sovereign of all sovereigns, one quickly attains the highest goal. "From Him alone, through the sequence of initiation, the supreme good, which is both liberation and perfection, arises; thus the purpose is established. Thus it has been said by us elsewhere.
Bow down with effort to Lord Śiva, the eternal one, for the sake of everlasting bliss, having abandoned with diligence the stubborn attachment to the service of other objects;
for he has not existed in this world, nor does he exist now, nor will he ever come to be.
That man who is endowed with happiness through devotion to Him and aversion to others [is truly blessed].
Thus [it is said].
Now he concludes:
"Thus, indeed, all investigation is preceded by the investigation of the person. (182)
For the benefit of those of mild intellect, this [work] was composed by that most excellent teacher Sadyojyotis— who was equal to Śiva himself— so that it might be exceedingly clear.
Indeed, out of compassion alone, he whose nature is a mine of fierce light and virtues bestowed his grace.

And thus, it is established that by the method just stated, the examination of the person is necessarily subsumed within the examination of God; therefore, it is proven to be purposeful by virtue of that very purpose. || 183 ||
Merely by being seen, the illustrious Sadyojyotis destroys fierce darkness;
but through constant observation, he increases right vision like the moon.
Because it is exceedingly profound, no one in this world— even among those possessing the speed of vast intelligence— attains a full understanding when examining the nature of the Lord of Men;
yet, out of a desire for the welfare of others, Rāmakaṇṭha [has undertaken this].
He has clearly established this illumination that dispels the darkness of fallacious reasoning.
Thus ends the third section, titled "The Refutation of the Lord as Established in Other Systems," in the *Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa* composed by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, son of Śrī Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha. 3.
And this *Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa* is now complete.
